en: Preface to the Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā Hu Zi Jin-yun of Qiantang questioned Danzi of Huazang, saying: "What is meant by the Way? Danzi replied: "It is nature.
Hu Zi was skeptical and asked: "Can cultivation then be abandoned? Danzi said: "A jade stone within its raw casing cannot be revealed without being cut open."
It is not seen. Gold in the ore is not pure without smelting; the nature within the entanglements is not manifest without cultivation.
If one insists that it is "nature" and thus cultivation can be abandoned, then among those who are so numerous, who does not possess this nature?
Thereupon, the teachings of the Elder of Lingfeng’s commentary on the *Nanyue Dacheng Zhiguan* were transmitted to Master Hu, who was told: "Cultivate!"
The essentials of the Way are fully contained within the single work *Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Furthermore, the essentials of the *Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā* are fully contained within the single phrase "the wisdom that turns away from objective dust. Why is this so? The mind is the substance of all phenomena. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"In the three realms there are no separate dharmas; they are created solely by this one mind. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "The arising of all dharmas is manifested only by the mind.
All causes and effects, worlds, and even the finest motes of dust, take their substance through the mind.

Ordinary beings do not understand the meaning of "mind-only" and are thus bound by the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); for them, these are truly the six sense objects. Śrāvakas likewise do not understand mind-only.
If one does not understand the meaning of "mind-only" and is bound by the Four Noble Truths, then the Four Noble Truths are also but dust.
If a Pratyekabuddha does not understand the meaning of "mind-only" and is bound by the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, then the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are also but dust.
If a Bodhisattva does not understand the meaning of "mind-only" and is bound by the Six Perfections, then the Six Perfections are also but dust. Not only that—
Consider this. Formerly, a monk asked a past master, "When one brushes away the dust to see the Buddha, what then? The master replied, "The Buddha is itself the dust.
Viewed from this perspective, if one perceives even the slightest phenomenon as existing outside the mind—be it ordinary or sagely—it is all dust.
Yet, do you not realize that the mind is itself the dust, and the dust is itself the mind? As the *Yuanlun* (Treatise on Conditions) states:
Furthermore, there are no phenomena external to the mind that can serve as conditions for the mind; all arise from the mind itself and in turn function as its manifestations.
This is because all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, are nothing but this single mind. If one truly understands this with certainty and without doubt, [one will realize the truth].
Then, with the emotions of acceptance and rejection forgotten and the mind of restless seeking stilled, the dustless wisdom begins to turn.

In these times, those who admire the Way are as numerous as cow-hairs, while those who clarify the Way are as rare as a unicorn’s horn. Those who cling to their inherent nature and abandon cultivation strictly adhere to non-action (*wuwei*);

those who cling to cultivation and abandon nature fail to know the fundamental wondrousness. Furthermore, there are those who engage in groundless, idle chatter, whose eyes— (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

If you can truly circulate this book, it will cause people to know that "quiescent illumination" is the essence of the nature. [Stop.]
Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is the function of the nature (*dharmatā*). From stillness (*śamatha*), one gives rise to contemplation, yet through that very contemplation, one accords with stillness.

From illumination (*prabhāsvara*), one gives rise to contemplation, yet through that very contemplation, one accords with illumination. Thus, cultivation arises entirely from the nature, and cultivation is entirely the nature.
There is nothing more detailed than this regarding the path of perfect awakening and perfect cultivation. Nevertheless, by means of a few skillful means...
To swiftly attain Bodhi is simply to turn the dust-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

Therefore, the essentials of the path of cultivation are fully contained within the single work, *Mahāyāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and the essence of the *Mahāyāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā* is fully contained within the single phrase "turning the dust-free wisdom.

Preface to the Mahāyāna Śamatha-Vipaśyanā of Nanyue,
composed by Zhu Di, Grand Master of the Court for Ceremonial Rank (Chao Feng Da Fu), Acting Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue (Shangshu Du-zhi Yuan-wai Lang),
Commander (Hu Jun) with Purple Robes, concurrently Commissioner for Encouraging Agriculture and Supervisor of Judicial Investigations in the Two Zhejiang Circuits.

From the time of his parinirvāṇa at the Crane Forest (Hèlín), there have been many sages and worthies who appeared in the world. All of them, through the six perfections and myriad practices, attained mastery of great wisdom;
they dwelt securely within the *dharmadhātu* and rescued the masses from delusion. Their golden words and precious scrolls are fully recorded in the treasuries of all dharmas.
As for the fact that all phenomena are empty and all natures are realized—such that they do not manifest within the three realms...
When body and mind reach the true source of perfect enlightenment and manifest the reality-mark (*dharmatā*) of Vairocana, one beholds the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the Great Master of Nanyue.

This Master was a holy member of the assembly at the Buddha’s Vulture Peak; he manifested his transformative influence throughout the three periods of time upon Mount Heng, secretly receiving the Buddha’s instructions and personally hearing the sound of the Dharma.
He synthesized the essential points of the minds of Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna and fully possessed the spirit of Bodhi.

This is the definitive meaning of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, I have composed the two treatises on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the upper and lower volumes, to dispel the distinction between the real and the false within a single thought-moment and to clarify that the essence and its manifestations leave no trace.
When the empty fist is opened and the hand is extended, nothing can be seen; thus, the principle of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is revealed from this very point.
Through this, one enters the gateway of tranquil illumination, which serves as the fundamental source for transcending the world and acts as the seed of Buddhahood.
The Guide. Without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one directly transcends to the ranks of the sages. Alas!
Although this teaching is vast and reveals the path for those who come after, it was not universally seen in the human world. It flowed abroad overseas until the fifth century [of the Buddha’s era].
During the Xianping era, the Japanese monk Jikishō (Jichō) crossed the sea with this teaching and returned to our sacred court in the fourth year of the Tianxi era.
In the fourth month of summer, Zunshe, the Master of Tiantong at Mount Lingyin, was about to manifest the seeds of Buddhahood for future lives;
thus, all were established in the most supreme and auspicious conditions. He therefore commissioned this text to be carved and further requested a preface.

Reflecting deeply, I consider that the wish-fulfilling pearl has already returned to Hepu, and within the empty chamber where white light arises, one sits and beholds the Dharmakāya. Yet, I am mindful that my own efforts in drilling and gazing have not yet reached [the depths].

I have arrived. I refrain from offering words of praise, for there is nothing therein to be grasped. I only wish that all who see this with faith may practice it; that those who practice may realize it;
that they remain unmoved amidst all objects and untainted by any phenomena; that having once received it, they do not regress, and having once attained it, they attain it forever;
and that until the end of the future, they may always be born together with the Great Master of Nanyue to carry out the work of the Tathāgata.
Preface to the *Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā* by the Chan Master of Nanyue, composed by the śramaṇa Zunshe of Tiandi Monastery.

The application of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is rooted in clarity and stillness. Clarity and stillness are virtues rooted in the single nature (*ekadhātu*). The essence of this nature is fundamentally awakened (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*).

What is called "clarity" (prajñā) refers to the essence of awakening being fundamentally quiescent; what is called "quiescence" (śamatha) refers to this very essence. That clarity and quiescence are non-dual is called the "essence" (tattva).

Since the essence is indivisible, clarity and quiescence find their secure resting place therein. Since the essence is all-encompassing, clarity and quiescence are present within it. To speak of the essence, it is not one yet ever one;
to speak of its attributes, they are non-dual yet ever dual. It is divided yet undivided; it is one yet not...
It is one and the same. That its essential nature (*tī*) and its qualities (*guṇa*) are unchanging is what we conventionally call the "nature" (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena.

That its essential nature and its qualities have no fixed abode is what we conventionally call the "root" (*mūla*) of all phenomena. Furthermore, what is meant by "all phenomena"? It refers to that which is produced by the total embodiment of luminous stillness.

How is this so? It is truly because the luminosity of primordial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) from time immemorial shines forth powerfully. When this shining arises, one becomes deluded by it and calls it "obscurity.
Because the fundamental state, which is beginningless and non-abiding, follows conditions, when these conditions arise, one becomes disordered by them and calls it "movement.

Once obscurity and movement have occurred, the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*) are born. Like flowers in the sky seen by one who rubs their eyes, how could they be anything other than [the mind] itself? Therefore, it is said: "The unchanging follows conditions."

That which is named "mind" (citta) undergoes change according to conditions; that which is named "nature" (prakṛti) remains unchanging amidst conditions. Mind is turbid and active; nature is luminous and still.
If one realizes that what has been luminous since beginningless time has become turbid, then one can understand that what is currently active can be made still.

Thus, the Sage perceives that this turbidity and activity can be immediately transcended and that luminosity and stillness can be restored. Therefore, he uses stillness to instruct [the disciple] in cessation.

It stops their movement. By means of clarity (*prajñā*), it teaches contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). It contemplates their obscurity so as to cause them to investigate how a single thought-moment is simultaneously movement and stillness, simultaneously obscurity and clarity.
Once obscurity and movement have ceased, the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*) naturally vanish, leaving only the essence of clarity and stillness.
This is called the Perfect and Sudden; this is called Non-action; this is the practice of the Tathāgata; this is cultivation perfected by illuminating the nature. Cultivation...
When [the practice] is accomplished, its application ceases. Who would discuss it? When the essence of *śamatha* (calm abiding) is manifest, its nature vanishes;

likewise, there is neither ignorance nor stillness. In this sudden clarity, where can anything be寄托 (entrusted)? It is nameless. To demonstrate the ultimate destination for beings: the accomplishment of *śamatha* is called liberation (*vimukti*);

the accomplishment of *vipaśyanā* (insight) is called *prajñā* (wisdom); the manifestation of the essence is called the *dharmakāya*. These three are one, and this one is the three, like the three dots of the character *ī*.
It is like the three eyes of a celestial being: neither vertical nor horizontal, neither one nor many.
This is the inconceivable Threefold Virtue; this is the Great Parinirvāṇa. Alas! This Dharma was concealed at the Śāla Grove and transmitted to Mahākāśyapa;
Kāśyapa transmitted it to Ānanda; from Ānanda downward, the lamps were passed from one to another until the eleventh, Aśvaghoṣa. Aśvaghoṣa...
It was transmitted to Nāgārjuna. Nāgārjuna expressed this Dharma through words in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.

Nanyue subsequently illuminated his mind and immediately returned to its original nature, attaining the purity of the six sense faculties and ranking as one adjacent to the sages. Thus, the efficacy of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* was verified. This, our Great Master—
Lamenting that it might not be heard by future generations, he produced these tens of thousands of words from his heart of great compassion.

the second fascicle demonstrates the practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā. With both exposition and practice complete, it is like having both eyes and feet, enabling me to dwell in peace.
While remaining unmoved in tranquility, his destiny led him to the Cool Lake (Sītavana). Alas, this literature! Through the vast passage of years and months, it was hidden away beyond the seas.

now returning once more to the East, it is like the ascending sun. Its pure radiance and perfect brilliance shall forever circulate within our land.

"Mahāyāna" is an alternative name for the nature of the mind. "Śamatha-vipaśyanā" is an alternative name for quiescence and illumination. As the world regards it...

To seek the Mahāyāna apart from the nature of the mind, or to discuss stillness and illumination separately from śamatha and vipaśyanā—how is this different from riding a cow while searching for the cow, or as the child of the south seeks fire?

The three methods—sudden, gradual, and indeterminate—are all perfected;

these were what Nanyue revealed as the essential points of the mind’s direct instruction, yet the world has remained unaware of them. Now, upon careful reading, one realizes they truly constitute the three perfect forms of śamatha.

Now, the transmission between Buddhas and patriarchs involves nothing more than using the mind to seal the mind. The essence of this mind is precisely the Mahāyāna.

To realize the Mahāyāna, there is nothing better than *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Through *śamatha*, one does not follow after deluded thoughts, and the single mark is eternally pure.
Contemplating thus, one does not stagnate in empty stillness, yet wondrous function constantly arises. One suddenly realizes all phenomena; wherever one touches, there is universal penetration.
This may be called attaining *bodhi* in the snap of a finger, a merit surpassing that of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; entering the *dharmadhātu* within a single atom, a principle beyond measure.

Among those who study the Tiantai school, many still follow the branches while losing sight of the source; how could those who receive divergent transmissions know how to explore the root and encompass the branches?
Reflecting upon myself, I am dim-witted, with both understanding and practice utterly desolate; yet I secretly look up to these numinous texts with the hunger of one longing for nourishment.

My thirst for this teaching is extreme; therefore, setting aside my humble ignorance, I shall briefly discern its essential purpose. I will explain the great text of this Dharma-gate by dividing it into two parts:
first, the title; second, the entry into the text. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, the direct explanation of the title;
second, the citation of the master’s name. Now, the first section.

The six characters of the general title of the *Mahāyāna-śamatha-vipaśyanā-dharmaparyāya* fully encompass: that which gives rise and that which is given rise to; that which relies and that upon which it relies; that which penetrates and that which is penetrated;

that by which one proceeds and that by which one proceeds; that which discriminates and that which is discriminated; that which accomplishes and that which is accomplished; that which expresses and that which is expressed; and that which understands and that which is understood.
Regarding the meaning of the eight pairs and sixteen aspects: first, as for that which can initiate [the practice], it is what is called the Mahāyāna in the Sanskrit language;

this is precisely the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*) of sentient beings. Based upon this, one can initiate and bring to completion the dharma-gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

For the nature of the sentient being’s mind is fundamentally quiescent and luminous: by virtue of its quality of quiescence, it can initiate sublime *śamatha*; by virtue of its quality of luminosity...
Therefore, one is able to give rise to wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Second, as for that which is given rise to, it is the dharma-gate of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

This is the essential technique by which the Buddhas of the three periods turn their backs on the dust [of delusion] and unite with awakening. It is because the nature of the sentient beings' minds is fundamentally quiescent and luminous;

yet, while they possess the virtue of their inherent nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), they have not yet attained the virtue of cultivation (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). Failing to realize this, thoughts arise and ignorance (*avidyā*) comes into being. As soon as thoughts arise—
The characteristic of movement contradicts original quiescence; ignorance thus becomes the characteristic of obscurity, contradicting original illumination.

Consequently, the entire substance of the mind-nature is taken as the *ālaya-vijñāna* and termed the "characteristic of karma" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). This is the transformation of the absolute reality into delusion, wherein delusion differentiates between subject and object.

The subject is called the "characteristic of transition" (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), and the object is called the "characteristic of manifestation" (*pratibhāsa-lakṣaṇa*). Once these three subtle characteristics have appeared, the six [consciousnesses]...
The coarse [realms] follow their respective conditions; the three links of affliction, karma, and suffering form an unceasing cycle. When suffering reaches its extreme, one contemplates its origin;
by reflecting back upon the source of suffering, one knows that suffering has no inherent nature. This arises from affliction and karma; yet affliction and karma have no inherent nature.

Though they exist, they are not truly existent—they are but the single mind. That all delusions are forever stilled is called "Cessation" (śamatha). One knows that suffering without inherent nature, as well as affliction and karma, are not real.

Yet there are myriad distinctions among them. To penetrate clearly into dependent origination is likewise but the one mind. The profuse arising of its great functions is termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
Both of these arise based upon the Mahāyāna’s intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*). Third, as for that which depends [upon the basis], it is precisely *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
This means that because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to know names and meanings, when one hears the teachings on all phenomena...
The intrinsic nature of phenomena is quiescent and primordially signless. It appears to exist through false causes and conditions, though it does not truly exist;
yet that which exists is itself non-existent, being nothing other than the single mind, and even this mental characteristic is ungraspable.

Because the mental consciousness can thus comprehend and realize this, the perpetual cessation of objective grasping is called *śamatha* (calm abiding). Thoroughly investigating according to reality is called [vipaśyanā].
Regarding "contemplation" (vipaśyanā): it should be understood that the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā is the function of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Regarding the "four bases": this means taking the Mahāyāna intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*) as the support;

one cultivates śamatha by relying on the meaning of primordial quiescence, and one cultivates vipaśyanā by relying on the meaning of primordial illumination. It should be understood that those who cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā must necessarily...
The nature of the mind (*cittaprakṛti*) serves as the basis. Regarding the five "gateways of penetration," these refer to the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. These, in turn, are threefold:

taking the teaching as the gateway enables the accomplishment of wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); taking practice as the gateway enables the accomplishment of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);

and taking principle as the gateway enables the accomplishment of wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Among these, one cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by means of the nature of conceptual differentiation (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); for the time being, this constitutes the teaching.
Regarding the gateways: practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by way of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is, for the time being, the gateway of practice;

practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by way of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is, for the time being, the gateway of principle. Regarding the six objects of penetration: these refer to the Mahāyāna’s intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*). This also has three aspects, namely:
the vehicle of principle (*tattva-yāna*), the vehicle of following (*anugama-yāna*), and the vehicle of attainment (*prāpti-yāna*). For the time being...
The "vehicle of speech" is that which is traversed by the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); the "vehicle of attainment" is that which is traversed by the gate of tranquility (*śamatha*);

and the "vehicle of principle" is that which is traversed by the gate of the non-duality of tranquility and contemplation. Furthermore, the Mahāyāna may also be called the "traverser," while tranquility and contemplation may also be called the "traversed.
By taking the teaching as the vehicle, one is traversed to a semblance of tranquility and contemplation; by taking practice as the vehicle...
It leads through to the true *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the stages of penetration; taking principle as the vehicle, it leads through to the ultimate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Seventh, regarding that which is "able to proceed": this refers to the Mahāyāna *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This, in turn, has three meanings. Regarding the three meanings of "Great" (*mahā*): they are great, many, and superior.
The three meanings of "vehicle" (*yāna*) are: the meaning of principle, the meaning of following, and the meaning of attainment. The three meanings of "cessation" (*śamatha*) are:

the meaning of pacification, the meaning of stopping, and the meaning of non-stopping-cessation. The three meanings of "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) are: the meaning of piercing through, the meaning of penetrating, and the meaning of non-contemplation-contemplation.
The present single thought-moment of the self-nature pure mind (*svabhāva-viśuddha-citta*) of sentient beings is "Great" because its essence is absolute and beyond duality;

it is "Many" because it is replete with all phenomena; it is "Supreme" because there is nothing that can be compared to it. These three meanings inherent in its nature are called the Vehicle of Principle (*li-sheng*).

To awaken to and reach these three meanings is called the Vehicle of Accordance (*sui-sheng*). To harmonize and accord with these three meanings is called the Vehicle of Attainment (*de-sheng*). When one realizes these three meanings within a single mind, it pervades everywhere.
It is capable. The cessation and extinction of the delusions of views, afflictions, and the dust-like ignorance of *saṃsāra* is the meaning of "stopping" (*shi*).

Abiding securely in the inconceivable realm of the three truths is the meaning of "staying still" (*ting*). In reality, there is no distinction between the one who stops and that which is stopped, nor between the one who stays still and that which is stayed;

this is the meaning of "neither stopping nor staying" (*bu zhi zhi*). To realize these three meanings within this single mind is to be able to universally penetrate through the obscurations of the three delusions.

The meaning of "hindrance" (*āvaraṇa*) is that of "observing and piercing. The meaning of "observing and penetrating" (*pratyavekṣaṇa*) is the thorough knowledge of the causes and conditions for the equality and differentiation of the three truths within a single object.

The meaning of "non-observation as observation" (*anupalambha-upalambha*) is that, in reality, there is no distinction between the piercer and the pierced, nor between the penetrator and the penetrated.

Only this Mahāyāna *śamatha-vipaśyanā* can proceed by way of the gates of the perfect teaching (*paripūrṇa-śāsana*), the perfect practice (*paripūrṇa-caryā*), and the perfect principle (*paripūrṇa-tattva*).

Regarding the eighth point, "that which is traversed": it means that within the Dharma-gates of the Mahāyāna, the three thousandfold nature-and-characteristics (*tri-sahasra-dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) are all termed "Dharma.

Furthermore, because these Dharmas can lead one through [to realization], they are also termed "gates" (*mukha*). The nature of all phenomena is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent.
There is nothing. It is perfectly free from the four propositions; it is utterly extinguished and pure. This is taught according to the *siddhānta*.

It possesses the four gates and the four non-definitions, each of which is perfectly interfused; this serves as the basis for both calming (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). If one wishes to provide a brief indication:

regarding the defiled portion of the *parikalpita-svabhāva*, the cultivation of calming and insight proceeds by way of the gate of emptiness. Regarding the defiled portion of the *paratantra-svabhāva*...

Cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* based on the nature of existence proceeds by way of the gate of "existence. Cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* regarding the true nature of the defiled portion proceeds by way of the gate of "both existence and emptiness.
Cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* regarding the three natures from the perspective of the pure portion proceeds by way of the gate of "neither existence nor emptiness.

Alternatively, one may also consider cultivation based on the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as proceeding by way of the gate of "existence," and cultivation based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as proceeding by way of the gate of "both. Regarding...

The true nature (*tathatā*) is the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*). Furthermore, each of the three natures may be discussed according to the four gates, because all three natures are equally free from the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*) and can be explained by means of the four gates.

Moreover, the cultivation of calm abiding (*śamatha*) proceeds by way of the gate of emptiness; the cultivation of the pair [of calm abiding and insight] proceeds by way of the gate of existence (*bhāva-mukha*);
and the simultaneous practice of both calm abiding and insight proceeds by way of the gate of both affirmation and negation (*ubhaya-anubhaya-mukha*). This is because...

To facilitate understanding, this analysis is composed. To express the essential meaning: when one gate is all gates, and all gates are one gate, this is precisely the gateway through which the Mahāyāna proceeds.
Ninth, regarding "that which can exclude": the two characters "Mahāyāna" exclude all other dharma-gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Tenth, regarding "that which is excluded": it refers to the fact that among the dharma-gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there are...

There are many types. If one practices "stopping by abiding in reality" (*tattva-śamatha*) and enters the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one can only save oneself and cannot save others; thus, it is not called the Mahāyāna.

If one practices "stopping by following conditions" (*prajñapti-anuśaraṇa-śamatha*) and emerges into the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), although one can save others, one does not reach the ultimate goal.

If one attains the cessation of the two extremes through the means of the two types of tranquility (*śamatha*), and attains the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way through the means of the two types of insight (*vipaśyanā*), this is generally described as the Mahāyāna.

However, if considered sequentially and individually, the former two are not "lofty" and the latter one is not "vast"; thus, they are not called "Great. Nevertheless, because they can transport one from the cause to the fruit, they are so designated.
Resting alone is not yet called "mounting" [the vehicle]. Now, taking the intrinsically pure mind as one's basis, one is still while moving and luminous within obscurity.

Adorned with the power of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one delivers sentient beings by means of this, until the end of the future without the notion of a limit—this is truly the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of the Mahāyāna. Eleventh, "that which can accomplish" refers to:
By the power of wondrous *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one is able to realize the Great Vehicle’s mind of self-nature purity, equality, and single reality.

Regarding the "twelfth accomplishment," this refers to the fundamentally original mind of self-nature purity; it is the unsurpassed ultimate fruit of the Great Vehicle that is realized through wondrous *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
This is because the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause. Thirteen.

Regarding the "expressive" (nengquan): these six characters in total are all expressive. "Great" (da) expresses the meaning of the three—essence, attributes, and function—as being beyond all relative dependence.
"Vehicle" (sheng) expresses the meaning of saving oneself and others, proceeding from cause to fruit.
"Cessation" (zhi) expresses the meaning of returning to the truth by subduing delusion. "Contemplation" (guan) expresses the meaning of arising function from within the essence itself.
"Dharma" (dharma) signifies the meaning of providing a standard for things and maintaining them; "gate" (mukha) signifies the meaning of following a path and entering a house.
Fourteenth, as for the "signified," this refers to the meaning revealed beneath these very characters, which can give rise in us to the wisdoms of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
Fifteenth, as for the "one who understands," this refers to one whose cognitive faculty is clear and sharp, such that they obtain the meaning from the text.
Unlike the gaze of cattle or sheep, which cannot distinguish the ultimate destination, that which is understood by the sixteen [aspects] refers to the spheres of names, phrases,
and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) as the objects traversed by the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*). Ultimately, because the power of wisdom is preeminent,
one is able to extensively traverse all objects within the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), thereby perceiving the Mahāyāna Dharma-gate of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within them all.
If one wishes to explain it according to the five aspects: its name is "Dharma"; its essence is the intrinsically pure mind;

its principle is *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; its function is the removal of hindrances and the attainment of benefit; and its characteristic is the unsurpassed *amṛta*. △ Second, the enumeration of the master’s titles.
The Great Meditation Master Si of Mount Nanyue personally transmitted the essentials of the mind.
His secular name was Huìsī; his family name was Lǐ. He was a native of Wǔjīn in the Southern Yù Prefecture during the Northern Wèi dynasty.
When he was a child, he dreamed of a foreign monk who exhorted him to enter the Way. He once dwelt in caves that he had excavated within empty tombs and relocated to ancient cities.
Throughout his life, except for the occasion of begging for alms, he read the *Lotus Sūtra* day and night. He prostrated with diligent devotion and did not attend to sleep or rest.
After enduring long rains and damp heat, his entire body became swollen; yet, with a heart of forbearance toward the scripture, his afflictions suddenly vanished.

Furthermore, in a dream, Samantabhadra mounted a white elephant king and rubbed the crown of his head; upon the spot where it was rubbed, a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) emerged. At the age of fifteen, he left home.
Having received full ordination at home, he dreamed that twenty-four monks performed the *karmavācanā* for him, thereby perfecting his precepts.

Subsequently, while reading the *Sūtra on the Wondrous and Supreme Samādhi*, he saw it extol the virtues of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Thereupon, he sought out teachers of Chan extensively. Later, he visited the Great Master Huìwén of the Northern Qi to inquire about and receive oral instructions.
Huìwén bestowed upon him the method of contemplating the mind (*guanxin*). He sat in meditation until dawn, whereupon he experienced eight [signs of spiritual attainment].
Chu (Touch). Due to his vision, he perceived the traces of the path of practice from three lifetimes prior.

At the end of the summer retreat, as he was about to receive the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he leaned his body against a wall and attained a sudden, great awakening to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. Thereafter, he propagated the Mahāyāna: first in Yanzhou in Henan; next in Yingzhou;
then at Kaiyue Temple in Guangzhou; and finally on Mount Dasu. Whenever he lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, [he would manifest miraculous signs].

Various malicious debaters vied with one another to end the Master’s life by administering poison. The Master focused his mind single-mindedly on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the poison was immediately neutralized.
Consequently, he made a vow to commission the transcription of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in golden letters.

Upon their completion, he composed one scroll of a Vow Text (*praṇidhāna-paṭala*) and commanded his disciple Zhiyi to lecture on it in his stead. When they reached the passage on “single-mindedness encompassing all,”...
Regarding the myriad practices, [Zhiyi] suddenly had some doubts. The Master said, "Your manner of doubting is merely the sequential approach of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;

it is not yet the perfect and sudden purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. In the past, during the summer retreat, I realized all dharmas in a single thought-moment, and they became manifest before me.
Since I have personally realized this, there is no need for doubt. Zhiyi asked, "Is what you have realized the stage of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*)? He replied: [It is].
"I had hoped throughout my life to enter the Age of the Bronze Wheel (Tāmra-yuga), but because I led disciples too early, I have harmed myself and benefited others;

thus, I shall dwell only in the Age of the Iron Wheel (Kāṃsa-yuga). Later, he sought refuge in the Southern Peak (Nanyue). While ascending Mount Zhurong, he encountered the deity of the mountain playing chess.

The deity approached the Master and asked, "Master, why have you come here? The Master replied, "I seek from you, O Patron (Dānapati), the space of a single sitting mat. The deity said, "Agreed. The Master—
He raised his flying staff to determine the location (which is the present-day Fuyan Temple). A deity said, "The Master has already occupied this blessed ground;
where should your disciple reside? The Master immediately turned a stone drum downward; it came to rest upon a level plain (the statue of the deity Yue still stands atop the stone drum today).
The deity Yue requested the precepts, and the Master immediately expounded for him the essentials of the Dharma. When the Master was about to pass away, he gathered his disciples in a great assembly.
Master Xue preached the Dharma day after day with such earnestness that it moved people to sorrow.

He then declared, "If there are ten people who do not begrudge their own lives and constantly practice the Lotus, Pratyutpanna, and Vaipulya repentances as well as the ascetic practice of constant sitting, I shall personally provide for whatever they require.
If there are no such people, I shall depart. Ultimately, no one answered. He then expanded the assembly.

As he was withdrawing his mind in preparation for entering nirvana, his disciple Lingbian involuntarily wailed aloud. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Evil Māra, get out! The assembly of holy ones is welcoming me.
I am currently discussing my place of rebirth; why do you startle me? He then sat upright and chanted, "The Buddha comes to welcome me," and passed away with palms joined.
His countenance remained as if alive, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room. (The ninth year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty.)
It was the twenty-second day of the sixth month of that year. His age was sixty-three; his years of the summer retreat were forty-nine. The Master’s physical form was exceptionally prominent:
his ears had the mark of the double-circle, and his crown possessed the mark of the flesh-tuft. He walked with the gait of an ox and the stride of an elephant, neither leaning nor slanting.
Throughout his life, he used only a single hempen robe to ward off the cold; he accepted no silk or cotton at all. As for the place where he resided—
Auspicious omens occurred in successive layers. The ritual offerings were solemnly prepared, and the water in the vases filled itself. Various celestial youths served as his attendants;
some manifested forms of varying sizes, while others remained silent and concealed their bodies.

These extraordinary fragrances and sublime traces are beyond recounting (the above is from the *Tiantai Shan Fangwai Zhi*). The title "Master Sida" used here is a term of honor bestowed by later generations. To speak of...

Someone asked a śramaṇa, saying: "Now, though our innate natures and physical forms are uniform, our cultivation differs. It is simply because the craftsman’s carving varies that the vessels produced are not identical.
I have heard that the Venerable One has penetrated the ultimate principle and discerned the profound and vast doctrine;
therefore, I have applied myself to cultivation in the hope of hearing the True Dharma."

The śramaṇa takes diligent cessation as his meaning. This is the general designation for those who have left the household life, whose name and nature do not change; it refers directly to the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*).

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) resulting from a single lifetime’s retribution are called the substance. Where there is substance, one must necessarily receive its nature—what is meant by the saying, "natures are similar.
That which is depended upon is called the objective support (*ālambana*); to advance through creation is cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which follows along with defilement.

Through pure conditions, the two types of cultivation—contrary and conforming—are accomplished, resulting in the differentiated fruits of the ten realms; this is what is meant by the "distinction of habitual characteristics.
The artisan is a metaphor for teachers and friends; carving is a metaphor for instruction and admonition; and the vessel is a metaphor for the student.

The fact that the fruits attained through upholding the teachings and practicing them are not uniform refers to the various distinctions among the three vehicles and the seven stages of expedient means. This is the ultimate point.

The principle of "this" refers to the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*); the doctrine of "mysterious vastness" (*xuankuo*) refers to wondrous cultivation. "Mysterious" means not being obstructed by the shallow or mundane;
"vast" means not being confined to a partial corner. Being neither obstructed nor confined is what is called the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
This effectively constitutes a secret request for the Mahāyāna *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* method. △ Second, the response.
The śramaṇa said: "Although I was young when I first entered the monastic life and tasted the flavor of the Way, my ignorance is deep-seated and difficult to change;
my conduct and principles remain untainted by it. Now, having been honored by your question, I do not know what to say."
This modesty is used to observe the capacities [of his audience]. That he "dyes his robes black" and "feeds on the wind of the Way" clarifies that he has practiced the orthodox teaching.

The statement that "the ignorant are difficult to reform" is a humble expression; because he has not yet reached the principle of practice—and since the principle of practice remains untainted—he is unable to discern the minds of others from afar.
Thus, he does not know what the questioner intends to say. Nevertheless, the Great Master manifested his presence.
The Iron Wheel [King] already belongs to the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*); what is now stated regarding his lack of defilement is merely a humble expression.
The second round of question and answer also has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. This is the first.
The outsider said, “Indeed, Venerable One! I pray that you will not disdain the labor; please explain for me the practices of the Mahāyāna.
I shall respectfully uphold them and dare not forget.”
Those who have not yet attained realization and whose minds wander outside of principle are called "outsiders.
Only those who have given rise to the Mahāyāna mind and seek the Mahāyāna Dharma may be spoken to regarding the Mahāyāna. △ Second, the response.
The śramaṇa said, "Excellent, son of the Buddha! You are indeed able to give rise to this unsurpassed mind and take delight in hearing the practices of the Mahāyāna.
You have already transcended the realm of the two vehicles at this very moment; how much more so when you wish to hear and practice them?

Nevertheless, although you have given rise to this sublime mind, it must rely upon practice to perfect its virtue. While the methods of practice are ten thousandfold and the ways of entering the Path are not one, for now..."

Based upon the sūtras and śāstras, I shall briefly explain for you, my son, the two gates of Mahāyāna *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. By relying on this Dharma, you will be able to swiftly fulfill your aspirations.
One who is able to give rise to the Great Mind is called a "Son of the Buddha," because such a person is capable of succeeding to the rank of the Buddha. Formerly, there was a *ra...* [text fragment]
Han kept a śrāmaṇera. Suddenly, the śrāmaṇera gave rise to the Great Mind (bodhicitta), whereupon his master immediately yielded to him and allowed him to go before.

Thus we know that the single thought of generating the mind truly transcends the realm of the two vehicles. Nevertheless, once this superior mind has been generated, one must especially cultivate superior practice.
Although practices differ in ten thousand ways, *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) are the essentials, for these two gates can encompass and give rise to all practices.
△ The third round of question and answer also has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Now, the first [the question]:
The outsider said: "Excellent! I pray that you will speak, so as to fulfill my own intent and also bring successive benefit to others.
Thus, by ensuring that the transmission of the lamp is never severed, one repays the Buddha's kindness."
The Buddha takes the salvation of sentient beings as his primary task; only by transmitting the Dharma can one repay the Buddha’s kindness.
This is precisely the profound mind of the Mahayana that seeks both self-benefit and the benefit of others. △ Second, the answer.

The śramaṇa said: "Listen attentively and hold yourself well; I shall explain it for you. As for what is called 'cessation,' it means knowing that all dharmas, from the very beginning, are by nature non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing.
It is only through false causes and conditions that they appear to exist where they do not.
Yet those existing dharmas, in their very existence, are non-existent; they are but the substance of the single mind, devoid of discrimination."
One who practices this contemplation is able to prevent deluded thoughts from flowing; therefore, it is called "stopping" (*śamatha*). As for what is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*):
although one knows that [phenomena] are fundamentally unborn and now unceasing, because the mind-nature arises through conditions, illusory worldly functions are not non-existent.
They are like illusions and dreams—neither existent nor non-existent—and thus it is called "contemplation."

First, he exhorted them to listen attentively so that they might give rise to the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Furthermore, he exhorted them to maintain proper composure so that they might give rise to the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), thereby ascending to the stage of the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
In Sanskrit, *śamatha* is translated here as "cessation" (*zhi*). It has three distinct types: first, the cessation of the true essence (*tattva-śamatha*).
Second is the cessation that accords with conditions through skillful means; third is the cessation that stills the discrimination of the two extremes.

Within each of these cessations, there are three meanings. First is the cessation of abiding in reality (*tattva-viśrānti*). This cessation stills view-delusions and afflictions (*kleśa*) and brings one to rest in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

View-delusions and the ultimate truth are like water and ice—they share the same nature of moisture. Since their nature is such, it is neither "cessation" nor "non-cessation. [The second is] the cessation that accords with conditions through skillful means.
Cessation. It ceases the sands of dust; it halts conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). These sands of dust and conventional truths are like ice and water:
their nature is neither cessation nor non-cessation. It ceases the discrimination of the two extremes; it ceases ignorance (*avidyā*); it halts the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*).
The truth within ignorance is also like ice and water; its nature is neither cessation nor non-cessation.

What is called "knowing all dharmas to be equal" refers to the character "contemplation" (guan) in the phrase "practicing this contemplation. This is because one enters cessation by means of contemplation.
"All dharmas" universally points to the ten realms and the ten suchnesses, encompassing both the provisional and the real, as well as their natures and characteristics.
This refers to the dharmas produced by causes and conditions. From the very beginning, their nature has inherently been non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing.
This is what I mean when I say they are "empty. The ten realms are all empty; this is not merely a state of simple emptiness.
It exists through false and illusory causes and conditions, yet it is not truly existent; this is what is called "provisional designation.
The ten realms are mutually inclusive, which differs from a partial or one-sided provisional designation. Yet those existing phenomena, though they exist, are in truth non-existent;
they are but the essence of the single mind, devoid of discrimination. This is what is called the meaning of the "Middle Way. Every phenomenon is the Middle.

It is not merely that they differ within the Middle Way; because one contemplates that which is identical to emptiness, the deluded thoughts of view and affliction (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within and without the realms do not flow forth.

Because one contemplates that which is identical to the provisional (*upāya*), the deluded thoughts regarding the sands of phenomena (*rajas*) within and without the realms do not flow forth. Because one contemplates that which is identical to the Middle.

It causes the ignorance and deluded thoughts within and without the realms to cease flowing. To facilitate easy understanding, it is explained through sequential analysis, using language that captures the essential meaning.

Because the three types of cessation are perfectly integrated within a single mind, it is called the "Mahāyāna Gate of Cessation. In Sanskrit, this is *vipaśyanā*, which is translated here as "contemplation" (*guān*).

This also has three distinct aspects: first, the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional; second, [the contemplation of entering the middle way from emptiness]; third, [the contemplation of the non-duality of emptiness and conventionality].

The contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness (*śūnyatā-praveśa-prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-prathamārtha-vipaśyanā*), and the contemplation of entering emptiness from the provisional (*prajñapti-praveśa-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) each possess three meanings.
The contemplation of entering emptiness from the provisional penetrates the views of afflictions (*kleśa-dṛṣṭi*) and reaches the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Since the nature of the views of afflictions and the ultimate truth is fundamentally non-dual, it is neither a matter of contemplation nor non-contemplation. The contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness penetrates the views of the *saṃsāra* of dust-like delusions (*rajas-sama-kleśa*) and reaches the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Truths. The nature of the mundane truths, as numerous as motes of dust, is fundamentally non-dual; it is neither something to be contemplated nor not contemplated.

Through the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way, one contemplates and penetrates the truth of the Middle. The nature of the truth of the Middle and ignorance is fundamentally non-dual; it is neither something to be contemplated nor not contemplated.
This indicates that the text concerning contemplation differs slightly from that concerning cessation (*śamatha*). The former was based on what is produced by causes and conditions. Now—
By clarifying wondrous stillness through emptiness, conventionality, and the Middle Way, the three wondrous contemplations are already contained therein.

This is simply a matter of revealing principle through phenomena and subsuming the branches back to the root, as elucidated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, where it is taught that the aggregates, bases, and elements are all the Tathāgata-garbha.
The present statement, "Though one knows they were originally unborn and are not now extinguished," directly cites the preceding text in its entirety.
Speaking from the perspective of phenomena as they are identical to principle (*li*), this means that what is called "following conditions" (*suiyuan*) is itself "unchanging" (*bubian*).

Yet, through the mind-nature’s dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is no absence of the illusory worldly functions; like a phantom or a dream, they are non-existent yet appear to exist.

Thus, it refers directly to all phenomena (*dharmas*), such that whichever single phenomenon one picks up is none other than the *dharmadhātu* of dependent origination—what is called "the unchanging following conditions."
This refers to the nature and its manifestations being both identical in substance and identical in function, as elucidated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Only when the seven elements within the Tathāgatagarbha are mutually interfused does it constitute the contemplative gate of the Mahāyāna.

Now, as for turning one's back on delusion and uniting with awakening, all three types of cessation and three types of contemplation are collectively termed "cessation" (*śamatha*). As for the entire substance giving rise to its function, all that is both quiescent and illuminating is termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).

Taken collectively, these are termed "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). Since this is not a practice of mere opposition, it is forever distinct from the tenets of the partial and limited vehicles (*hīnayāna*).

Having grasped this intent, one will see that throughout the subsequent sections on defilement and purity and the three natures—whether considered vertically or horizontally—all varieties of *samatha* and *vipaśyanā* from beginning to end are nothing other than perfectly consummate.
Only then will one know that Master Zhiyi established the ten objects (*daśaviṣaya*) and exhaustively discussed the ten [stages]...

The vehicles do not transcend this. It is solely because of the varying capacities of the faculties—some sharp and some dull—that the teachings are presented with varying degrees of detail and brevity.
How could one revere the son while, conversely, disparaging the father? This concludes the initial brief presentation of the essential framework.
△ Second, the extensive analysis has two parts: first, the reiterated questioning; second, the detailed response. Now, the first.

The outsider said: "My understanding is dim and my consciousness is subtle; having heard this, I have not yet been able to attain immediate awakening. I pray that you will use skillful means to explain it further for me.
△ Second, the detailed response, which has three parts: first, the promise to speak; second, the establishment of the outline; third, the explanation. Now, the first.
The śramaṇa said: "Indeed. I shall further provide you with a detailed analysis, so that those who have not yet heard it may seek it out and attain awakening.
△ Second, the establishment of the topical outline.
Within the extensive analysis of the gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, five sections are established: first, clarifying the basis of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;

second, clarifying the objects of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; third, clarifying the essential nature and characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; fourth, clarifying the abandonment and attainment of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; and fifth, clarifying the functions of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

First, the clarification of the basis for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, consisting of two and a half fascicles; this is what Ciyun referred to as the first fascicle, which opens up the exegesis of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Second, the clarification of the spheres of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, continuing through the fifth section, the clarification of the functions of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
There is a half-fascicle of text, which is what Ciyun referred to as "the second fascicle showing the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Regarding the sequence:
the basis (*āśraya*) is the source of both delusion and awakening. Due to delusion, there arise the distinctions among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) of objective realms.

Because there is an object of observation, one can discern the essential characteristics of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). Because one cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there is abandonment and attainment.
Because one attains their essence, there is functional activity. △ Third, the explanation consists of five parts: first, clarifying the basis of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
[continuing] up to fifth, clarifying the functional activity of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the division of the topical outline; second, each...
Commentary: First, regarding the first section on "reliance," it is further analyzed through three gates: first, clarifying what is relied upon; second, clarifying why one relies [upon it];
and third, clarifying by means of what one relies [upon it].

△ Second, the individual explanations. This consists of three parts: first, clarifying that which is relied upon; second, [clarifying the nature of the reliance]; third, clarifying by means of what one relies.
Regarding the first of these, there are two sections: first, the headings and enumeration; second, the detailed exposition. Now, the first.
First, to clarify that upon which one relies: it means relying on the single mind to cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā. Within this, there are three further distinctions:
first, enumerating the various names; second, explaining the meaning of those names; and third, discerning their essential characteristics.
First, "one mind" is indicated; next, the three distinctions are enumerated. "One mind" refers to the present, momentary thought of each of us—the so-called *kṣaṇika-citta*.
Its nature is fundamentally equal to that of all Buddhas and sentient beings; this is what is meant by the "threefold non-differentiation.
Since the true is entirely manifested as the deluded, the deluded is likewise entirely the true. Therefore, it is called "one mind," and not...
This establishes a single true mind as distinct from the deluded mind. It is like this: the nature of water is identical to the waves, and the nature of the sea is identical to the bubbles.
△ Second, the explanation and establishment [of this principle] consists of three parts: first, the presentation of various names; second, the explanation of the meanings of those names;
third, the discernment of their essential characteristics. Now, the first part.

Regarding the phrase "initially appearing with manifold names": this mind is the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*). It is also called *tathatā* (suchness), and it is further called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

It is also termed the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and is likewise designated as the Tathāgata-garbha. It is also named the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and further called the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
Names such as these are immeasurable and boundless; therefore, they are said to be "manifold names."
This is a brief listing of seven names to serve as the basis for explaining their meanings. △ Second, the explanation of the names and meanings has three parts:
first, the presentation of the headings; second, the detailed explanation; third, the conclusion. Now, the first part.
Next, the definitions and meanings are explained.
△ Second, the detailed explanation is divided into seven parts: first, the explanation of the intrinsically pure mind (up to) seventh, the explanation of the *dharmatā*.
Now, the first.
Question: What is meant by the "intrinsically pure mind" (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*)? Answer:
Although this mind has been covered by the defiled dharmas of ignorance since beginningless time, its nature is pure and unchanging; therefore, it is called "pure. Why is this so?
Because the defiled phenomena of ignorance are fundamentally separated from the mind, how is this separation to be understood?

It means that because the essence of ignorance is a non-existent thing (*abhāva*), its existence is itself non-existence. Since it is non-existent, there is nothing that can be associated with the mind; therefore, it is said to be "separated.

Because no defiled phenomenon of ignorance is associated with it, it is called "intrinsically pure" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*). Thus, it is the true, central, original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Therefore...
It is called "mind"; therefore, it is termed the "intrinsically pure mind" (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*).
This refers to the intrinsic nature of this very thought-moment of the present.
Although from time immemorial it has been shrouded by the defiled dharmas of ignorance, it remains pure as before; its nature cannot be altered. It is, for example, like space, which—though...
While delusory flowers arise and perish within it, emptiness remains unchanged. Because the substance of those delusory flowers does not exist, one cannot say that they correspond with emptiness;
this is called "separation. It is not like two distinct objects situated in different places that are called separate.
As for what is called the "Middle Real Original Enlightenment," its nature is neither existent nor non-existent; thus it is named the "Middle. It is not...
The principle that the name "existence" is derived in contrast to emptiness is not false or erroneous; thus, it is designated as "substantial.
Unlike emptiness, which is manifested through form, [the mind] fundamentally lacks non-awakening and is therefore called "original awakening" (*mūla-bodhi*).
Unlike emptiness, which is obscure and devoid of cognition, it can only be compared to emptiness; one must not mistake emptiness for the mind. △ Second, the explanation of *tathatā* (suchness).
Question: What is meant by "True Suchness" (tathatā)? Answer: All phenomena (dharmas) exist in dependence upon this mind;

taking the mind as their essence, when compared to all phenomena, those phenomena are entirely false and illusory. Since they exist yet are not truly existent, and because they are contrasted with these deceptive phenomena, they are designated as "True.
Furthermore, although all phenomena are in reality non-existent, they arise solely through false causes and conditions.
Regarding the characteristics of arising and ceasing: when those empty phenomena arise, this mind does not arise; when all phenomena cease, this mind does not cease.
Because it does not arise, it does not increase; because it does not cease, it does not decrease. Because it is without arising or ceasing, and without increase or decrease, it is called "True.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time and all sentient beings alike share this one pure mind.
It is the essence. While all phenomena of ordinary beings and sages possess their own distinct differences and characteristics, this true mind is without difference and without characteristic;
therefore, it is named "Suchness" (*tathatā*). Furthermore, regarding "True Suchness," because all phenomena are truly thus and are solely this one mind, this one mind is designated as True Suchness.
If there were any phenomena existing apart from the mind, they would not be real.
It is not like this; rather, it constitutes a false appearance of difference. Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:

"All dharmas, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names, and free from the characteristics of mental objects; they are ultimately equal."
It is without change and cannot be destroyed; it is solely this single mind, and is therefore called *tathatā* (suchness).
For this reason, the intrinsically pure mind is further named *tathatā*.
The first two sections explain "Reality" (*tathatā*); the next section explains "Suchness" (*tathā*); and the final section explains "True Suchness" (*tathatā*) by combining them.
"Real" (*tathā*) means not false; "Such" (*tathā*) means not different. Regarding the initial explanation of "Real":

all the various distinctions among phenomena are entirely false and deceptive appearances. The mind, however, is both the distinctions and non-distinction, just as gold is both the substance and the vessel.
The vessels have distinctions, but the nature of gold has no distinction. The appearance of the vessel is false; the substance of the gold is true. Furthermore, to explain "true":
while all phenomena are illusory, arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, the mind, though appearing to arise and cease, does not truly arise or cease.
It is like gold that constitutes a vessel. The vessel undergoes formation and destruction, but the gold itself has neither formation nor destruction.
Formation and destruction are the delusions of arising and ceasing, or increase and decrease; that which is devoid of formation and destruction is called "True.

The next passage explaining "like" (ru) cites the myriad differences between ordinary beings and sages as being of one and the same essence within the true mind. Since this essence is not dual, it is said to be "without difference," even though their appearances differ.
Because it is only the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is said to be "without marks" (*animitta*). Next, to explain *tathatā* (suchness) by combining its aspects:

there are no phenomena outside the mind; phenomena are solely the mind. Because it is truly thus, it is called *tathatā*. The citation from the treatise that establishes this is easily seen in the text.
△ Third, the explanation of Buddha-nature has two parts: first, a brief explanation; second, an extensive analysis. Now, the first.
Question: Why is this mind further designated as "Buddha-nature"? Answer: "Buddha" means awakening (*bodhi*), and "nature" (*prakṛti*) means mind.
Since the essence of this pure mind is not non-awakened, it is therefore called the "awakened mind."
△ Second, the detailed exposition has three parts: first, the exposition based on non-awakening; second, the exposition based on awakening; third, the resolution of remaining doubts.
Within the first part, there are two sections: first, directly clarifying that the mind is not non-awakened; second, the dual manifestation of the meaning of Buddha-nature. Now, the first section.
Question: How is it known that this true mind is not non-enlightenment? Answer: Non-enlightenment is precisely the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āvasthā-bhūmi*).
If this pure mind were itself ignorance, then when sentient beings attain Buddhahood and ignorance is extinguished, there would be no true mind.
Why is this? Because the mind would be ignorance. Since ignorance is extinguished of its own accord, the pure mind [remains].
Because it exists, we know that the pure mind is not non-awakening. Furthermore, it is only when non-awakening is extinguished that one realizes the pure mind;
thus, one should know that the mind is not non-awakening.

When ignorance is extinguished of its own accord, the pure mind attains sovereignty; this is explained in terms of True Suchness within the entanglements (*saṃvṛta-tathatā*) to clarify that it is not non-awakening (*a-prabodha*).

Because non-awakening is extinguished, one then realizes the pure mind; this is explained in terms of True Suchness beyond the entanglements (*niḥsaṃvṛta-tathatā*) to clarify that it is not non-awakening.
Although this mind differs in being either within or beyond the entanglements, they are identical in that it is fundamentally not non-awakening.
...and so forth. △ Second, the dual manifestation of the two meanings of Buddha-nature. Question:
Why is it not called "awakening" (bodhi) by virtue of its own essence being awakening, but rather is said to be awakening because it is not non-awakening?
Answer: The essence of the mind is equal, being neither awakening nor non-awakening; it is only to clarify the Tathāgata that [it is so designated].

Therefore, it is metaphorically described as "awakening" (*bodhi*). Thus, the Sūtra says: "There is no nirvāṇa at all; there is no Buddha who has entered nirvāṇa, nor is there nirvāṇa belonging to a Buddha.
It is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened. Whether 'existent' or 'non-existent,' one is entirely free from both.

This is explained specifically with respect to the equality of the essence of mind. If, however, one proceeds from the perspective of the functional meaning of the *dharmadhātu* within the essence of mind...

Regarding "clear awareness" (prajñā): this essence of mind possesses three kinds of great wisdom—namely, teacherless wisdom (anācārya-jñāna), spontaneous wisdom (svayambhū-jñāna), and unimpeded wisdom (asanga-jñāna).
Because this essence of the awakened mind inherently possesses these three natures of wisdom, this mind is designated as the nature of awakening.
Therefore, one must understand the meaning of identity and difference. What is meant by identity? It means that the essence of mind is equality, which is itself awakening-wisdom (*jñāna-bodhi*);

and awakening-wisdom is itself the essence of mind as equality. Hence, they are said to be identical. Furthermore, what is meant by difference? It means that the principle of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is its functional activity.
In ordinary beings, it is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and it is also called the nature of the three kinds of wisdom. When it emerges from hindrances, it is called the Buddha of Wisdom.
Furthermore, the meaning of the equality of the essence of mind is the substance; therefore, there is no duality between ordinary beings and sages, for they are merely named "Tathāgata Buddha.
Thus, although the names differ, one should understand them in this way.
The question intends to grasp the meaning of "awakening" (*bodhi*) alone; the answer, however, negates both extremes.

Nevertheless, the essence of the mind is in reality neither awakening nor non-awakening, yet it can also be described as "awakening" because it possesses the two meanings of the Buddha of Suchness (*tathatā-buddha*) and the Buddha of Wisdom (*jñāna-buddha*).
From the perspective of the Buddha of Suchness, it is neither awakening nor non-awakening; yet, since it is designated as "Buddha," it may also be figuratively [described as such].
This is what is called "Awakening" (Bodhi). Since the Buddha of Wisdom possesses the functions of the three types of knowledge, he may be directly designated as "Awakened.

Unlearned Knowledge (*asikṣita-jñāna*) is identical to All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); for it is the thorough realization that the ten realms share a single characteristic, attained without depending on the enlightenment of another.

Natural Knowledge (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is identical to the Knowledge of the Paths and Species (*mārgajñatā*); for it is the thorough realization of the infinite distinctions among the natures and characteristics of the three thousand worlds.
Due to mental attention (*manasikāra*), unimpeded knowledge (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) is itself the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

It thoroughly penetrates that the single characteristic is the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), and that this absence of characteristics is not a non-characteristic. Within each and every characteristic, one perceives the true characteristic of all phenomena (*dharmas*), because it exhausts the limits and depths without obstruction.
Furthermore, "knowledge without a teacher" refers to the three knowledges, such as the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*).

Because it is attained within a single mind and is not received from another, "spontaneous wisdom" (svayambhū-jñāna) refers to the fact that the single-mind dharma-nature is inherently endowed with the three types of wisdom.

"Unobstructed wisdom" (anāvaraṇa-jñāna) means that for all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), the three truths are simultaneously empty; for the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (mārgajñatā), the three truths are all conventional designations;
and for the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), the three truths are simultaneously the Middle Way. Because there is no obstruction or hindrance, this is indeed Suchness (tathatā).
The Buddha and the wisdom-Buddha are such that the whole substance is function and the whole function is substance; how could they not be identical?
Yet, while ordinary beings possess only the nature of the wisdom-Buddha without yet manifesting its function, the Tathatā-Buddha neither diminishes in the ordinary nor increases in the sage;
how could they not be distinct? Furthermore, one should know that the nature of the wisdom-Buddha in ordinary beings...

Although its function is not manifest, its nature is fundamentally without decrease. Such is the Buddha-nature of *tathatā*. Although the essence of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) does not decrease, they are deluded and do not realize it themselves;

thus, while they appear different, they are not actually different. It is simply that they are neither identical nor different; it is only for the sake of discourse that the meaning of identity and difference is spoken of.
△ Second, distinguishing the four [aspects] based on awakening: 1. Distinguishing the Buddha-nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). 2. Distinguishing the [Buddha-nature of] retribution (*vipāka*).

1. The Buddha-nature of the Response-Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*). 2. The Buddha-nature of Wisdom-Buddha (*jñānakāya*), which is the *svasaṃbhogakāya*. 3. The Buddha-nature of the Fruition-Buddha (*vipākakāya*), which is the *parasambhogakāya*. 4.
The Buddha-nature of the Response-Buddha, which comprises both the superior and inferior response-bodies as well as the response-body that accords with the species of beings.

5. The Buddha-nature of the Transcendent-from-Obstructions, which is the Dharmakāya at the stage of fruition. 6. The Buddha-nature of Equality, which is the Dharmakāya while still enmeshed in afflictions (*saṃkleśa*).
The Body. Thus, these three bodies—both singular and plural—are all characterized by pure mind as their nature;
therefore, they are all termed "Awakening" (*bodhi*). This section has three parts: first, a dual acknowledgment of two meanings; second, a detailed explanation based on cultivation;
and third, a conclusion through analogy. Now, the first part.
Question: Regarding the Buddha of Wisdom, is he called "Buddha" because he is able to awaken to the pure mind, or is he called "Buddha" because the pure mind awakens itself?
Answer: Both meanings apply. First, awakening to the pure mind; second, the pure mind awakening itself.
Although two meanings are spoken of, their essence is not distinct.
△ Second, the detailed explanation based on cultivation has two parts. First, the meaning of "non-awakening" (abodha) is established by showing how delusion regarding reality gives rise to falsehood.

Second, the meaning of possessing the two types of awakening is established by showing the return from falsehood to reality. Within the first part, there are four sections. First, the clarification of the two types of perfuming. Second, the enumeration of names and characteristics.
The three clarities are mutually dependent; the fourth is the flow of the fetters. Now, for the first: what is the meaning of this?

It means that when all Buddhas were originally in the state of ordinary beings, their minds, depending on habitual perfuming and undergoing transformation, moved involuntarily through non-awakening, manifesting as empty forms.
These "empty forms" are precisely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) of ordinary beings; they are also called...
It resembles consciousness (*vijñāna*), resembles form (*rūpa*), and resembles objects (*viṣaya*). That which resembles consciousness refers to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.

When these resembling consciousnesses arise moment by moment, they fail to understand that the dharmas resembling form and so forth are merely the mind’s fabrication of empty appearances and lack reality.
Because they do not understand this, they falsely grasp these empty appearances as real entities. At the time of such false grasping, they in turn perfuse the pure mind.
Furthermore,
regarding the initial statement that "the mind transforms according to perfuming," it means that although the essence of the single True Suchness Mind is eternally unchanging,
it inherently possesses the capacity to follow conditions. Because it has not yet attained awakening, it cannot avoid depending on perfuming.

Transformation. Because there is only the nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) and not yet the cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), non-awakening gives rise to thoughts, falsely constituting "enlightened awareness" (*vidyā-bodha*).
This enlightened awareness is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). Once ignorance moves, the three subtleties and six coarsenesses are fully present;

this is called the manifestation of empty forms, namely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are termed "semblances."
Consciousness (*vijñāna*). The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is called "resembling form," and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are called "resembling objects.

They are all said to be "resembling" because they are illusory reflections manifested by the single mind, lacking any substantial reality. Since the objects are themselves form, it need not be stated explicitly;
consciousness refers to the first six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness. These seven all lack a separate essence and arise dependent upon the mind, just as waves arise from water.

This is because of the waves. This clarifies the power of the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) to permeate and transform. Next, regarding the statement "by this, the semblance-consciousness arises moment by moment," etc.:
false attachment is merely the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); it is also called the branch-and-tip ignorance (*śākhāgra-avidyā*).

Through the superior permeating power of this ignorance, it causes the originally pure mind to be obstructed and concealed, transforming into the ground-abiding ignorance (*mūlasthāna-avidyā*) within the five turbidities.
This clarifies the power of the perfuming and transformation of ignorance (*avidyā*) at the level of the branches and subordinates.
II. Naming the Characteristics: However, the meaning of "resembling consciousness" while being non-comprehending is precisely ignorance at the stage of the fruit;

it is also termed "ignorance regarding deluded objects. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Because of delusion (*moha*) with respect to conditions. The meaning of the false attachment of what resembles consciousness is precisely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); that which is attached to...
The state of the objective realm thus becomes a delusory realm. Because ignorance (*avidyā*) perfumes the mind at the stage of fruition, it causes the mind to lack awakening;

this is precisely the ignorance of the causal stage (*bīja-kāla*), also termed the "ground-abiding ignorance" (*sthiti-bhūmi-avidyā*). Because false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) perfumes the mind, it causes the mind to undergo fluctuation; this is precisely the *karma-vijñāna*.
Because the delusory realm perfumes the mind, it causes the mind to form seeds resembling external objects; these are the semblance-consciousnesses (*pratibimba-vijñāna*).

Because the mind is perfumed, it causes the mind to become seeds that resemble consciousness. These two kinds of seeds—those resembling objects and those resembling consciousness—are collectively termed "seeds of illusory forms."
First, the meaning of "deluded consciousness that does not comprehend" is clarified: it is termed "confusion regarding the object at the time of the fruit.

This ignorance (*avidyā*) is the branch of ignorance within the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) pertaining to the realm of desire; it is also termed "delusion" (*moha*), because it fails to comprehend that objects are empty.

Among the three outflows (*āsrava*), it is the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
