The remaining afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) pertaining to the three realms are termed the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*).

Next, the meaning of the deluded attachment of what resembles consciousness is explained as being false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), namely, the afflictions of views and thoughts within the three realms.
Next, the objects grasped by that attachment are shown to constitute false objects; if the mind does not grasp them, they do not exist.

The objective realm is fundamentally empty. Next, it clarifies how delusion regarding the realm causes ignorance to reflexively permeate the pure mind, causing that pure mind to become non-enlightened;
this means that the derivative ignorance permeates the fundamental ignorance, bringing about its manifestation as active functioning.
Next, it clarifies how the false thoughts of views and afflictions reflexively permeate the pure mind, causing the entire substance of that pure mind to undergo transformation and fluctuation.

This is called "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*). This refers to the manifestation and transformation of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, which perfumes the *ālaya-vijñāna* to produce manifest activity.

Furthermore, when delusive objects perfume the mind, they immediately form seeds that appear as sense-objects (*viṣaya*), because the *ālaya-vijñāna* inherently contains the seeds of the eleven material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).
When delusive consciousness perfumes the mind, it immediately forms [seeds] that appear as consciousness itself.
The seed: this refers to the fact that within the *ālaya* are contained the seeds of the preceding seven consciousnesses as well as their associated mental factors (*caitta*).
Although there are two kinds of seeds, they share the same illusory appearance and lack any distinct substantial reality;
they are nothing other than the entirety of a single mind taken as their essence. △ Third, the mutual dependence.

However, although these factors such as ignorance (*avidyā*) at the time of fruition are said to be distinct from one another, they must be combined simultaneously in order to perfuse and give rise to a single dharma;

therefore, they act as the perfumers. Why is this? Because they are inseparable and exist in mutual dependence. If there were no semblance-consciousness, there would be no ignorance at the time of fruition;
if there were no ignorance, there would be no delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*); and if there were no delusive conceptualization, [the result] would not be established.
This is the false object. Therefore, it is only when these four factors are simultaneously combined that they can manifest as a fruit of illusory appearance.
Why is this? Because they are inseparable. Furthermore, the seeds of illusory appearance abide in ignorance during the stage of the "seed-time."
Furthermore, because empty appearances cannot manifest as a fruit independently, if there is no seed, then ignorance is likewise absent and the karma-consciousness does not exist.
If the karma-consciousness is absent, then empty appearances cannot manifest to form a fruit; thus, their own substance would not be established.
Therefore, it is only through their conjunction that empty appearances manifest as a fruit. Consequently, within these empty appearances, [the fruit] returns...
This refers to the false attachment of ignorance (*avidyā*), which resembles consciousness and resembles objects.
This explains the two types of ignorance—the fundamental and the derivative—as well as the first seven [consciousnesses] and the eighth;
whether manifest or latent, they necessarily rely upon and mutually perfuse one another. As previously stated, at the time of fruition, ignorance perfuses the mind to serve as its seed.

At that time, ignorance delusively perfumes the mind to constitute the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). While it appears as though these are perfumed and arise individually, in reality they must necessarily be in simultaneous conjunction for the meaning of "perfuming" to be established.
This is because the four characteristics, such as the semblance-consciousness (*pratibhāsajñāna*) and so forth, exist in mutual dependence and are not separate from one another.
One should know, therefore, that the perfuming that gives rise to active manifestations does not occur individually. Furthermore, there are the seeds of the empty forms of matter and mind.

It necessarily abides in dependence upon fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). It necessarily arises as the fruit of active manifestation in dependence upon the karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).

Once the fruit has been produced, it again possesses the semblance-consciousnesses of the sixth and seventh [minds]. These can permeate the mind to once again form the seeds of semblance-consciousness.
Furthermore, it possesses the semblance-objects consisting of the eleven material dharmas; these can permeate the mind to secretly form the seeds of semblance-objects.
When the ignorance at the time of the fruition, which fully possesses delusion, can further permeate the ignorance at the time of the seed,
and when the false conceptualization of grasping can further permeate the karmic consciousness, one should know that the present and the seeds mutually permeate one another.
They must also necessarily be in simultaneous conjunction; they are not separate entities. △ Fourth, the conclusion on the cycle of transmigration:
For this reason, it is explained briefly: "Because of non-awakening, there is movement," which manifests as empty forms.
Thus, the mutual generation of cause and fruit in a beginningless cycle of transmigration is called "sentient beings."
Fundamentally, there is nothing that is not non-awakening; there is nothing that is not deluded movement; there is nothing that is not a hollow manifestation.

Since the fruit gives rise to the seed, and the seed in turn gives rise to the fruit, this cycle has flowed and turned since beginningless time. How could there be even the slightest real dharma outside of the mind?

This concludes the explanation of the meaning of "non-awakening" as arising from the delusion of the True. Next, regarding the return from delusion to the True, it possesses the two meanings of awakening.

Two. First, the clarification of the meaning of the pure mind as the subject of awakening; second, the clarification of the meaning of the pure mind as self-awakening. Within the first, there are five parts: first, awakening by name;
second, awakening through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*); third, awakening resembling the ultimate; fourth, partial true awakening; and fifth, ultimate awakening.

First: Later, encountering a virtuous friend who explained to him that all phenomena are produced by the single mind, appearing as if they exist while being without reality. Having heard this teaching:
△ Second, the awakening of contemplative practice.
Practicing in accordance [with this], one gradually comes to know that all dharmas are produced from the mind and are merely empty and without reality.

△ Third, the semblance awakening, which has two parts: first, the explicit clarification of awakening regarding pervasive afflictions; second, the incidental clarification of the gradual elimination of specific afflictions. Now, the first part.
When this understanding is established, it is the time when the fruit arises and ignorance ceases. Because ignorance ceases, one no longer clings to illusory appearances as real;
this is the cessation of deluded thought and deluded objects. At that time, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is transformed and termed "non-objective wisdom" (*nirviṣaya-jñāna*).
Because one knows that external objects have no reality, ignorance ceases at the stage of fruition;
this corresponds to the initial stage of the first *śraddhā* (faith). Delusive thoughts and delusive objects cease, extending through the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

This is because within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), both the active (*pravṛtti*) and latent (*vāsanā*) aspects of delusive thoughts and delusive objects exist. The wisdom that perceives the absence of objects is the "wonderful observation" (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
Wisdom. △ Second, a concurrent clarification of the gradual elimination of specific delusions, which has two parts: first, the presentation of the characteristics of specific delusions;
second, the elucidation of the reasons for their gradual elimination. Now, the first part.
Although it is known that because the object is empty, ignorance ceases at the time of the fruit, one still perceives the existence of its empty appearance.
Existence is non-existence; its original nature is unarisen and thus now does not cease. It is solely this single mind.

Because one does not know this principle, it is also called "ignorance at the time of the child" (the causal stage) and "ignorance of delusion regarding the principle. However, it is subtler than the aforementioned ignorance of delusion regarding phenomena.
Furthermore, because those coarse [defilements] have been extinguished, it is said that at the time of the fruit, ignorance is extinguished.

Moreover, because one no longer clings to illusory appearances as real, it is said that deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is extinguished. Even seeing illusory signs and thinking there is a distinct mind—this clinging is itself a form of deluded conceptualization.

It is also called the "illusory characteristic" (*śūnyalakṣaṇa*). It is merely subtler than the former; because that coarse [characteristic] has ceased, it is said that "deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) ceases.
Furthermore, because this illusory object is grasped by subtle ignorance and deluded conceptualization, it appears as if distinct from the mind, and its various characteristics are not uniform.
This is precisely the delusive object, though it is subtler than the former. Because it is subtle, it is called a "void object.
Furthermore, because the attachment to the reality of those coarse characteristics has ceased, it is said that the delusive objects have ceased.

To still perceive the existence of illusory appearances refers to the habitual tendencies of the delusions of view within the realm of transmigration (*dhātu*), as well as the delusions of view beyond that realm;
therefore, it is also called "ignorance at the stage of the child" and "ignorance that is deluded regarding principle.

To still perceive illusory appearances means to believe there is a distinct mind, not knowing that the mind has no distinct characteristics, and to cling to illusory objects as if they were different from the mind, not knowing that [the mind is one with them].
There is no external object. These are all the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions of thought within the realms, as well as the afflictions of thought outside the realms;
therefore, they are likewise deluded thoughts and deluded objects. △ Second, explaining the reasons for their gradual elimination, which has three parts. First, using the end to verify the root.
Second, the explicit explanation of the causes for cessation; third, the application of the latter to conclude the former. Regarding the first:

according to this treatise, it is not only that the ignorance which deludes regarding phenomena ceases at the time of fruition, but the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is also partially eliminated.
If it were not eliminated portion by portion and gradually, the ignorance at the time of fruition could not be extinguished portion by portion and gradually either.
However, because these signs are subtle and difficult to manifest, I have not yet spoken of the gradual extinction of the dwelling-place (sthānabhūmi) divisions.

For now, let us explain the causes and conditions for the gradual extinction of the dwelling-place based on the extinction of ignorance regarding phenomena after [the initial awakening]. By this, one should know that from the moment a single thought-moment of cultivation is initiated, it is also capable of gradually extinguishing [ignorance].

This clarifies that within the stage of the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*), although the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) outside the realm have not yet been permanently severed, they have already been thoroughly suppressed.

Therefore, it is said that the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-ālaya-bhūmi*) is also partially eliminated. If ignorance were not eliminated even in part, by what means could the afflictions of views and thoughts be extinguished?
It is like a tree: if the root is not shaken, the branches and leaves will certainly not fall. However, their...

It is simply not mentioned because its subtlety makes it difficult to manifest. In reality, at the very moment one initiates the cultivation of the perfect contemplation within a single thought-moment, one has already perfectly subdued ignorance;
how much more so during the stage of the ten faiths! △ Second, the explicit explanation of the cause for extinction.

What is the meaning of this? It refers to two causal conditions by which the ignorance-abiding-ground (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), and so forth, gradually become attenuated.

What are these two conditions? First, because the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of objects permeates the mind, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the former ignorance-abiding-ground and the karma-consciousness are gradually eliminated.
Why is this? Wisdom is a luminous dharma; its essential nature is capable of counteracting [ignorance].

Because of ignorance. Second, because subtle ignorance and false attachments, as well as false objects, permeate the mind, even though the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) and so forth arise again, they are immediately weak and feeble, unlike those [states] previously produced by the permeation of deluded objects.
Why is this? Because the permeating factors are subtle, the resulting lack of awakening (*abodhi*) is likewise thin. For this reason, it abides...
The stages of ignorance, karmic consciousness, and so forth are gradually diminished and extinguished.
Knowing that objects are empty is the wisdom that is devoid of objective dust. This wisdom counteracts ignorance, causing it to become thin;

this is the condition for gradual extinction. That which is produced by the subtle permeation of ignorance and is consequently slight and weak is the cause of gradual extinction. The rest may be understood accordingly.
△ Third, the conclusion following the examples:

Just as this principle applies after the cessation of ignorance regarding phenomena (*vastu*), one should know that at the very moment of first initiating cultivation, the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is partially extinguished. Because it is extinguished part by part, the wisdom that arises is also partial.
Because the increasing illumination is divided [into stages], there is no separate cessation of delusion regarding phenomena at the time of attaining the fruit.
At the moment one first initiates cultivation, it is said that one enters the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) from the level of names (*nāman*).

Within this stage of contemplative practice, one is also able to know that the object is empty; this wisdom that knows the emptiness of the object serves as the antidote to ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore...

Once one knows that objects are empty, one no longer clings to these empty forms as being real. At that time, because coarse perceptions and coarse objects have been subdued, they no longer permeate the mind;
there remains only the permeation of subtle ignorance (*avidyā*) and its clinging to emptiness, along with the permeation of empty objects.
How could the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) not be partially extinguished? Furthermore, if the ground of abiding ignorance were not partially extinguished...
Extinction. By what means could ignorance be extinguished spontaneously at the time of fruition so as to attain Perfect Faith? △ Fourth Division:
True Awakening.
Following the extinction of the ignorance of deluded phenomena, because the karmic consciousness and the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) gradually thin out, that which arises is empty...

The resulting retribution likewise becomes increasingly subtle and refined, differing from what preceded. For this reason, the semblance-consciousness (*vijñapti*) becomes progressively clearer and sharper;
the semblances of dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) no longer cause delusion to arise in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Because the internal consciousnesses that produce external objects such as forms are both subtle and sharp, wisdom devoid of objects becomes doubly luminous, while ignorance and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) become extremely thin, continuing to permeate the mind.
Furthermore, it causes the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the karma-consciousness within the ground-abiding ignorance (*avidyā-sthiti-bhūmi*) to gradually tend toward exhaustion.

The wisdom that perceives the absence of objective dust (*nirviṣaya-jñāna*) becomes doubly clear. Thus, through the successive perfuming of each thought-moment, as the ground-abiding ignorance approaches its end, the wisdom that perceives the absence of objective dust is able to know that the nature of the essence of those illusory fruit-retributions is non-existent; they have been so from the very beginning.
That which arises now has no cessation; it is solely the essence of the one mind, free from discrimination, because there are no phenomena external to the mind alone.
This wisdom is precisely the unimpeded Vajra-wisdom.

The extinction of the ignorance of deluded phenomena specifically refers to the simultaneous exhaustion of both the active and latent afflictions (*kleśa*) regarding the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kāma*) within the three realms during the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
From this point on, the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) and the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) gradually thin out;

this is the aspect of severing delusions stage by stage throughout the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) up to the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*). Consequently, the resulting illusory retributions that arise also become progressively lighter and more subtle; this is the reality.

This refers to the characteristics of the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) existing within the Buddha-land; it differs from the three realms mentioned previously because it is not of the nature of segmented birth-and-death (*āntarābhava-jarāmaraṇa*).
"Gradually tending toward exhaustion" refers to the stage of the tenth bhūmi. "About to be exhausted" refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

"The unimpeded diamond-wisdom" refers to the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the wondrous enlightenment following the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*). △ Five: Ultimate Realization.

Upon the realization of this wisdom, it in turn perfumes the mind. Because the mind is perfumed by this clear wisdom, the habitual tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*) are extinguished in that very instant.
Since ignorance is exhausted, the seeds and habitual tendencies of the defiled dharmas of the *karma-vijñāna* likewise follow suit and cease.
It is destroyed. Therefore, the meaning of the scriptural statement, "When that ground is destroyed, those [seeds] are also destroyed accordingly," is precisely this.
"That ground" refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance; "those" refers to the seeds of defiled phenomena within the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
This refers to the fact that after the adamantine path (*vajra-mārga*), the maturation (*vipāka*) becomes empty. All of the above clarifies the meaning of the pure mind as the subject of awakening.
△ Next, the meaning of the pure mind’s self-awakening is explained.
Because the seeds and habitual tendencies are destroyed, the illusory forms are forever extinguished. Because the illusory forms are extinguished, the essence of the mind is quiescently luminous;

this is called the realization of the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Why is this? Because there is no distinct phenomenon that serves as the means of realization, it is itself quiescent luminosity. There is none.
The distinction between the subject that realizes and the object realized is termed non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Why is this?

Because apart from this wisdom, there is no separate suchness (*tathatā*) to be conceptualized. This is precisely the mind manifesting as wisdom; wisdom is the function of the mind, and the mind is the essence of wisdom.
Since essence and function are a single dharma whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is non-dual, it is called the realization of the essential nature.
Non-conceptual wisdom is precisely the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). The rest may be understood accordingly.
The above concludes the extensive explanation based on cultivation. △ Third, the conclusion by means of analogies.

It is like still water: its internal illumination and its moistening are distinct in meaning, yet it remains eternally profound and one. Why is this? Because illumination moistens and moistening illuminates; the mind is likewise thus.
Its tranquility and illumination are divided in meaning, yet their essence is harmonious and non-dual. Why is this? Because illumination is tranquility and tranquility is illumination.
Illumination in tranquility accords with the essence, while tranquility in illumination accords with function. This illumination of its own essence is called awakening within the pure mind.
The essence illuminates itself, which is precisely what is called the pure mind’s self-awakening; therefore, it is said that these two meanings constitute a single essence.
This takes non-conceptual wisdom as awakening. Since time immemorial, this pure mind has possessed the nature of this wisdom, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, the pure mind is taken as the Buddha-nature. This explains that, with respect to the Wisdom-Buddha, the pure mind is clarified as the Buddha-nature.
"Like water being still" first presents a metaphor for the mind; "is also like this" next applies the dharma to correspond [to the metaphor].
"The pure mind, from its origin... concludes by establishing that the pure mind is named the Buddha-nature. [This section extends] from the question, "As for the Wisdom-Buddha," up to this point.

This concludes the first section of the second part, which distinguishes the Buddha-nature in terms of awakening, specifically the wisdom-Buddha-nature. II. Distinguishing the Retribution and Response Buddha-natures:
Furthermore, this essence of the pure mind is fully endowed with the nature of merit and the nature of skillful application; it is moreover pure.
Perfumed by karma, these give rise to the two Buddhas of retribution and response; therefore, this mind is taken as the Buddha-nature.
The nature of merit and virtue gives rise to the Buddha of retribution, which is common to both self-enjoyment and other-enjoyment.

The nature of skillful application gives rise to the Buddha of response, who possesses both superior and inferior forms and appearances. All of these arise from being perfumed by pure karma. This Buddha-nature of retribution and response is not...
This is external to the pure mind. △ Third, distinguishing the Buddha-nature that transcends obstacles:
Furthermore, because non-awakening has ceased, the mind is taken as awakening; because the meaning of movement has subsided, the mind is said to be unmoving;
because delusive appearances have dissolved, the mind is said to be signless. Yet the essence of this mind is neither awakening nor non-awakening, neither moving nor unmoving.
It is neither with marks nor without marks. Nevertheless, because non-awakening has been extinguished, the mind is spoken of as awakening; this also presents no contradiction.

This discussion of awakening is based on the essential nature of the mind as it emerges from obstacles through counteractive measures; it does not rely upon the functional activity of wisdom as awakening.
Although it is neither awakening nor non-awakening, because non-awakening is extinguished, it does not preclude speaking of awakening.
This Buddha-nature of the Dharmakāya at the stage of fruition is nothing other than the pure mind. △ Fourth, the discernment of the equal Buddha-nature.

Furthermore, although the pure mind is fundamentally without non-awakening, it is described as "fundamental awakening"; although it is fundamentally without movement or change, it is described as "fundamental stillness";
and although it is fundamentally without illusory characteristics, it is described as "fundamentally equal. Nevertheless, the essence of this mind is neither awakening nor non-awakening.
It is neither moving nor non-moving; it is neither with marks nor without marks. Nevertheless, because there was originally no non-enlightenment, it is called "original enlightenment" (*mūla-bodhi*);
thus, there is no error. This explains that the substance of the mind is the Tathāgata-as-suchness (*tathatā-buddha*) by way of the non-duality of ordinary beings and sages;
it does not concern the functional aspect of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*) which is inherently possessed by the substance of the mind.
Although it is neither awakening nor non-awakening, because there is fundamentally no non-awakening, it is nonetheless not precluded from being called "original awakening" (*mūla-bodhi*).
This Dharma-body of the Buddha within the bonds of affliction, the Buddha-nature, is non-dual for both ordinary beings and sages; it is simply the one pure mind.

The above constitutes the extensive analysis of Buddha-nature, specifically the second section concerning its distinction through awakening. △ Third, the resolution of remaining doubts, in four parts.

First, the explanation dispels the doubt regarding the attachment to inherent nature and the neglect of cultivation; second, the explanation dispels the doubt regarding the existence of fundamental non-enlightenment; third, the explanation dispels the doubt regarding spontaneous causes and conditions;
fourth, the explanation dispels the doubt regarding ignorance and the nature of the mind. Now, the first.
Question: If one is called a Buddha based on the fact that there is originally no lack of awakening, then ordinary beings are already Buddhas; what need is there for the cultivation of the path?
Answer: If one considers the equality of the essence of mind, then there is neither cultivation nor non-cultivation, neither accomplishment nor non-accomplishment.
Furthermore, there is neither awakening nor non-awakening; it is only for the sake of clarifying the Buddha of Suchness (tathatā) that we provisionally speak of "awakening" in contrast [to it].
Moreover, if one relies on the equality of the essence of mind (citta-tattva), there is no difference between sentient beings and all Buddhas regarding this essence of mind.
Thus, a verse in a sutra says: "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Nevertheless, the nature of the mind is the dharma of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
Because the nature of the dharmas of the realms is inherently indestructible, they are both eternally equal and eternally distinct.

Because they are eternally equal, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three—are without distinction. Because they are eternally distinct, those who transmigrate through the five paths are designated as "sentient beings."
To turn back the flow and exhaust the source is what is called "Buddha. Because this meaning of equality exists, there is neither Buddha nor sentient being.
Yet, because of these distinctions within dependent origination, sentient beings must cultivate the path.
This raises a doubt based on the preceding meaning of the equal *dharmakāya*.

In the response, it is first clarified that when explaining "awakening" (*bodhi*) through the lens of correspondence, the Tathāgata-as-such (*tathatā-buddha*) is merely manifested through cultivation; it is not produced by cultivation.

Next, it clarifies that equality does not obstruct differentiation. It is precisely because these two meanings—equality and differentiation—exist that the mind-nature (*cittatā*) is established as having conditions.
This is the Dharma-gate of the Arising of the Dharmadhātu. In terms of equality, the six are eternally identical; in terms of differentiation, the identical is eternally six.
Because one knows equality, one does not give rise to despondency; because one knows differentiation, one does not give rise to arrogance.
△ Second, the explanation of the doubt regarding the original non-awakening.
Question: How can it be known that the substance of the mind is fundamentally non-awakened? Answer:

If the substance of the mind were fundamentally awakened, then when a sage realizes the pure mind, he would no longer be awakened; and when an ordinary person has not yet realized it, he should already be awakened.

Since there is no witness who is not in a state of non-awakening, and one who has not yet realized [this] cannot be called awakened, we know with certainty that the essence of the mind is fundamentally devoid of non-awakening.
Question: Sages attain the pure self-realized mind by extinguishing non-awakening. If non-awakening does not exist, how can you speak of its extinction?
Furthermore, if there were no non-awakening, there would be no sentient beings. Answer: This has already been fully explained previously.
The essence of the mind is equal, being neither ordinary nor sagely; therefore, it is said that fundamentally there is no non-awakening (*abodhi*).

Yet, because the mind-nature’s dependent origination is not non-existent, there is cessation, there is realization, and there are the ordinary and the sagely. Furthermore, the existence of this dependent origination is such that existence is itself non-existence;

thus, it is said that fundamentally there is no non-awakening, and now too there is no non-awakening. Nevertheless, it is not that [dependent origination] does not exist; hence it is said that there is cessation and there is realization.
There are both ordinary beings and sages. However, when one realizes that by following the functional application one enters the essence, there is no lack of awakening.

Thus, it can be verified that the substance of the mind fundamentally has no lack of awakening; it is only because ordinary beings oppose its function and perceive the single essence as being diverse that they are unable to realize and know the essence of equality.
The previous question asked how one knows that this true mind is not non-awakening (*abodhi*), as it was assumed that the entire substance of the true mind is non-awakening;
therefore, the answer was given that when ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases, the true mind should likewise cease to exist.

This present question asks how one can know that the essence of the mind is fundamentally devoid of non-awakening, as it was assumed that the true mind possesses both awakening and non-awakening as two distinct entities.
Since both [the awakened and unawakened] exist within the substance, he answers by stating that while the Sage corresponds to non-awakening, the ordinary person corresponds to awakening.
Next, he raises another question, intending to say: since the Sage has already extinguished non-awakening, there should be no principle for non-awakening to arise again.

However, if non-awakening did not exist within the causal state (*hetu*), why would it need to be said that it is "extinguished"? Furthermore, if non-awakening were absent, how could one be called a "sentient being" (*sattva*)?

In the response, there are three successive clarifications of the doubt. The first clarifies that equality is spoken of in terms of the essence of mind, while differentiation is spoken of in terms of dependent origination.
The second clarifies that within dependent origination alone, both the meanings of equality and differentiation are simultaneously present.
The third clarifies the reason for differentiation within equality: it arises from the two functions of opposition and compliance.
The essence is truly equal. △ Third, resolving doubts regarding natural causes and conditions. Question:
When the mind manifests as wisdom, is it because ignorance has been exhausted that this nature is inherently wisdom, or is there yet another distinct cause and condition?
Answer: While this mind is in a state of defilement, it fundamentally possesses the two natures of merit and wisdom; they are not lacking in the slightest.
There is one Dharma that is no different from the Buddha; however, because it is shrouded by defiled dharmas of ignorance, its manifest function cannot be realized.
Later, through being perfumed by the two kinds of pure karma—merit and wisdom—all defiled dharmas are completely exhausted.

At the moment this pure karma eliminates defilement, it is able to manifest that twofold nature and bring about its functional activity, namely: the primary marks and secondary signs (laksana and vyañjana), as well as all the environments and rewards (āśraya and vipāka).

Regarding "wisdom" and so forth: the essence of wisdom is the inherent capacity of the true mind’s nature to illuminate; the function of wisdom is formed through conditioning. The question contains both types of conceptualization:
it naturally conceives of wisdom as being spontaneous (*svabhāva*), and it separately conceives of it as arising from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
In the answer, there are two successive refutations of both positions. The first states that while the two natures of merit and wisdom are inherently present, they are not [spontaneous].
If it were due to causes and conditions, being obscured by defilements and thus unmanifest would mean it is not spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Next, it says it is perfumed by two kinds of pure karma;
this means it is not spontaneous. That these two natures manifest and bring about functional efficacy means it is not merely due to causes and conditions.

Its essence is the capacity for the illumination of nature, while its function is established through perfuming. This may be called "the entirety of nature giving rise to cultivation" and "the entirety of cultivation residing in nature," transcending all [dualistic extremes].
This is mere conceptual proliferation. △ Fourth, resolving the doubt regarding the nature of the mind in ignorance.
Question: Since the mind manifests as wisdom, the mind is taken as the Buddha-nature; yet since the mind gives rise to non-awakening, it should likewise be taken as the nature of ignorance.
Answer: If one discusses this from the perspective of the meaning of *dharmatā*, it may indeed be considered the nature of ignorance.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The nature of clarity and ignorance is non-dual; this non-dual nature is the true nature.
Wisdom is like water, and ignorance is like ice. Water has moisture as its nature, and ice also has moisture as its nature. If...
Knowing that the nature of moisture is non-dual, one realizes that water and ice merely possess provisional names, while moisture alone is the true nature.
However, because the conventional usage of the term "water" is more prevalent, it is sufficient to speak simply of "the moisture of water"; why must one necessarily say "the moisture of ice"?

Furthermore, once one knows that the nature of ice is fundamentally moisture, one will certainly not seek water apart from ice, nor will one ever cling to ice as being [something other than moisture].
[This concludes the section on] Water. The above concludes the explanation of *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature).
△ Fourth, the explanation of *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body). Question: Why is this mind designated as the *dharmakāya*? Answer: "Dharma" (*dharma*) has the meaning of functional capacity;
"body" (*kāya*) has the meaning of a basis or support. Because the essence of this mind possesses the function of following along with defilement, it serves as the basis for all defiled phenomena.

It is that which is perfumed. Because this mind follows along with defilement, it is able to sustain the fragrance of perfuming; furthermore, it is able to manifest defiled phenomena based upon that perfuming.

Thus, the two functional capacities of this mind—its ability to sustain and its ability to manifest—as well as the two types of defiled phenomena sustained and manifested, all depend upon this single mind for their establishment. They are neither identical to nor different from the mind.

Therefore, this mind is named the *dharmakāya*. Because its capacity to sustain [phenomena] is in union with the phenomena it sustains, it is called the *ālayavijñāna* of the causal stage (*bījakāla*).
Because its capacity to manifest phenomena through perfuming is in union with the appearances thus manifested, it is called the *ālayavijñāna* of retribution (*vipākaphala*).
These two consciousnesses are identical in essence but differ in function.
Furthermore, within this ālayavijñāna there are two divisions: first, the defiled division, which consists of the characteristics of karma and its retribution;
second, the pure division, which consists of the nature of mind (cittatva) and the purifying dharmas that act as perfumers—this is termed the pure division.

Because the nature of defilement is itself the nature of purity and there is no other distinct dharma, and because this mind-nature serves as the basis for those defiled phenomena that are the fruits of karma, it is said that birth-and-death (saṃsāra) relies upon the Tathāgatagarbha; this is precisely the Dharmakāyagarbha.

Furthermore, although this essence of mind is shrouded by immeasurable defiled dharmas, it nonetheless fully possesses untainted (anāsrava) qualities of nature exceeding the sands of the Ganges in number.
Because it is perfumed by immeasurable pure karmas, these pure natures are able to sustain the latent impressions (vāsanā) of that perfuming;
moreover, they can manifest the functional power of the Buddhas' merits based upon that perfuming. That is to say:
These sands-of-the-Ganges-like qualities of inherent purity, as well as the two functional capacities of sustaining and manifesting,

along with the two pure functions of that which is sustained and that which is manifested, all depend upon this single mind for their establishment. Because they are neither identical to nor different from the mind,
this mind is named the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
In the response, first the *dharmakāya* conforming to defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is clarified;

subsequently, within the clarification of the *dharmakāya* conforming to purity (*vyavadāna*), both the defiled and pure aspects are fully explained as being fundamentally non-dual in their nature. This serves to conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one.

Both defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭadharma*) and pure phenomena (*viśuddhadharma*) are termed "Dharma" because they both possess functional efficacy. They are both termed "body" (*kāya*) because they both serve as a basis of support (*āśraya*). Because...
This nature of mind possesses two functional capacities—those of maintaining and manifesting—as well as the two categories of phenomena maintained and manifested, which are the defiled and the pure.

Because these are neither identical to nor different from the mind, that which maintains is the seeds of the *karmic-consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*), and that which manifests is the active functioning (*pravṛtti*) of the *karmic-consciousness*.

That which is maintained consists of the seeds of defiled phenomena, and that which is manifested consists of the active functioning of defiled phenomena. [The seeds... *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "種不" [seeds not...]. The translation reflects the available portion of the passage.)*
Manifestation is not the seed; the agent is not the object, and the object is not the agent; therefore, they are said to be not one. Apart from the mind there is no seed;
apart from the mind there is no manifestation; apart from the mind there is no agent; apart from the mind there is no object; therefore, they are said to be not different.
Since all phenomena are mind, the mind is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). That which is capable of sustaining the vital energies (*vāyu*) that are sustained is the seed;
therefore, it is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* at the stage of the seed. "Vital energy" refers to the category of vital energies.

That which is capable of manifesting the appearances (*nimitta*) that are manifested is the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*); therefore, it is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* as karmic fruition. As for these appearances...

This refers to their characteristics. Active manifestations also infuse seeds, and seeds also infuse active manifestations. From the perspective of infusing active manifestations, they are termed "seeds";
from the perspective of infusing seeds, they are termed "active manifestations. Therefore, it is said that their substance is one while their functions differ.
The above explanation has merely clarified the *dharmakāya* in relation to the aspect of defilement (*saṃkleśa*).

However, within the *ālayavijñāna*, it not only contains the defiled portion but also fully contains the pure portion. This is because the two natures of defilement and purity are not distinct dharmas; the nature of defilement is itself the nature of purity.
It is only when one is deluded that it becomes the basis for the defiled phenomena of karma and its fruits, falsely giving rise to the two types of death (*dvividha-maraṇa*).
At the time of awakening, the dharmas of the untainted nature and its meritorious qualities are manifested; the pure functions are fully perfected.
The mutual perfuming between the seeds and manifestations of the pure dharmas may be understood by analogy with what preceded. △ Fifth, the explanation of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Question: For what reason is this mind further called the *tathāgatagarbha*? Answer: There are three meanings. First, that which can contain is called a "store" (*garbha*).
Second, that which is contained is called a "store. Third, that which can produce is called a "store.
Regarding that which can contain, there are two kinds: first, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata’s resultant virtue; second, the pure mind of the sentient being’s inherent virtue.
Furthermore, it can encompass both the two natures of defilement and purity, as well as the two phenomena of defilement and purity, without any obstruction;

therefore, it is said that its capacity to "contain" (zàng) is called a "treasury" (zàng). The essence of this treasury is equality, which is termed "Suchness" (rú); this equal dependent origination is designated as "coming" (lái).

This is what constitutes the "Tathāgatagarbha" (the Treasury of the Thus-Come One) as the "container. Second, regarding the "treasury" as that which is "contained," this refers to this very True Mind.

Because it is concealed and hidden by the "egg-shell" (kośa) of ignorance, it is called the "concealed" (*saṃcita*). Its essence is undifferentiated and signless, which is termed "Suchness" (*tathatā*);
its essence is endowed with the two functions of defilement and purity, which is designated as "coming" (*āgata*). Therefore, that which is concealed is called the "Concealed.
Third, regarding that which is called the "Concealed" because it can produce: just as a woman’s womb (*garbha*) can give birth to a child, so too does this mind.

This is so because its essence possesses the functional capacity for both defiled and pure natures; thus, by the power of these two types of perfuming—defiled and pure—it is able to produce mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Furthermore, another sutra asks: "The nature of the mind is one; how can it produce various kinds of karmic retributions? Moreover, another sutra states: "All..."
The Buddha, the Perfectly All-Knowing One, arises from the ocean of mental conceptions; therefore, the equality of defilement and purity is termed "Suchness" (Tathatā).
That which can give rise to defilement and purity is designated as "Coming" (Āgata); thus it is said that that which can give rise [to them] is called the Tathāgatagarbha.

The meanings of "store" (*ālaya*) include that which stores, that which is stored, and that which gives rise [to phenomena]. "That which stores" refers to both the state of being bound in affliction (*saṃkliṣṭa*) and the state of being free from them (*niḥkleśa*).
"That which is stored" refers solely to the state of being bound in affliction. "That which gives rise" refers directly to the single thought-moment of the present.
The text is easy to understand. △ Sixth, the explanation of the *dharmadhātu*. Question:
Why is the pure mind further named the *dharmadhātu*? Answer: "Dharma" (*dharma*) refers to its being *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena);
"realm" (*dhātu*) refers to its specific character (*gotra*). Because this essence of mind inherently possesses all phenomena by its very nature, it is called the *dharmadhātu*.
△ Seventh, the explanation of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
Question: Why is this pure mind designated as *dharmatā*? Answer: "Dharma" refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
"Tā" (nature) has the meaning of "distinct essence. Because this pure mind possesses a distinct nature, it is able to serve as the essence for all phenomena.

Furthermore, "nature" (xing) signifies the meaning of being substantially real and unchanging. Since all phenomena take this mind as their substance, the characteristics of these various phenomena inherently undergo arising and ceasing;
therefore, they are termed "illusory. This mind, however, is real, unchanging, and non-perishing; therefore, it is termed the "Dharma-nature" (dharmatā).

The first explanation concerns the nature of differentiation, wherein the unchanging follows along with conditions; the subsequent explanation concerns the nature of reality, wherein that which follows along with conditions remains unchanging. △ Third, the conclusion.
The remaining infinite names, such as "the reality-limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*) and "the true mark" (*lakṣaṇa*), cannot be explained in detail. The explanation of the names and meanings is now complete.
"Reality" (*bhūta*) means that which is real; "limit" (*koṭi*) means the boundary. There are no phenomena external to the mind; phenomena are solely the mind, and there is no boundary beyond it.
Therefore, it is called the "Limit of Reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*). Because it is free from deluded conceptualization, it is called the "True Aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The term "etc.
includes other designations such as the abiding of dharmas in their own positions, the Middle Way and true principle, the single reality of the mind, and so forth.

△ Third, the discernment of the essence and characteristics, in two parts: first, the brief indication by marking the headings; second, the detailed explanation according to those headings.
Now, for the first part: next, the presentation of the essence and characteristics. Regarding what is called "essence and characteristics," there are therein three further distinctions:
first, citing the transcendence of marks to clarify the pure mind; second, citing neither identity nor difference to discuss the *dharmatā*; third, citing the two kinds of *tathatā*.

The *ālayavijñāna* is used to distinguish *tathatā*. Although there are three distinct types, they collectively only clarify the essential nature and characteristics of this pure mind (*viśuddha-citta*).
Furthermore, the phrase "there are three distinctions" and so forth serves as a topical outline; it collectively clarifies that this specific sentence is a brief indication. Someone may ask:
With what intention are these three distinctions used to clarify the essential nature of the pure mind? The answer is: The essential nature of the pure mind cannot be expressed in words.
Because all marks are themselves non-marks, it is clarified as being free from marks. If one reckons that there are marks to be abandoned, then it would not be "not different" [from them].
If one reckons that the marks are identical to the mind, then it would not be "not one. Now, it is said to be neither one nor...

"Different" means being free from the characteristics of identity and difference. However, although one is free from the characteristics of identity and difference, one must not again conceptualize a characteristic of "neither identical nor different.
One must know that the pure mind is neither identical nor different; yet, identity is the pure mind and difference is also the pure mind.
In terms of identity, it is the meaning of emptiness as it truly is; in terms of difference, it is the [phenomenon] as it truly is.
This is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). By seeking it through these three meanings, one may perhaps comprehend the essential nature of the pure mind.
Part Two: Extensive Explanation According to the Sections (Three). First: Citing the absence of characteristics to clarify the pure mind. Second:
Citing neither identity nor difference to discuss the *dharmatā*. Third: Citing the two kinds of *tathāgatagarbha* to distinguish *tathatā*. In the first [section], there are two parts.
First, the correct elucidation of the pure mind as free from marks; second, the skillful demonstration of the expedient means for entering [the path] in accordance [with it]. Now, for the first:
regarding the clarification of being free from marks, this mind is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the *tathatā*-mind.

Its self-nature is perfectly interfused, its essence is fully endowed with great function, and it is known only by the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana-jñāna*); it cannot be fathomed by the measures of ordinary consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that "the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases. It cannot be named by names, nor can it be characterized by characteristics.
Why? Because the essence of the mind is detached from names and characteristics. Since its essence is detached from names, one cannot employ names to explain that essence;
since the mind is devoid of characteristics, one cannot rely on characteristics to discern that mind. Thus, now, wishing to...

To discuss its essential nature and characteristics is indeed difficult; one can only describe the aspect of what it is free from, thereby attuning oneself through the reversal of those characteristics and their cessation.
That is to say, this mind, from the very beginning, is free from all characteristics, being equal and quiescent.
It is neither with marks nor without marks; neither not with marks nor not without marks; neither both with and without marks nor neither with nor without marks.
It is neither past, present, nor future; neither superior, middling, nor inferior; neither that nor this; neither still nor chaotic; neither defiled nor pure;
neither eternal nor annihilated; neither light nor dark; and it is free from all fourfold conceptual categories (*catuskoṭi*) such as oneness and difference.
In summary, it refers even to those dharmas that are neither expressible nor conceivable, yet they are also not dharmas that are inexpressible or inconceivable.
Why is this? Because that which is inexpressible and inconceivable arises in contrast to the expressible and conceivable;

it is not a dharma that exists by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, it is not the pure mind. Therefore, one should simply know all that is expressible, conceivable, and inexpressible.
Phenomena such as "unthinkability" and so forth are all not the pure mind itself; they are merely illusory appearances manifested by the pure mind.
Yet these illusory appearances each lack inherent reality. What exists is not existence. Even the appearance of non-existence cannot be grasped. Why is this?
Because that which has no fundamental existence does not exist. If there is no fundamental existence, how could there be the characteristic of non-existence?
Therefore, one should know that the essence of the pure mind cannot be known through conceptualization or cognitive objects, nor can it be reached by verbal expression.
Why is this? Because there is not a single dharma outside of the pure mind. If there is no dharma outside the mind, who else could there be to engage in conceptualization?
Can this mind be spoken of? Therefore, one should know that all things capable of cognizing or speaking are merely existing as false and unreal;
when examined in reality, they do not exist. Since the cognizer is not real, how could the object of cognition be real?
Because both the cognizer and the cognized are entirely unreal, the pure mind is a real dharma; therefore, it is not [affected by them].

Objects of cognition are that which are taken as conditions for mental engagement. For example, the eye cannot see itself; it is only by means of another eye external to this one that this eye can be seen.
In that case, there would be both a self-eye and an other-eye. The mind is not like this; it is simply suchness (*tathatā*).

Since there is no phenomenon outside of suchness, and furthermore, the pure mind does not engage in self-discrimination, how could there be anything capable of discriminating and grasping this mind? And yet, all...
Those who deludedly discriminate regarding their own pure mind are like foolish people who, with eyes wide open,
search for their own eyes and further claim that various appearances are their own eyes, yet ultimately fail to know the location of their own eyes. Therefore,
one should know that the so-called "subjective perceiver" and "objective perceived" are merely one's own pure mind, permeated by beginningless false conceptualization.
Therefore, being unable to know its own nature, it gives rise to false discrimination.

It establishes the appearance of a pure mind outside of its own mind, and then, by means of deluded thought, grasps that appearance, taking it to be the pure mind. To speak of the reality of the matter, the appearance thus grasped is precisely the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*); it is truly not the pure mind.

Since its self-nature is perfectly interfused, it cannot be grasped through various characteristics. Since its essence is replete with great function, it cannot be sought through quiescent extinction.
The characteristics to be abandoned refer to the four propositions and the hundred negations. The characteristic of reversal refers to seeking the source by following the current.
The characteristic of cessation refers to stilling the waves to obtain the water. The eye cannot see itself; yet there is another eye that can.

When seeing my eyes, the mind does not know itself; nor can any other mind know my mind. For all that belongs to spatial directions and formal characteristics is grasped through delusive thought (*vikalpa*).
Even if one further attempts to conceive of something without spatial direction or formal characteristic as the characteristic of the pure mind, this too is delusive thought.
What is grasped in either case does not transcend the realm of consciousness and emotion (*vijñāna*).

The characteristics of conceptual discrimination are certainly not the essence of the pure mind; this is why [the text says so]. The remaining passages are easy to understand. △ Second, the skillful demonstration of the expedient means for entering in accordance [with reality].
Question: Since the substance of the pure mind cannot be conceptually discriminated, how can sentient beings, such as ourselves, accord with it?

And yet one is able to enter [it]. The answer is: If one knows that the essence of all false thoughts and discriminations is the pure mind, and understands that they are said to be contrary to principle only because discrimination does not cease—having gained this knowledge, one should contemplate that all phenomena and all conditioned thoughts exist and yet are non-existent.
Therefore, it is called "conformity. If, through long-term cultivation, one becomes free from discrimination, it is called [enlightenment].

To "attain entry" means to realize the true suchness (tathatā) by being detached from all marks. This concludes the first section, which clarifies detachment from marks in order to distinguish the essential nature.
To know that the essence of all deluded thoughts and discriminations is the pure mind is like knowing that something is water; it is simply—

Because conceptual discrimination does not cease, it is said to be contrary to principle (*yukti*). This is, for example, like saying that waves which do not cease are contrary to the nature of water’s stillness.
Having understood this, one initiates contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) from names and designations. One should contemplate all phenomena as being thus.

From this contemplative practice, one enters the stage of semblance (*pratirūpa*). By practicing for a long time, if one becomes free from conceptual discrimination and so forth, [one attains the true nature].
This is because one enters the stage of semblance through resemblance; the essentials of the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are entirely contained herein.
△ Second, citing non-identity and non-difference to discuss the Dharma-nature.
Next, to clarify the state of being neither identical nor different in order to distinguish its essential nature:

although it has been explained above that the pure mind is free from all conceptualizing minds and the characteristics of objective realms, these various characteristics are nonetheless not different from the pure mind. Why is this so?
Although the substance of this mind is equal, it inherently possesses the two functions of defilement and purity.
Furthermore, due to the power of the habitual perfuming of beginningless ignorance and deluded thoughts, the defiled function of the mind’s substance manifests based upon that perfuming.

These illusory appearances have no substantiality and are nothing other than the pure mind; therefore, it is said they are not different. Yet, they are also not identical. Why? Because of the pure mind’s...
Although the substance possesses both defiled and pure functions, it lacks any characteristics of dualistic differentiation; it is of a single flavor and equal.
These various differences in illusory appearances merely manifest according to the power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Yet, while these illusory appearances arise and perish, the substance of the pure mind is eternally without arising or ceasing, constant and unchanging. Therefore, they are said not to be one. This clarifies the second point: non-identity.

Having finished distinguishing the essence and its characteristics through non-difference, first, clarifying non-difference means not seeking a pure mind apart from its manifestations. It is like when water in its entirety forms waves;
thus, the waves in their entirety are simply water. Next, clarifying non-identity means not reckoning differentiated characteristics as being the pure mind.
The mind is like waves: although they arise and perish, one cannot say that the water has arising and perishing.
△ Third, citing two kinds of Tathāgatagarbha to distinguish the two aspects of True Suchness (Tathatā). First, clarifying the meaning of emptiness; second, clarifying the meaning of non-emptiness.
Although it is said there are two kinds of Tathāgatagarbha, they are in fact a single entity possessing two meanings. This is because when it follows conditions, it is precisely [non-empty].
Because of transformation, the nature of the dharmas within the ten realms—whether defiled or pure—is inherently non-existent; this is termed the "empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Because it is unchanging yet capable of following conditions, it fully possesses the natures and characteristics of both the defiled and the pure;

their identity and difference are inconceivable, and thus it is termed the "non-empty Tathāgatagarbha. Its essence is truly neither empty nor non-empty; therefore, it can simultaneously illuminate both emptiness and non-emptiness.
The first section has two parts: first, the explicit clarification of emptiness; second, the resolution of doubts through question and answer. Now, for the first part:
next, the third section clarifies the two kinds of *tathāgatagarbha* to distinguish their essential characteristics. First, it clarifies the empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

For what reason is it called "emptiness"? Because although this mind-nature establishes through dependent origination phenomena such as saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, or those that are contrary and compliant, the essence of the mind remains equal and sublime, transcending the marks of defilement and purity.
Not only is the self-nature of the mind's essence equal, but the phenomena of defilement and purity that arise from it are likewise non-existent by nature. It is like looking at a cloth...
The rabbit. The substance of the rabbit is non-existent; it only appears as a rabbit due to the power of illusion. The rabbit that appears exists yet is not existent. The mind is also like this:
because it is perfumed by the illusory power of the two types of karma—defiled and pure—it appears as the two phenomena of defilement and purity.
If one regards those two phenomena from the perspective of the mind, the phenomena are not existent. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is precisely birth and death; non-cycling is *nirvāṇa*. Both birth and death and *nirvāṇa* are equally unapprehendable.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are like an illusion, even up to Great Parinirvāṇa being like an illusion.
If there were any phenomenon that transcended *nirvāṇa*, I would likewise say that it is like an illusion. Moreover, a sutra states: "There is no *nirvāṇa* at all; nothing exists..."
The Buddha is *nirvāṇa*; there is no Buddha apart from *nirvāṇa*. It is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened, and from both existence and non-existence;
it is entirely free from these two. These scriptural passages all rely upon the equality of the essence of mind to dissolve the dual functions of defilement and purity.
Since the nature of mind is thus quiescent, the essence of mind is empty and pure. For this reason, the essence of this mind is called "empty-like" (*śūnyatā*).
The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) does not mean that the essence of mind is empty and non-existent.
By means of the impartial mind, one realizes the phenomena of differentiation; there exists only the essence of impartiality, while from the beginning there is no reality of differentiation.
This is what is called "emptiness. It is as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "One is not, and all are not," regarding the ten realms.
It is neither both nor neither; it is simply emptiness. △ Second, the fivefold interrogation and response to dispel doubts: First, dispelling the doubt that sentient beings currently exist.

Second, dispelling the doubt regarding the cause of delusion and falsehood. Third, dispelling the doubt that ignorance has a substantial essence. Fourth, dispelling the doubt that the perfuming agent constitutes the essence.
Fifth, dispelling the doubt regarding the identity or difference between cause and effect. Now, the first.

Question: The Buddhas have realized the pure mind through their essential nature (*dharmatā*). Because the essence of the mind is equal, the Buddhas employ it while remaining eternally quiescent, and thus it is said to be non-existent.
Since sentient beings have not yet realized this principle, the distinctions of the six realms currently exist; how can it be said that they do not exist? Answer:

If even true wisdom and true illumination are said to be empty when their very functioning is eternally quiescent, how much more so is this the case for delusion, darkness, and false conceptualization?
Seeing what could it not exist? Existence is itself non-existence.
△ Second, dispelling the doubt regarding the cause of delusion and confusion.
Question: Since you say it does not exist, how can this delusion and confusion arise? Answer: Having realized that it does not exist, yet one deludes...
Seeing that there is existence, why should one fail to attain freedom from delusion and instead give rise to delusion at random? The analogy of flowers in the sky is appropriate to cite here.
That one gives rise to delusion at random while actually free from delusion refers to what is called "delusion having no fundamental cause.

Just as there are no flowers yet one falsely sees flowers, one can likewise understand by analogy that it is unnecessary labor to falsely gaze until the eyes become fatigued. △ Three: Dispelling Non-existence.
Clarifying the doubt regarding the substantiality [of ignorance].
Question: While other defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) may be said to be non-existent, since ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of defilement, how can it be non-existent?
Answer: Both the seed and the fruit aspects of ignorance are fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they have only the pure mind as their essence. It is merely due to...

Due to the causal conditions of perfuming (*vāsanā*), there is the function of delusion; yet, when the mind is gathered back through its own activity, that [delusion] is not existent, for it is but the single mind.

It is like millet or barley, which originally have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and have only atoms (*paramāṇu*) as their substance; they exist merely through the causal conditions of seeds (*bīja*).
Therefore, there is the utility of millet and wheat; yet when one examines them through their constituent particles, they are not truly existent, being nothing more than subtle atoms.
Ignorance is likewise: that which exists is not truly existent.
△ Fourth, dispelling the doubt regarding the nature of the perfuming agent.
Question: Since it is said that delusive activity exists due to the causes and conditions of perfuming, the perfuming dharma itself should constitute the essence of ignorance.
Why then is the pure mind taken as its essence? Answer: Although the perfuming agent is capable of perfuming others...
It causes [a thing] to arise, yet it perishes of its own accord in every moment. How could it then serve as the very substance of that which has arisen?
It is like a grain of barley which can only produce fruit; its own substance decays and returns to minute particles. How could the barley seed of springtime itself come forth as the fruit of autumn?
If that were possible, the barley seed from the beginning of the eon should still exist today. [But] the past does not exist.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise. It can only permeate and give rise to subsequent moments of ignorance; it cannot, while its own substance remains unextinguished, directly become the subsequent moment of ignorance.
If that were possible, ignorance would be a permanent phenomenon (*nityadharma*) rather than something that perishes moment by moment.
Since it is not permanent, it arises through the mutual causality of preceding and succeeding moments, like the flame of a lamp; its essence is solely the pure mind (*viśuddha-citta*).
Therefore, it is subsumed under the mind. That which exists is in fact non-existent. Because that existence is non-existence, this pure mind is called the "empty Tathāgatagarbha."
"Capable of perfuming" (*nengxun*) refers to the two types of ignorance—cause and fruit—in the past; "ignorance" (*wuming*) refers to the two types of ignorance—cause and fruit—in the present.
The remainder of the text is self-evident. △ Fifth: Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Identity or Difference between Cause and Effect.
Question: At the time of the fruit, is ignorance one with or different from delusive thought?
At the time of the seed, is ignorance one with or different from the karmic consciousness? Answer: It is neither one nor different. Why? Because the pure mind moves due to non-awakening.
Non-awakening is itself non-movement. Furthermore, if there were no ignorance (*avidyā*), there would be no karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
Moreover, movement and non-awakening arise together in conjunction and cannot be distinguished; therefore, at the moment of conception, ignorance and the karma-consciousness are not different.
Furthermore, non-awakening is inherently the sense of deluded darkness, as it arises from being perfumed by ignorance during the past stage of fruition.
This means that at the time of the fruit, ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the cause. "Movement" (*iñjita*) inherently signifies transformation;

because it arises through being perfumed by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), false conceptualization itself serves as the cause. Therefore, at the stage of the seed, ignorance and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) are not identical.
This is the sense in which, at the stage of the seed, ignorance and the karmic consciousness are neither identical nor different. At the stage of the fruit...
Regarding the fact that ignorance (*avidyā*) and deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) are neither identical nor different: ignorance, by its very nature, carries the meaning of non-comprehension;
because it arises from the stage of the "seed" (*bīja*), it takes that seed-stage ignorance as its cause.

Deluded conceptualization, by its very nature, carries the meaning of the surging forth of discrimination; because it arises from the *karmic-consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*), it takes that karmic-consciousness as its cause. Therefore, ignorance...
Delusive thoughts are not uniform. Furthermore, because the mental consciousness does not realize that objects are empty, it gives rise to false discrimination.
If one realizes their emptiness, false attachment and discrimination will not arise. Moreover, if there is no ignorance, there is no delusive thought;
if there is no delusive thought, there is also no ignorance. Furthermore, these two factors arise together in conjunction, such that they cannot be distinguished as separate.
Therefore, they are not different. This is the sense that at the time of fruition, ignorance (*avidyā*) and delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*) are neither identical nor different.

For this reason, the two kinds of ignorance constitute the essence (*svabhāva*), while the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) and delusive conceptualization constitute the function (*vṛtti*). The two kinds of ignorance act as cause and effect for one another;
the karma-consciousness and delusive conceptualization likewise act as cause and effect for one another. If the causal and resultant ignorances act as causes for one another...

This refers precisely to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). That false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) act as mutual causes is also a causal condition.
If, at the stage of the seed, ignorance gives rise to the karmic consciousness, this is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If, at the stage of the fruit, ignorance gives rise to false conceptualization, this is likewise a dominant condition. Thus far, the explanation of the empty *tathāgatagarbha* is complete.

In the response, first the meaning of neither identity nor difference is clarified; next, the meanings of essence and function, cause and effect, as well as the conditions of direct cause and dominant condition, are clarified.
These various meanings are established based solely upon the single mind through false construction; though they exist, they are not truly existent.

Thus, the conclusion is reached that the *tathāgatagarbha* is empty. At the stage of the cause (*hetu*), it is first explained that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) are not different;
next, it is explained that they are not identical. At the stage of the fruit (*phala*), it is first explained that ignorance and delusive thought (*vikalpa*) are not identical;

next, it is explained that they are not different. Through fundamental ignorance, the function of the karmic consciousness comes into being; through derivative ignorance, [the function of the evolving consciousnesses] comes into being.

The function of false conceptualization (vikalpa) takes the two kinds of ignorance as its substance. From the ignorance of the causal stage (bīja-kāla), the ignorance of the resultant stage (phala-kāla) arises;
furthermore, from the ignorance of the resultant stage, the ignorance of the causal stage is perfumed and established.

Thus, these two kinds mutually serve as cause and effect for one another, and are termed "direct causal conditions" (sākṣāt-hetu-pratyaya). From the karmic consciousness (karma-vijñāna), false conceptualization arises; furthermore, by means of...

Because deluded thoughts permeate and form the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), these two types [of ignorance] also serve as cause and effect for one another; they are also termed "direct causal conditions" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

If, at the stage of the seed, ignorance gives rise to the karmic consciousness, and at the stage of the fruit, ignorance gives rise to deluded thoughts, this merely constitutes the mutual formation of distinct phenomena and is designated only as a "predominant condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
II. Clarifying the Meaning of Non-Emptiness. As stated in the *Great Buddha-Crown Sūtra* (*Mahā-buddhōṣṇīṣa-sūtra*):
What is meant by "one is all, and all is one"? It refers to the ten realms being mutually identical; this is not a partial or provisional identity. The text is divided into two parts:
first, the general establishment of the various categories; second, the detailed explanation according to each category. This is the first part.
Next, the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha is explained. Within this, there are two types of distinctions: first, explaining its non-emptiness by way of its possession of both defiled and pure dharmas;
second, explaining its substantial existence by way of the identity or difference of the essence of the garbha.

Regarding the first, the explanation of the two dharmas—defiled and pure—there is first the explanation of the pure dharmas, followed by the explanation of the defiled dharmas. Within the initial explanation of the pure dharmas, there are again two parts.
There are two types of analysis: first, clarifying the possession of the qualities of untainted nature; second, clarifying the possession of the pure dharmas that transcend obstacles.

△ Second, the detailed explanation according to the sections consists of two parts: first, clarifying the possession of both defiled and pure dharmas; second, clarifying the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
One and different. This consists of two parts: first, the clarification of pure phenomena; second, the clarification of defiled phenomena. The first part further has two sections:

first, the clarification of the complete possession of the qualities of untainted nature; second, the clarification of the complete possession of pure phenomena that emerge from obstructions. Now, the first [of these].
First, regarding the possession of the qualities of the untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharmatā*):

although this pure mind is of a single, equal flavor and its essence is without differentiation, it nevertheless possesses untainted qualities of the nature that exceed the sands of the Ganges in number. These are:
the sense that its self-nature possesses the radiance of great wisdom; the sense of true and authentic cognition; and the sense of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Such immeasurable and boundless dharmas of intrinsic purity are possessed solely by the one mind, as is extensively elucidated in the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra*.
Because the pure mind possesses these dharmas of intrinsic purity, it is called "not empty."
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "When non-awakening gives rise to thought, one perceives various objective realms; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
When the nature of the mind does not arise, this is precisely the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom.

If the mind is in motion, it is not true cognition; it is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure. When the nature of the mind is unmoving, it is the meaning of true cognition and so forth. This nature...
The "pure dharmas" are not spoken of in terms of their functional efficacy. △ Second, clarifying that the pure dharmas which emerge from obstructions are complete [in nature].

This has two parts: first, clarifying that the nature of the fruit is possessed solely by the mind; second, clarifying that the perfuming agents are also possessed solely by the mind. Now, the first part:
Second, regarding the pure qualities that emerge from the removal of obstacles: this very essence of the pure mind possesses the quality of intrinsic purity.
Consequently, it is able to sustain the power of the habitual perfuming of pure karma. Through the force of this perfuming, its virtuous functions manifest. What is the meaning of this?
By means of the wisdom of the practice on the causal ground, the nature of the threefold wisdom is perfumed, causing its functional manifestation to arise;

this is precisely the Tathāgata’s fruition-merit of the three great wisdoms. Furthermore, by means of all modes of practice such as the five pāramitās on the causal ground, the nature of the marks and signs is perfumed, causing its functional manifestation to arise; this is precisely the Tathāgata...
These are the rewards of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Although these dharmas of the fruition-merit (*phala-guṇa*) have distinct characteristics, their essence is the one mind.
Because the essence of the mind possesses these merits, it is called "not empty" (*aśūnya*). This does not mean that "not empty" is explained solely in terms of the meaning of the mind's essence.
Why? Because the essence of the mind is equal, being neither empty nor not empty.
△ Second, it is clarified that the perfuming agent is also comprised solely within the mind.
Question: Does the perfuming pure karma arise from the mind, or is there a distinct pure dharma external to the mind that serves as the perfuming agent?
Answer: All dharmas that act as perfuming agents are produced by the one mind alone. How is this so? It is said that...
One hears that the entirety of the Dharma teachings is the creation of the minds of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Because the mind of the Buddhas, the mind of the Bodhisattvas, and the mind of sentient beings are one and the same, the Dharma teachings do not exist apart from the mind. Furthermore, by using these teachings to permeate the mind, the nature of understanding (*jiesing*) is awakened;
