Furthermore, there is no separate dharma that comes to realize it; rather, it is like waves subsiding back into the water. This *tathatā* is thus termed the "Gate of Great Quiescent Stillness.

Moreover, by means of the power of the gates of contemplation and skillful means, as well as the power of the熏習 (*vāsanā*) of compassion and vows, cultivated since the initial arousal of the bodhicitta...
Therefore, within meditative concentration itself, one gives rise to great function;

or, upon emerging from concentration, there are various distinctions such as mindfulness, vision, mind, and objects—this is precisely the meaning of the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This is called "arising of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) from stillness (*śamatha*)."

From the first stage of the Perfect Enlightenment (yuan-chu), it is called "conforming to True Suchness" (*tathatā-anuloma*). Having passed through all forty-one stages, it is called "long-term perfuming.
The fundamental wisdom of reality (*mūla-jñāna*) realized upon the initial attainment of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is called the "Gate of Great Tranquil Cessation" (*mahā-śamatha*).

The subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that arises thereafter, which functions as a constant great application until the end of the future, is called the "Gate of Following [the World]."

This is the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) based on quiescence (*śamatha*). Furthermore, the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) may also be called "conforming to True Suchness" (*tathatā-anuloma*), and from the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) upward, they may also be called "partial realization of True Suchness.

These two gates of quiescence and contemplation are fully detailed below in the section on "Attainment through Severance. △ Fourth, the repeated practice of quiescence and contemplation clarifies their simultaneous manifestation.

Furthermore, while intense conceptualization is eternally quiescent in its essence, and though it is eternally quiescent in its essence, it is precisely the conceptualization of dependent origination;
this is called the simultaneous practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
This encompasses the gate of the great tranquility of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the meaning of the functional activity of True Suchness, thereby clarifying that [the two] are not separate.

This refers to a different time. This simultaneous practice of equalizing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* pertains specifically to the fruit of Buddhahood, yet it applies generally to both the innate nature (*prakṛti*) and its cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Why is this so? Because those of the Two Vehicles possess much concentration (*samādhi*) but little wisdom (*prajñā*), and thus do not see the Buddha-nature.

Bodhisattvas possess much wisdom but little concentration; although they see the Buddha-nature, they do not see it clearly. This continues up to the Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avakrānti-bhūmi*), who sees...
Regarding the Buddha-nature, it is like viewing the moon through a fine silk screen; thus, one knows that [the previous stages] were restricted solely to the fruit of Buddhahood.

Nevertheless, although all sentient beings possess the blazing conceptualization of the two kinds of ignorance—delusion regarding principle and delusion regarding phenomena—their essence is fundamentally and eternally quiescent.
Within this essence of eternal quiescence, they are fully endowed with all dependent origination and conceptualization; this is called "identity with principle" (li-ji).

The Twofold Practice. If, through a spiritual friend or from scriptural texts, one hears this principle of the mind-nature’s quiescence and function, and is able to understand and know it, this is called the twofold practice at the level of names (*nāma*).

From this point on, if one moment by moment realizes its fundamental quiescence and is well able to discern dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), this is called the twofold practice of contemplative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Because one is able to realize quiescence, one accords with the path of *śamatha*.

Because it is capable of discernment, it accords with *vipaśyanā*. This is called "concordant dual practice. When the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*) manifests, it is named the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*;
when the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*) manifests, it is named *Mahāprajñā*. This is called "partial realization of dual practice.
Because habitual tendencies are exhausted, the *dharmadhātu* is of a single characteristic; because the great function is manifested, the three wheels are universally displayed.

This is called ultimate dual cultivation: the wondrously luminous is itself wondrous, and tranquil illumination is itself tranquil. From beginning to end, there is nothing that is not the inherent virtue of nature (*xingde*).
Within the stage of principle (*liju*), it is termed "contrary cultivation" (*nixiu*); from the stage of names (*mingzi*) onward, it is entirely termed "conformable cultivation" (*shunxiu*).
Although the directions of following and reversing differ, they are one in their fundamental nature. Therefore, it is only by awakening to this nature that one achieves wondrous cultivation.

Having understood this principle of the fourth stage—the simultaneous practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā—one will realize that the śamatha and vipaśyanā cultivated regarding the two natures previously discussed, as well as the three preceding sets of śamatha and vipaśyanā within the *tathatā* (true reality) nature, are likewise each a simultaneous practice of both. The difference lies only in their degree of clarity or obscurity.

There is a distinction, which results merely in differences of depth and shallowness. Having completed the division of sections and the individual explanations based on the three natures within the defiled and turbid states, [the following] section three provides a comprehensive clarification in three parts:
first, the formal clarification and demonstration; second, by means of the analogy of an illusion; and third, by means of the analogy of a dream.

The first section has four parts: first, distinguishing the functions of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; second, distinguishing the profound meaning of the four grave offenses; third, distinguishing that cultivation follows a specific sequence;
and fourth, distinguishing that false attachments must be eliminated. Now, the first part.

The preceding three sections have clarified the two gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). One should know that the gate of insight (*vipaśyanā*) is able to establish the dependent origination of the three natures as existent;

the gate of calm abiding (*śamatha*) is able to eliminate the three natures so that one may enter the three non-natures. To enter the three non-natures means: by eliminating the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one enters the signless nature (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*);
by eliminating the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one enters the birthless nature (*anutpāda-lakṣaṇa*); [and by eliminating] the true... [nature].
The true nature enters into the nature of non-substantiality.

Regarding the establishment of the three natures as dependent origination through the gate of contemplation: this means that by contemplating how phenomena such as the five aggregates and the six sense objects are fundamentally empty, yet are merely false imaginings grasped as real, one is able to establish the dependent origination of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature). This is because one knows all phenomena...

Since the nature of mere conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks any real dharma, one next contemplates that all dharmas—the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth—are entirely produced by the mind and their essence is empty;
thus, one can establish the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of dependent origination.
This is because one knows that all dharmas arise dependently and are merely empty appearances. Next, one contemplates that all dharmas are fundamentally only mind, and outside of the mind—

It is not possible. One does not take the two absences as the characteristic of mind; rather, one can establish true reality and dependent origination by knowing that all phenomena exist yet are non-existent, because they are solely the pure mind. Regarding the gate of cessation (*śamatha*), which eliminates the three natures and enters the three non-natures:
this means forcefully contemplating that all phenomena are merely mental characteristics, empty appearances without substance, and further contemplating—

The mind that is capable of observation likewise lacks any real thought. Because this grasping mind ceases, it is called "removing the nature of conceptualization" and entering the "nature of signlessness.
Next, one observes that empty phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind; existence is non-existence, and there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Because this grasping at empty appearances is extinguished, it is called "removing the dependent nature" and entering the "nature of non-arising. Next...
Contemplating the pure mind as perfect and transcending the four propositions—it does not belong to existence or non-existence, nor is it an object of perception or thought.
Therefore, it is called "removing the nature of reality to enter the nature of non-nature. △ Second, distinguishing the profound meaning of the four layers.

Regarding the reason why *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are elucidated in four successive stages within the context of ultimate reality (*tattva*): it is because this point of ultimate profundity is subtle and difficult to comprehend.
Therefore, first, the emptiness of delusion is shown to be unreal; by eliminating the emptiness of delusion, *śamatha* is clarified as being the nature of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Next, one stage reveals that the false is itself the true; by ceasing divergent attachments, tranquility (*śānti*) is distinguished as being the absence of a "true" [nature].
Nature. Therefore, "no-nature" (wuxing) is the nature [of no-nature], or it is called "no non-nature," or it is said to be "no true nature.

The third layer of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is precisely the fundamental samādhi of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The final fourth layer of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is the simultaneous manifestation of both.
How could there be a "non-existence" (abhāva) that serves as the pure mind? Therefore, it is said: "To show that false emptiness is not real, the mind that clings to non-existence is extinguished.
Thus, it is said: "Eliminating false emptiness clarifies cessation (śamatha). Even if one were to engage in discrimination, this is precisely the discrimination of the pure mind.
Therefore, it is said: "Revealing that the counterfeit is itself the true. How could there be any separate dharma to be objectified or recollected? Therefore, it is said: "Cessation."
Distinguish quiescence by means of the distinct attachments. The remainder may be understood as explained above. △ Second, distinguishing that there is a sequence in cultivation:
Furthermore, if a practitioner possesses sharp faculties and deep insight, they need not cultivate from the first [nature], the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature);

rather, they proceed directly to cultivate based on the second, the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). This *paratantra-svabhāva* may also be termed the *parikalpita-svabhāva*, because it possesses...
There are two natures. If one is unable to practice in this manner, one must proceed step-by-step from the first nature, and thereafter practice according to the second nature;
advancing in this sequence, one must never bypass the preceding two natures to practice directly according to the third nature.
Furthermore, although one is a beginner, it does not hinder the three cycles within every moment of thought.
To study both [the provisional and the ultimate] constitutes the second stage of completion.
"Sharp faculties" refers to wisdom that is quick and keen; "profound realization" refers to insight that is far-reaching. Being sharp means knowing immediately upon contact;
being profound means not becoming mired in emotional attachments. This is because one has already previously realized that all is but mind and that all phenomena lack substantial reality.

Therefore, one may directly observe the dharma of fundamental emptiness (*mūla-śūnyatā*). By means of this dharma of fundamental emptiness, non-attachment is precisely the *paratantra* (dependent nature);

attachment, however, constitutes the deluded *vikalpa* (discrimination). Originally, there are not two essences or two characteristics. Furthermore, even illusory karmic retribution is termed a dharma of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

If one cannot thoroughly comprehend that objects are empty, then one must—as follows— [Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Yogācāra doctrine, likely from the *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya* or a related work by Sthiramati or another commentator. The final sentence is incomplete.]

The preceding sequential cultivation is easy to understand. Nevertheless, even those with the sharpest faculties cannot directly perceive the dharmas of true reality, because sentient beings have fallen entirely into the nature of dependence (paratantra-svabhāva) since beginningless time.
Apart from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is no perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). It is like water that does not exist apart from its flow.

Even if one were to directly perceive the perfected nature, that perfected nature would instead become a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For example, it is like seeking water by abandoning the flow; this is not true water. Therefore, the *Awakening of Mahāśrī* Sūtra says:

"If one attempts to discern perfect enlightenment (*bodhi*) without having realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), that nature of perfect enlightenment will be identical to the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*). This...

This means that if one can clearly contemplate and discern the *parikalpita* (imagined) and *paratantra* (dependent) natures, one will spontaneously realize the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature, just as touching the waves and currents is entirely touching the water. The Great Master Zhi refers here to the single thought-moment of the present.
The conscious mind is taken as the object of contemplation. Is the conscious mind not the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature)?
To contemplate this is precisely the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). Since it is inconceivable, is it not the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature)?

If one does not establish the objective realm of phenomena but speaks only of the contemplation of principle, and intends to grasp the ultimate meaning, it is merely pure *tathatā* (suchness). In the case of a beginner, this mostly belongs to...
One must be cautious not to misapprehend or harbor perverse attachments. Furthermore, one should understand the reason for observing the *parikalpita* (the imagined nature):

it is because one wishes to realize that the imagined nature lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in order to enter the *paratantra* (the dependent nature). Observing the *paratantra* is because one wishes to realize that the dependent nature lacks intrinsic nature in order to realize the *pariniṣpanna* (the perfected nature).
Thus, the former two serve as skillful means, truly intended to support and bring about the third stage.

Furthermore, if we consider the general course: within the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), the practice of the three stops and three contemplations proceeds from the provisional toward emptiness;

within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), the practice of the three stops and three contemplations proceeds from emptiness toward the provisional; within the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), the practice of the three stops and three contemplations precisely manifests the wondrous samādhi and wondrous prajñā of the Middle Way.
Nevertheless, for a person of the Perfect Teaching at the initial stage of practice, the three stops and three contemplations are fully present within a single mind.

Because one practices in the interim, it does not hinder the simultaneous study of the three phases in every moment of thought. From the three phases of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), one enters the three phases of semblance (*sādṛśya*).

From the three phases of semblance, one enters the three phases of partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*). From the three phases of partial realization, one enters the three phases of ultimate perfection (*niṣṭhā-gata*).
Upon reaching the ultimate, although it does not hinder the continued discourse on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*), [the ultimate is realized].
[The nature] is ultimately and exclusively the true nature (bhūtatathatā). △ Fourth, distinguishing false attachments that must be eliminated.
Question: Since you speak of the dharmas of true nature, what is there to eliminate? If something can be eliminated, it is not the true nature.
The answer is: Those who grasp at the two absences as being the true nature must eliminate them; therefore, it is said that there is no "absence of nature.

Furthermore, those whose deluded intellect discriminates the pure mind and considers it an object of contemplation must also cease this discrimination of distinct characteristics, demonstrating that there is no separate true nature that can be discriminated;
therefore, it is said that there is no "true nature. One should merely eliminate these [misconceptions] regarding the truth.
The "true" [nature] that is erroneously clung to upon the fundamental nature does not mean that the substance of *tathatā* (suchness) is eliminated.

This concludes the precise clarification. △ Second, the section on the analogy of illusion has three parts: first, the heading; second, the formal exposition; third, the concluding application by example.
Now, first:
there are further analogies that can clarify the two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā regarding the three natures; these shall now be explained. △ Second, the actual exposition has three parts:
first, an analogy for the gate of vipaśyanā; second, an analogy for the gate of śamatha; third, a combined analysis of śamatha and vipaśyanā. Now...
First: For example, a handkerchief originally has no rabbit; the dharma of true nature is likewise thus—it is the single pure mind whose self-nature is free from characteristics.
When augmented by the power of illusion, the handkerchief appears as if it were a rabbit; the dharma of the dependent nature is likewise thus.
This is so: the false perfuming of the true nature manifests the appearances of the six realms. The ignorant and small-minded, lacking knowledge, claim these to be real.
The dharmas of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) are likewise thus: the deluded consciousness clings to the unreal as real. Therefore, the Sūtra says, "All dharmas are like illusions.
This is an analogy for the contemplative gate of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
This analogy is identical in meaning to the preceding passage which distinguishes the three natures based on the single mind; the text may be understood accordingly.
△ Second, the section on the cessation gate using the analogy of the three non-natures.

If one knows that this rabbit is merely dependent on the handkerchief and appears to exist, yet is purely empty and lacks reality—its nature being without marks (animitta)—then the wisdom of the nature without marks is likewise so (excluding the *parikalpita-svabhāva*).
One is able to know that all phenomena depend upon the mind and appear to exist, yet are merely empty forms lacking any real nature or marks.

If one knows that the appearance of the rabbit is merely the handkerchief itself, then the existence of the rabbit upon the handkerchief is in fact non-existence; it has never existed from the beginning.
The wisdom of the nature of non-nature is likewise so (excluding the dependent nature). It is able to know that false appearances are merely the true mind;
the appearances manifested by the mind exist yet are not existent, for their self-nature is unarisen. If one knows that the handkerchief was originally existent...
One does not take that which is non-existent as a hand-towel; the wisdom of the nature of non-nature is likewise so (excluding the true nature).

One is able to know that the fundamental nature of the pure mind exists inherently, and does not regard the non-existence of the two natures as the true nature. This is the metaphor for the gate of cessation through the three non-natures.
△ Third, the combined analysis of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Therefore, if one wishes to relinquish conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one should cultivate the gate of *śamatha* to enter the three non-natures (*tri-niḥsvabhāva*).

If one wishes not to destroy dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) while establishing conventional truth, one should cultivate the gate of *vipaśyanā* to understand and know the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). If one does not cultivate the gate of *vipaśyanā*, then...
If one does not understand the dependent origination of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one will not know why ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is eternally quiescent.

If one does not cultivate the gate of tranquility (*śamatha*), one will not know that the ultimate is itself the conventional; if one does not cultivate the gate of insight (*vipaśyanā*), one will not know that the conventional is itself the ultimate.
For this reason, one must rely on the analogy of illusion to penetrate the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three non-natures (*triniḥsvabhāva*).
Regarding nature:

the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) refers to the provisional establishment of the distinctions among the ten realms as nominal designations; this is the "three thousand [realms] produced by phenomena.

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) refers to the fact that phenomena produced by causes and conditions are empty, yet provisionally existent, and identical with the Middle Way; this is the "three thousand [realms] inherent in principle. In the ultimate sense, all three truths are equally true.
In the conventional sense, the three truths are all conventional; the real is itself the conventional, and the conventional is itself the real.

This is truly because they are neither real nor conventional that one can simultaneously illuminate both the real and the conventional; thus, the three truths are all the Middle Way. If the analogy of illusion is such, other cases may be understood accordingly.
Part Two: The formal explanation of the analogy of illusion is concluded. △ Part Three: The analogical conclusion.
The analogy of illusion can penetrate the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*).

As for the other analogies—those of dreams, transformations, reflections, the moon in water, mirages, cities of the gandharvas, hungry ghosts, and so forth—they all represent the arising of the unreal based upon the real; those who cling to the unreal as being real are all illustrated by the three natures.

This can be understood by analogy. If one were to take these various analogies directly as illustrations solely because they represent the arising of the unreal based upon the real, [it would be incomplete].

The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is also attained [through these analogies]. However, that which is empty yet substantial can be used as an analogy for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);

that which is empty and follows the movement of grasping can be used as an analogy for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Therefore, these various analogies collectively illustrate the three natures.

When one understands the sequence of these illustrative methods as being without characteristics (*animitta*), they can be used as an analogy for the three absences of intrinsic nature (*trisvabhāva-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

In this passage, first there is a summary conclusion. Next, with the words "If one directly [considers] these... and so forth, various analogies are again employed to illustrate the preceding text, specifically the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as distinguished according to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Within the summary conclusion, that which is relied upon as real is an analogy for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);
that which arises as unreal is an analogy for the dependent nature; and the grasping of the unreal as real is an analogy for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). These are the three natures.

This being so, the meaning of the three natures (trisvabhāva) may be understood by analogy with this. Next, in the text, "the empty substance is real" serves as a metaphor for the True [Nature] when defiled, namely the pure portion (*śuddhabhāga*).

"The empty follows the turning of grasping" serves as a metaphor for the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*) and the empty marks of retribution, namely the defiled portion (*kliṣṭabhāga*). △ Third, the analogy of a dream.
Furthermore, the analogy of a dream is further analyzed to clarify the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*).
For example, because ordinary beings are habituated to all phenomena, various phenomena manifest within their minds even during dreams. The *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is likewise:
due to the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of true nature by ignorance and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) throughout beginningless time, the true mind relies upon [the dependent nature].

The perfuming manifests as the fruit of illusory appearances. Because that person in the dream is shrouded by the veil of sleep, they are unable to know for themselves that their own body and the bodies of others are all produced by the dreaming mind;
they instead grasp them as real entities. For this reason, the various experiences of self and other within the dream are established.
The nature of dharmas characterized by conceptual discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is likewise so. [This applies to] the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because they are deluded by ignorance at the time of fruition, they do not know that both self and others are entirely the true mind produced through the influence of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
They then falsely grasp [these phenomena] as being real; therefore, the various experiences and enjoyments of self and others are established. For this reason, the Sūtra says:
"This body is like a dream, a false and illusory vision. Here, "illusory" (*khu*) refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and "false" (*wang*) refers to...
The nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). This constitutes the gate of contemplation for the three natures as dependent origination.

Now, that which is grasped as real within this dream is merely a manifestation of the dreaming mind; it fundamentally lacks any reality. The phenomena of the nature of discrimination are likewise thus.
However, these empty conceptions arise from the mind; they are fundamentally without reality, which is precisely the nature of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇatā*).

Furthermore, those empty appearances within a dream exist yet are not existent; they are solely the dreaming mind, with no other phenomena present. The nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is likewise:
the empty appearances of self and other exist yet are not existent; they are solely the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), with no other phenomena present.
This is precisely the nature of non-arising. Furthermore, that dreaming mind is identical to the awakened mind of the original state;
it is only due to the causal conditions of sleep that it is called the "dreaming mind. Apart from the dreaming mind, no separate awakened mind can be found.
The reality of dharmas is likewise thus: they are equal and non-dual. It is only because of the causal conditions of the perfuming of the defiled dharmas of ignorance that [this distinction arises].

That which is conjoined with defilements is called the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). However, in reality, there is no separate true mind (*tathatā-citta*) to be found apart from this fundamental consciousness;

it is precisely the dharma of the nature of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). This constitutes the gate of cessation for eliminating the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). It is by means of this analogy [that this is understood].

The three natures and the three absences of nature can thus be clearly elucidated. This concludes the explanation of the essential characteristics of śamatha and vipaśyanā as categorized according to the three defiled natures within the clarification of the essential characteristics of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Above, the eight metaphors beginning with dreams were presented collectively; they may be understood through the analogy of an illusion.

Now, they are further analyzed in order to make śamatha and vipaśyanā increasingly clear. Regarding the fact that the "perfected nature" (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) was not explicitly mentioned among the three natures in the preceding metaphors:
it refers to the dreaming mind itself as the perfected nature. Based upon this, the various things seen within the dream arise.
The Dharma is named the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). To falsely grasp it as real within a dream is named the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
There are no distinct phenomena within the three realms; they are produced solely by the one mind. Failing to realize that all is but mind, one falsely discriminates between self and dharmas.

When one contemplates this analogy deeply, how could one not feel a sense of chilling clarity? The analogies for the three gates of cessation are clear from the text. Second, [the section] concerning the three aspects of purity.
The Nature [of the Three Natures] has three parts: first, the general outline; second, the individual explanations; third, the comprehensive clarification. Now, for the first part:

next, we clarify the essence and characteristics of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) within the three natures of purity. Within this, there are also three sections: first, clarifying the essence and characteristics of calm abiding and insight within the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of conceptual construction);

second, clarifying the essence and characteristics of calm abiding and insight within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the nature of dependent origination); third, clarifying the [essence and characteristics of calm abiding and insight within the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the nature of ultimate reality)].
The essential nature of cessation consists of the characteristics of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).

△ Second, the individual explanations of these three [natures]: first, regarding the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature); second, regarding the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature); third, regarding the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). Now, the first.
Regarding the nature and characteristics of meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) within the first [of the three] natures, the *parikalpita-svabhāva*:

it refers to knowing all the form-bodies (*rūpakāya*), voices, great compassion, and great vows of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; their various forms of dependent rewards and requisites; their manifestations and arrangements throughout the six realms of existence;
and even the appearance and passing away of their golden bodies, the distribution of their relics, and the sites where they are commemorated through clay, water, carvings, and paintings.

As for the monasteries, as well as the teachings of the sūtras, the codes of conduct, and the methods of maintenance—whatever can benefit sentient beings—one should know that these all arise from the permeation of great compassion and great vows, as well as the power of the responsive resonance of sentient beings' capacities. Because the causes and conditions are fully present, they permeate the pure mind;
thus, the nature of the mind manifests these phenomena based upon such permeation. Therefore, this is exclusively the dependent origination of true nature.
The principle is that there is no reality [to them]. It is only because sentient beings possess ignorance and delusive conceptualization that their distorted views are not empty.
A practitioner need only observe and know that this mind of attachment to distorted views is itself ignorance and delusive conceptualization.

This is precisely what is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*), because one knows that this seeing is delusive and false; one forcibly applies the mind and observes that it has no reality, being merely a product of one's own mind.
Because one knows thus, the grasping at reality ceases, which is precisely what is called "quiescence" (*śamatha*).
This is the entry from contemplation into quiescence within the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The sequence of first observing and subsequently ceasing can be understood from the text. All Buddha-activities, including the maintenance of the Triple Gem, fundamentally derive their capacity from the dependent origination of true nature (*tathatā*).
True nature is the pure, ultimate nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), while dependent origination is the pure, other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
It is only because sentient beings fail to understand this and falsely conceptualize it as being real that it is termed the "discriminative nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

[It is] the ear. Since it is a conceptualization of ignorance and delusion, it is further called "pure" because its object of perception arises from great compassion and great vows, and can serve as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for sentient beings;
thus, even if one does not realize that [all things] are mind-only, one will not increase the karma of the fetters. However, to enter the gateway of the Mahāyāna, one must...

One must forcefully cultivate the contemplation of the mind to know that it lacks substantial reality; otherwise, one will conceptually construct phenomena as existing outside the mind, which is forever contrary to the essential path of liberation.
△ Second, regarding the other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
As for the gate of cessation and contemplation within the second [nature], the other-dependent: because of the preceding gate of cessation, one realizes herein that—
The pure virtues of all Buddhas are produced solely by the mind; they are the manifestations of provisional emptiness.

Because these empty manifestations arise through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), their pure functions are fully revealed, manifesting as a response to the perfuming causes accumulated over vast eons.

Furthermore, because they respond to conditions to gather and transform sentient beings, their grace moistens even the lowliest grass, expressing the power of boundless resonance. This is precisely the dependent origination of the pure mind.
It is that which is quiescent yet constantly active. To form such an understanding is called the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Because one employs skillful means based on this gate of contemplation, one is able to know the virtues of benefiting oneself and others that arise from the pure mind.

That which is non-active yet constantly quiescent—such an understanding is called the gate of tranquility (*śamatha*). This tranquility and contemplation should be practiced in tandem, both sequentially and simultaneously.
Practicing them together is also permissible.
Those of sharp faculties may practice both simultaneously; those of dull faculties may practice them sequentially. The meaning of this can be understood accordingly.
△ Third, regarding the nature of reality (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Next, to clarify the gate of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within the nature of reality (*tathatā*):
because of the preceding practice of *śamatha*, one realizes that the pure virtues of all Buddhas are nothing other than the single mind; this is termed *vipaśyanā*.

Furthermore, one realizes that the pure mind of all Buddhas is the pure mind of sentient beings, and the pure mind of sentient beings is the pure mind of all Buddhas—non-dual and without distinction. Because there is no distinction, one does not...
Externally contemplating the Buddha with a pure mind, because one does not seek the Buddha’s mind outside of one's own mind, conceptual discrimination is naturally extinguished.

Once the deluded mind has ceased, one further realizes that one's own mind and the Buddha’s mind have been fundamentally identical from the beginning; therefore, this is called *śamatha* (calm abiding).
This is known as the gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* within the true nature.

The meaning may also be understood thus. Someone asks: "Regarding this and the preceding passage on the defiled and turbid three natures (*trisvabhāva*), are they practiced sequentially as calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), or are they practiced simultaneously? Is there a sequence, or is there no sequence?
Must they be practiced together, or need they not be practiced together? The answer is: "There is both sequence and simultaneity; there is both order and lack of order."

In sequence, there is both the complete cultivation and the incomplete cultivation. Why is this so? The former refers to the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) of defilement;

this is the samādhi of contemplating the true reality of the body while recollecting one’s own Buddha. The latter refers to the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* based on the three natures of purity;
this is the samādhi of contemplating the true reality of the Buddha while recollecting another Buddha. If one recollects only oneself...
As for a Buddha, it is not necessary to fully cultivate the latter three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

This is because once the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* has been perfected within the defiled true nature (*tathatā*), and habitual tendencies have been exhausted such that one realizes *tathatā*, one spontaneously attains penetration into the pure three natures and three non-natures.
If one merely contemplates other Buddhas, it is likewise unnecessary to further cultivate the former three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
When practice is perfected through the purity of true reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), my own mind and the Buddha-mind become equal and of one suchness;
thus, one no longer gives rise to delusion regarding the three natures and three non-natures within the defiled state.

Furthermore, when cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) are established within the purity of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), this refers to the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) corresponding to the mindfulness of "mind-only. This is the purity of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) of the Buddha of the Mind-Only Recitation Dharma-gate is the cessation and contemplation of the pure, true nature.
This is the cessation and contemplation of the Buddha of the True Mark of Mind-Only. It may also be called "reciting both self and other," for it is not merely reciting another Buddha.
If one were to discuss the general practice of reciting both the Buddhas of self and others, then one must cultivate both types [of recitation].

Regarding the dharma-gate of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* for the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), there are four further meanings within it: sequential priority and posteriority, simultaneity, and the non-sequential.

As for "priority and posteriority," one first practices according to the defiled *parikalpita-svabhāva*, next according to the pure *parikalpita-svabhāva*, and subsequently according to the defiled and pure *paratantra-svabhāva*, and the defiled and pure *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*, practicing each one in succession.

One must practice these in sequence; one may not skip over the stages. Regarding "simultaneity": this means practicing the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) of the ten realms all at once, followed by practicing the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) of the ten realms, and then practicing the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) of the ten realms.

Thus, defilement and purity occur simultaneously, without priority or posteriority. Regarding "sequence," this is as explained below in the section on "severance and attainment. Regarding "not... [the text continues].

As for the "next" [point]: it was stated above that within every thought-moment one studies all three phases simultaneously; by analogy, one may likewise say that defilement and purity are observed together.

Furthermore, as stated in the following text, the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) are practiced in every stage. Thus, we know that the perfect fusion and sequential arrangement encompass both the horizontal and the vertical;
they include both the sudden and the gradual, and benefit those of both sharp and dull faculties. The subtlety of this dharma-gate is beyond compare.

Furthermore. △ Third, the threefold elimination of six [points]. First, eliminating the characteristics of quiescence and function; second, eliminating the names of "sentient beings" and "Buddha"; third, eliminating the meaning of sameness and difference;
fourth, eliminating the benefits of self-cultivation and other-cultivation; fifth, eliminating whether the Buddha's virtues are real or empty;
sixth, eliminating permanence and birth-and-death. Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, revealing the nature through cultivation; second, arising in accordance with the nature.
Cultivation. First, regarding the initial stage:
within the aforementioned purification of the three natures, one first enters cessation (*śamatha*) from contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) within the first nature;

then, from this cessation, one proceeds to enter contemplation within the second nature; then, from this contemplation, one enters cessation; and then, from this cessation, one enters the third [nature].
Contemplating the nature, one further enters into *śamatha* (calm abiding) from this contemplation; thus, one attains the equality and oneness of one's own mind and the Buddha-mind.

This is precisely the single path through which cultivation reaches fulfillment. Furthermore, because the mind has been perfumed since first resolving to attain enlightenment through the skillful means of great compassion, activity arises within meditative concentration in manifold abundance.
There is no task that is not performed, and no characteristic that is not enacted. Thus, the Dharma...

When the great function of the realms is without obstruction or hindrance, this is termed "emergence from cultivation. Functioning while in stillness, and being still while functioning—this is the simultaneous manifestation of both.

Entering cultivation in a single track to fulfillment refers to the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), beginning from the stage of response and transformation and culminating in the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Relying on the external meaning, one accomplishes the contemplation of Mind-Only, establishing that "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha," whereby the self-nature is ultimately and perfectly manifested.

This constitutes the gate of Great Quiescent Stilling (*mahāśānti*) of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Furthermore, through the power of the habitual perfuming of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), the great function flourishes profusely;
this is precisely the wisdom of differentiation (*viśeṣa-jñāna*). Thus, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is eternally so. Great.
Regarding the application of this gate: it is applied through the application of profound stillness. Although there is a sequence in the teaching, there is no sequence in the essence;
therefore, it is called "simultaneous manifestation. △ Second, the cultivation arising in accordance with the nature.
Even an ordinary person can, at this very moment, practice the simultaneous cultivation of tranquility and function in this way. What does this mean?
It means that knowing all phenomena to exist is precisely their non-existence; this is "constant tranquility during the time of function.

That they do not exist yet appear to exist as if they were phenomena is called "constant function during the time of tranquility. Therefore, form is itself emptiness; it is not that emptiness results from the extinction of form.
Form is itself emptiness; existence is itself non-existence. This is the meaning of the quiescent nature of the *dharmadhātu*, which is its inherent law (*dharmatā*).

It is not that form ceases for there to be emptiness; it is not the absence of phenomena that resemble [them]. This is the meaning of the functional aspect of the *dharmadhātu*, which is its inherent law.

Because this nature is replete with both quiescence and function, they are fundamentally neither prior nor posterior. Therefore, illumination of the nature constitutes cultivation, beginning from the stage of names and continuing until the end.
Ultimately, there is no time when these two do not manifest together. Why wait until after the attainment of Buddhahood for them to be called "manifesting together"?
△ Second, distinguishing the names of the ordinary being and the Buddha.
Question: Since it has been stated that the Buddha-mind and the sentient-being mind are neither two nor distinct, why is it said that there are different names for "Buddha" and "sentient being"?
Answer: While the essence of the mind is the same, there is also a distinct nature characterized by non-obstruction.

Because this distinct nature exists, one receives the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) from beginningless time. Due to the distinctness of this power of perfuming, the nature of the mind— [is differentiated].

Based on the manifestations produced by habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), distinct characteristics appear. It is because these are the characteristics of this self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) that the difference between the two names—Buddha and sentient being—is spoken of.
Identity does not obstruct difference, and difference does not hinder identity; therefore, it is called the "unobstructed nature of difference. The rest may be understood accordingly. △
Third, distinguishing the meanings of identity and difference.

Question: Since all Buddhas have already abandoned the grasping for a self (*ātma-grāha*), how can there be distinctions between the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time? Answer:

At the moment when one abandons the grasping for a self and realizes the equality of the essence of mind (*citta-tattva*), in reality there are no [distinctions of] the ten directions or the three periods of time.

It is different. However, when originally in the stage of practice (*yindì*) and not yet free from attachment, each [Buddha] made individual vows, cultivated their own pure lands (*jingtu*), and transformed sentient beings individually.

Such various karmic distinctions perfumed the pure mind. Because the nature of the mind relies on the power of these distinct perfumings, the two retributions—the primary and secondary—of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and three periods of time appear with distinct characteristics. This does not mean that True Suchness (*tathatā*) itself is diverse.
The essence of this [Dharmakāya] possesses these marks of differentiation. For this reason, all Buddhas are both eternally identical and eternally distinct;
this is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of past and present. Therefore, a sutra says: "The Dharma of Mañjuśrī is ever thus; the Dharma-King has but one Dharma.
All those who are unimpeded emerge from birth and death by means of the One Path. The bodies of all Buddhas are but this single Dharmakāya. This is precisely...
This is discussed through the dual perspective of identity and difference. If there were only absolute identity and no distinction, why would the Sūtra say:
"The bodies of all Buddhas are one; all are unimpeded persons"? If there were only absolute difference and no identity, why would the Sūtra say:
"There is only this single Dharma-body; through this single path, one transcends birth and death"? For these reasons, although the True Mind is indeed equal, it is also...

It possesses a nature of differentiation. If one understands that a single substance in a bright mirror possesses the nature of manifesting myriad images, then one will not be deluded regarding the dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm.
△ Fourth, distinguishing between the benefits of cultivation for oneself and others, which has two parts: first, clarifying the benefits; second, resolving doubts. Now, the first part.
Question: If it is because the true mind possesses a differentiated nature that Buddhas and sentient beings are each distinct and not the same;
yet, because the essence of the true mind is non-dual, all ordinary beings and sages constitute a single *dharmakāya*, then there should likewise be a distinct nature [in that unity].

Since the essence is one, when another practices, I do not practice; yet since the essence is one, when another practices, I attain the Way. Answer: Because there is a sense of distinction, when another practices...
It is not that I practice, for their essence is one; thus, practice and non-practice are equal.
Nevertheless, if one understands this meaning of the identity of essence, then the virtues practiced by others also possess the capacity to benefit oneself. Therefore, a sutra says:
"If a bodhisattva knows that all the merits of the Buddhas are themselves his own merits, this is a marvelous and extraordinary dharma. Furthermore,
The Sūtra states: "One shares the same treasury of roots of goodness as all Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, practitioners should know that the merits performed by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, those of the Two Vehicles, noble ones, ordinary beings, devas, and humans are all one's own merits;
for this reason, one should rejoice in them with sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).

In the response, it is first clarified that the essence of cultivation and non-cultivation is one and the same in order to refute the attachment to the notion that "I have attained what others have cultivated.

Next, he further exhorts the cultivation of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) toward merit; if one can deeply give rise to sympathetic joy toward the merits of both ordinary beings and sages, then the principle that "I have attained what others have cultivated" is also established.
This is because when one understands that the essence is identical, [the two are realized as one].
This is wondrous wisdom. To rejoice in every thought-moment while breaking through the obstacle of jealousy is itself wondrous practice.
When both wisdom and practice are possessed, one is no longer someone who relies solely on others to seek the Way. △ Second, resolving doubts.
Question: If that were so, all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should naturally attain the Way. Answer:
If this true mind possessed only the meaning of sameness, it would not require cultivation and one could attain the Way by relying on others;

furthermore, there would be no distinction between the characteristics of self and other bodies. Since True Suchness (*tathatā*) also possesses the meaning of difference, the distinction between self and other can exist.
Why must you rely exclusively on others to seek the Way? You should simply cultivate merit for yourself, knowing that what others cultivate is itself your own virtue;
thus, by mutually supporting one another’s accomplishment, you will be able to attain the Way with extraordinary swiftness. How can you rely entirely upon others?
Furthermore, you must understand that if you only cultivate for yourself and do not recognize that what others cultivate is your own [virtue], [you will fail].

As for those who possess [the potential], they likewise cannot obtain benefit from others; this is like the impoverished son who did not know that his father was his own father or that the wealth was his own property.
Thus, for over twenty years, he endured the suffering of poverty while dwelling in a grass hut—this is the meaning.

Therefore, by relying on causes and depending on conditions, one quickly achieves fulfillment. If one were to seek [enlightenment] alone without borrowing from others, one could only achieve [a limited result].
Regarding the price for clearing away filth:

in the response, it first clarifies that one must not rely entirely upon others for cultivation; next, it clarifies that one must recognize that "others" are oneself. The meaning of the text is clear.
However, this benefit of cultivation regarding self and others must be analyzed according to four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): the first is seeking only for oneself.
If one does not rely on others, yet achieves the state of the Two Vehicles, it is because one has not realized that self and others are of the same essence.

Second, if one relies solely on others and seeks nothing from oneself, one becomes a being of the human or celestial realms; this is likewise because one does not know that self and others are of the same essence.
Third, if one neither cultivates [the path] oneself nor seeks others to do so, one will constantly remain in the three miserable realms (*trāya*), because both cause and condition have perished.

Fourth, if one knows that others [are practicing] and inwardly gives rise to deep sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), one will swiftly attain the Buddha-way, because one relies upon causes and entrusts oneself to conditions.
△ Fifth, distinguishing whether the Buddha’s virtues are real or false, which has two parts: first, showing the characteristics of these virtues; second, the distinction.
Reality and Emptiness. First: Question:
How many kinds are there of the pure virtues of all Buddhas mentioned above? Answer: Briefly stated, there are two kinds.
The first is self-benefit; the second is benefiting others. Within self-benefit, there are further three kinds: first, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
second, the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); and third, the Pure Land. Within benefiting others, there are further two kinds: first, transformation through compliance.

Second is contrariety to transformation (*viruddha-vikurvaṇa*). Within accordance with transformation (*anuloma-vikurvaṇa*), there are two kinds: first, the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the *māyopama-nirmāṇakāya*;
second, the pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*) and the defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭakṣetra*). These constitute the pure virtues of all Buddhas.
The two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—are spoken of in terms of the "supported," while the Pure Land is spoken of in terms of the "support.
In reality, the supported and the support are non-dual; they are distinguished only for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain the four benefits.

The Dharma-body is the essence of the self-nature purity revealed by principle. The Reward-body is that which is accomplished through the three wisdoms and four wisdoms of the single mind, as well as permanence.

It is the immeasurable accumulation of dharmas characterized by bliss, selfhood, and purity. The nature of the merit of the principle and wisdom upon which the Pure Land relies is precisely the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
In accordance with transformation, it manifests as the body of a Buddha; in opposition to transformation, it manifests as bodies within the various realms of existence (*saṃsāra*).
The response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are either superior or inferior: the superior rely on the Pure Land, while the inferior rely on the defiled realms. This also applies to the *māyāmaya* [body].
It is called *manomaya*; this translates as "body born of mind" (*yishengshen*), and it is also translated as "body accomplished by mind" (*ychengshen*).
△ Second, distinguishing the real from the false, which has two parts: first, distinguishing by way of cultivation; second, distinguishing by way of nature. Now, the first.

Question: The virtue of benefiting others is established in relation to conditions; as a provisional manifestation of skillful means, it may be said to lack substantial reality, being merely a false appearance that exists yet is not existent.
The virtue of self-benefit, however, is precisely the two bodies of Dharma and Reward, the perfect enlightenment of great wisdom.
It manifests the principle and thereby achieves permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity. Why, then, do you say that existence is non-existence? The answer is:
the virtue of self-benefit is indeed permanent, blissful, self-natured, and pure—unmoving and unchanging—precisely because it is accomplished by manifesting the principle; therefore, it is so.
Furthermore, precisely because it is accomplished by manifesting the principle, it is the very function of the mind-nature’s dependent origination. However...

Function has no function apart from itself; function is entirely mind. Mind has no mind apart from itself; mind is entirely function. Therefore, by means of the essence, the essence and function are identical yet not existent;
they are but the one mind, without abandoning the constant utility of function. By means of function, the function and essence are non-existent yet existent;
they blaze forth throughout the Dharma-realm without hindering its eternal quiescence. This quiescence is itself function, which is called the gate of contemplation (*guanmen*).
Functioning is itself quiescence, which is termed "cessation" (śamatha); this is a single essence acting in tandem.

However, it is for the sake of leading practitioners to dissolve appearances and enter into quiescence that cessation and insight (vipaśyanā) are explained separately as preceding and following one another. This does not imply that the Buddha's virtues undergo any transition or change.
When it is manifested through principle and thus perfected, the entire body is principle; therefore, it is called "existence.
Furthermore, because it is manifested through principle and thus perfected, its perfection is non-different from its source, which is simply principle; therefore, it is "non-existence.

However, since sentient beings have, from time immemorial, been attached to the reality of phenomena with great weight, one now wishes to lead students to dissolve appearances and enter quiescence; for this reason, *śamatha* (calm abiding) is taught first.

The subsequent discussion concerns the contemplation of the ear. Fundamentally, these two are of one essence and function as a dual practice; how could there ever be any transition or change? △ Second, the analogy based on nature to clarify:
furthermore, that "form is itself emptiness" is termed *śamatha* (calm abiding); that "emptiness does not annihilate form" is designated as *vipaśyanā* (insight). These are worldly dharmas...
If this is so even for worldly phenomena, how much more so must it be for the Buddha’s virtues, which cannot fail to be eternally active and eternally quiescent?

Even mundane material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are themselves immediately quiescent and immediately observed; such is the principle of the inherent nature (*dharmatā*) that possesses both quiescence and activity.

How much more so for the Buddha’s virtues, which are perfected through cultivation in accordance with the nature (*xing*), wherein the entirety of cultivation manifests the nature itself. How could one allow for any distinction between quiescence and activity?
It is the essence! From the perspective of quiescent stillness, it exists yet is not existent; from the perspective of function, it is non-existent yet existent. What further doubt could there be?
△ Sixth, distinguishing between the eternally abiding and the subject to birth and death.
Question: If the virtues of the Buddha exist and yet are non-existent, and this does not preclude their being eternally abiding, then sentient beings also exist and yet are non-existent;
it should likewise not preclude their being subject to extinction. Answer: The virtues of the Buddha manifest as the principle (*li*) and thereby constitute a conforming function;

therefore, they are eternally abiding. Sentient beings, however, conceal the principle and thereby constitute a contrary function; therefore, they undergo birth and extinction. Although these eternally abiding virtues—
Existence is itself non-existence, yet it is non-existent while being existent; thus, its permanence is not obstructed.
The functioning of arising and ceasing is likewise existence that is itself non-existence, yet non-existent while being existent; thus, its arising and ceasing are not obstructed.
This concludes the explanation of the essential characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* according to the three natures of purity.
The general heading and detailed explanation regarding the essential characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are now complete. △ Third, the summary.
This concludes the third section on the essential characteristics.
Someone may ask: "Are these essential characteristics of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* the same as or different from the ten stages of contemplation (*daśa-yāna-darśana-dharma*)? The answer is: Ten...
The practice of contemplating the Dharma benefits all three faculties. Now, this dharma-gate is taught for those of superior faculty;

therefore it is said that those of superior faculty employ only one [nature], those of middling faculty employ two through seven, and those of inferior faculty employ all ten. Indeed, by means of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), one enters the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature);
by means of the *paratantra-svabhāva*, one enters the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). Thus, by means of the three natures, one enters the three non-natures.
This is precisely the first contemplation of the inconceivable realm: while abiding in the three natures of non-substantiality, one does not destroy the dependent origination of the three natures.
Although the remaining nine dharmas are not explicitly detailed here, each single dharma inherently contains all ten.
Why is this so? The opening passage states: "Excellent, Son of the Buddha, that you are able to give rise to this unsurpassed mind.
Is this not the true and correct arousal of the bodhicitta? Each successive practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—is this not skillful settling of the mind (*anxin*)?

The three natures are non-natures; is this not the universal refutation of all dharmas? Through *śamatha*, one knows that the conventional is itself the ultimate; through *vipaśyanā*, one knows that the ultimate is itself the conventional.

Is this not skillfully discerning what is permeable and what is obstructed? Furthermore, the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the three natures are precisely the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

From this, the evils of two lifetimes are extinguished and the virtues of two lifetimes are produced, giving rise to the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), and the powers (*bala*).

Awakening to the Path—is this not the harmonization of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*)? The subsequent text’s sequential treatment of matters through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—is this not the application of remedies to assist in awakening?
The differences in the removal of hindrances and the attainment of benefits—are these not the successive stages (*bhūmi*)? Cultivating with a resolute mind—is this not patient endurance (*kṣānti*)?
Taking the fruit of Buddhahood as one's goal—is this not the departure from attachment to the semblance-path? △ Fourth, clarifying the severance of hindrances through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
There are three parts: first, the outline; second, the individual explanations; third, the general analysis. Now, for the first [part]:
next, the fourth section clarifies the cessation of hindrances and the attainment of benefits through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Within this, there are again three gates of differentiation:

first, clarifying the cessation of hindrances and the attainment of benefits by way of the *parikalpita-svabhāva*; second, clarifying the cessation of hindrances and the attainment of benefits by way of the *paratantra-svabhāva*.
Third, clarifying the removal of obstacles and the attainment of benefits by means of the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

△ Second, the individual explanations of the three [natures]. First, [the explanation] by means of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) [up to] third, by means of the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*. Within the first [of these], there are two parts.

First, the attainment through the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is explained; second, the attainment through the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*) is explained. The first [section] further has three parts: first, the formal explanation;
second, the illustration by means of a metaphor; third, the application of the principle. Now, the first [part].

First, to clarify the obstacles to be eliminated within the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): this refers to the mind that, failing to understand that objects are empty, clings to them as real.
Since this is ignorance and deluded conceptualization (*avidyā-vikalpa*), it is through the perfection of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) that these are removed.

Because contemplation is perfected, one can eliminate the delusive confusion inherent in ignorance and conceptualization. What is meant by "delusive confusion upon delusion"? It means not knowing that such delusive confusion itself is a delusion.
"Delusion" (*māyā*) is precisely confusion. Because of this confusion, one clings to it as if it were not confusion; this is further delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
This layer of delusive confusion arises based upon the preceding layer; therefore, it is called "delusive confusion upon delusive confusion.
For this reason, although a practitioner has not yet been able to eliminate it or realize that objects are empty, they can nevertheless recognize that this mind is...
"Delusion and falsehood" refers to the higher delusions and illusions that can be eliminated by it; this constitutes the removal of hindrances.
Because the hindrances are removed, one is able to advance in the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding), which constitutes the attainment of benefit.
To eliminate delusion upon delusion is itself cessation; to be capable of practicing the conduct of *śamatha* is itself attainment.
This marks the initial arising of contemplative practice from names. The text is clear and may be understood accordingly. △ Second, the manifestation through analogy.
Furthermore, this delusion upon delusion is further clarified by means of an analogy. For example, when a person mistakes the east for the west, this is a false attachment;

this constitutes one layer of delusion. When another person says to them, "You are currently deluded, mistaking the east for the west," that person still thinks, "What I see is not a delusion. Because they do not understand, they remain attached to it.
To act as one who is not deluded while still harboring delusive thoughts is to generate further delusion upon delusion.
What fault does such a person have? It is said they have the fault of turning their back on their home and wandering aimlessly.
If this person, though not yet awakened, merely follows the words of others and knows with certainty that this mind is delusive, then there is no delusion upon delusion. This...
What benefit does the person obtain? It means that although they have not yet awakened from delusion and ignorance, they nonetheless derive the benefit of heading toward their home.
△ Third, the correspondence with the Dharma:
Although one has not yet realized that all phenomena are empty, merely being able to know that objects are empty is [the cessation of] ignorance; to cling to them as real is delusion.

As for "conception" (*saṃjñā*): it refers to constantly disbelieving that which one clings to, thereby being capable of advancing in the practice of *śamatha* and gradually proceeding toward *nirvāṇa*.
If one is entirely ignorant of this, one will follow the current into the ocean of suffering, increase the three poisons, and turn one's back upon the peaceful abode of *nirvāṇa*.
This clarifies the meaning of severing and attaining through contemplative practice within the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
To know that objects are empty is ignorance; it should be stated that "to know [objects] while failing to realize they are empty is ignorance.

The two characters "failing to realize" (bùliǎo) are missing from the text, but their meaning must be supplied. "Gradually approaching nirvana" corresponds to the benefit of heading toward one's home.

This increases the three poisons and pursues the fault of following along with the surging waves; the rest may be understood accordingly. △ Second, clarifying the cessation-practice for severing and attaining.

Regarding what is called the cessation-practice for removing hindrances and gaining benefit within the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it refers to the method of practice based upon that contemplative cultivation.
Because of this, one is able to know that all phenomena (*dharma*) are originally without reality.

As the grasping at reality ceases, one is thus able to eliminate the ignorance regarding objects and discursive conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that exist at the time of the fruit. Furthermore, greed and hatred gradually become attenuated;

although there may be defilements, they do not constitute karmic bondage. Even if one undergoes suffering and pain, by understanding that suffering is without suffering, one eliminates obstacles. Furthermore, relying upon this...

Because cessation can accomplish the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and because the function of non-objective wisdom (*nirālambana-jñāna*) operates in accordance with the mind, this constitutes the attainment of benefit.
This clarifies that within the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the practice of cessation removes obstacles and brings about benefit.
When the ignorance that deludes regarding phenomena during the stage of fruition is eliminated, one immediately severs the delusion (*moha*) within dependent origination;

furthermore, when false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is removed, one completely severs the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) throughout the three realms. Greed and hatred gradually become thin and faint; this means that while there remains only the affliction that moistens rebirth (*janma-pratisaṃdhāna-kleśa*), the affliction that initiates karma (*karma-samutthāpaka-kleśa*) no longer exists.
Although the conditions for rebirth have not yet been permanently severed, one is already vastly different from those who cling to substantiality, and is thus capable [of further progress].
The function of the wisdom of non-dust arises. △ Second, regarding the dependent nature, there are two parts: first, clarifying the attainment through the severance of contemplative practice;
second, clarifying the attainment through the severance of quiescent practice. Now, the first.
Next, we clarify the cessation and contemplation for abandoning [the dependent nature]. First, we clarify the gate of contemplation.
This gate of contemplation is not different from the gate of cessation regarding the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), yet it possesses a slight distinct meaning. What is this?
It means that the gate of cessation therein necessarily takes all phenomena as objects by way of their being empty; thus, it can dispel ignorance. Because ignorance is extinguished, attachment...

When the mind of reality and falsity ceases, this very elimination of the objectification of the unreal is itself the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
there is no other distinct method. Therefore, when that cessation (*śamatha*) is accomplished, this contemplation is also perfected.

However, because it is able to extinguish the attachment to reality by means of the objectification of the unreal, it is called "cessation. This is precisely because, through knowing the absence of reality, one understands that all phenomena are unreal.

Because the arising through the collection of causes and conditions is not devoid of mental characteristics, it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). That [system] takes the refutation of attachment by means of the reality of cessation as its primary tenet;

this [system] takes the establishment of empty dependent origination as its essential aim. Thus, there is a distinction between them. For this reason, they are identical in their sense of eliminating hindrances.

The benefits obtained are somewhat distinct. What is this distinction? It refers to the fact that by practicing and advancing through these contemplative skillful means, one becomes capable of entering the gate of *śamatha* (calm abiding) regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, one further differentiates into samādhis such as "like an illusion" and so forth; thus, it is said that benefits are obtained.
This is the attainment through the severance of afflictions via contemplative practice within the dependent nature.

The cessation of reality and the breaking of attachments constitute the entry from the conventional into emptiness; the establishment of illusory dependent origination constitutes the entry from emptiness into the conventional.

Thus, one is able to attain samādhis such as "like an illusion" and so forth. The rest may be understood. Part Two: Explaining the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) regarding the abandonment and attainment.
This has two sections: first, the formal explanation; second, the analytical examination. Now, the first section.
Regarding what is called the gate of cessation (*śamatha*) within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which removes obstacles and brings benefit:

it means that by relying on meditative cultivation as a skillful means, one is able to know that all false appearances have the single mind alone as their essence. Therefore, the existence of false appearances is in fact non-existence.

Because one understands in this way, one is able to extinguish the attachment to false appearances; thus, it is named "cessation. By means of this cessation, [one attains the aforementioned benefits].
One is able to eliminate the ignorance regarding the principle that causes delusion at the time of fruition, as well as its illusory manifestations.

Furthermore, as the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) gradually becomes attenuated, this is termed "removing obstacles. One also attains the accomplishment of samādhis such as those of illusion and transformation.

Moreover, the function of the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) manifests before one, whereby one further accomplishes the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) within the sphere of true reality (*tathatā*); this is termed "attaining benefits."

At the stage of fruition, the ignorance that deludes regarding principle consists of the residual habits of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa-vāsanā*) as well as the "dust-like" afflictions within the realms (*dhātu*).
The function of the wisdom of non-arising is the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (*mārgajñatā*). The remainder may be understood accordingly. △ Second, the detailed analysis.

Question: Within the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one also achieves samādhis such as "like an illusion" (*māyopama*). Within this gate of cessation (*śamatha*), one also achieves samādhis such as "like an illusion.
What is the distinction between them? Answer: In the gate of contemplation, one attains them partially; here, in this gate, one achieves them fully.

Furthermore, in the gate of contemplation, one knows that the phenomena of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are like illusions; here, one knows that the phenomena of dependent origination are... [as before].

Quiescence, too, is like an illusion or a magical transformation; thus there is a distinction between them. This clarifies that within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), one practices cessation and cultivation to eliminate hindrances and attain benefit.

One knows that the dependent origination of phenomena is like an illusion; this is merely entering the provisional from the empty. To know that the dependent origination of phenomena is itself quiescent is [the realization of the ultimate].
As for "illusion," it both negates the two extremes and simultaneously illuminates them. △ Third, regarding the nature of reality, there are two parts:

first, clarifying the attainment through the practice of contemplation; second, clarifying the attainment through the practice of quiescence. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the direct explanation;
second, the analytical examination. Now, the first section.

Next, regarding the explanation of the cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) within the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and the resulting benefits from the removal of hindrances: first, the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*) is explained.

This gate of contemplation is initially no different from the gate of cessation (*śamatha-mukha*) within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), yet it possesses a slight distinct meaning. What is this?
This means that the gate of *śamatha* necessarily takes all phenomena as its object, [realizing] they are merely the products of mind. That which exists is itself non-existent;

their essence is the single mind. Therefore, one attains the cessation of the attachment to false appearances. Thus, this is the capacity to know that the essence of all phenomena is solely the single mind.

This means that within this context, there is no other method for the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Therefore, if that tranquility (*śamatha*) is accomplished, this contemplation is immediately realized;

they are not separate from one another. Nevertheless, although both take a single mind as their object, the former takes the characteristic of cessation as its primary tenet, whereas here, although one knows that empty characteristics are non-existent, the aim is to establish the mind.
Thus, there is a distinction between them. Consequently, while their meaning regarding the removal of hindrances is the same, [the methods differ].
