The benefits are slightly different. What is this difference? It means that by relying on this contemplation as a skillful means (*upāya*), one is capable of superior progress into the gate of *śamatha*.
Taking the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) as its thesis negates the two extremes; taking the establishment of the mind as its purport correctly reveals the Middle Way. △ Second.
Discernment. Question:
Is that which is produced by mind-only identical to, or different from, the single mind itself? Answer:

That which is produced by mind-only refers to the arising of all phenomena based upon the mind—appearing as if they exist though they do not—which is precisely the manifestation of characteristics (lakṣaṇa) from the essence (tattva). This is the realization.
"Only this single mind" means that one knows the characteristics arising therein exist yet are non-existent, their essence being the single mind;
this is the realization of entering reality by extinguishing those characteristics. This clarifies the attainment through the practice of contemplation within the nature of ultimate truth.

Arising from the essence as characteristics remains illusory existence; extinguishing these characteristics and entering the reality is to return to the Middle Way. △ Second, clarifying the practice of cessation (*śamatha*), the severing of obstacles, and the attainment of benefits:
what is called the practice of cessation that removes obstacles and gains benefit means that by relying on the aforementioned contemplative practices as skillful means, one comes to know that...
The essence of the single mind is beyond differentiation; from the very beginning, it has been eternally quiescent.

By forming this understanding, the movement of thought ceases, which is termed *śamatha* (calm abiding). Through this practice of *śamatha*, one can extinguish the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-ālaya*) and the habitual tendencies of deluded thoughts;
this is termed the "removal of obstructions. When great awakening manifests and the power of a Buddha is fully realized, this is termed "attaining benefit. This...
This concludes the section on the cessation of practice, the removal of obstacles, and the attainment of benefits within the clarification of true reality (*tattva*).

The headings for the sections and their respective explanations regarding the abandonment and attainment through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are now complete. △ Third: A General Examination of Four Points. 1.
Examining the meaning of the removal of obstacles. 2. Examining the cause for the permeation of the mind. 3. Examining the characteristics of the stages and levels. 4. Concluding with a summary.
[The section on] Clarification. Now, first: Question:
At the time of removing hindrances, is it removed by way of opposing adversaries, or is it removed by the permeation of wisdom? Answer: It cannot be removed through mutual opposition.
Why is this so? Because while the deluded mind is present, that wisdom has not yet arisen; and when that wisdom arises, [the delusion has already ceased].
Delusion has already been extinguished previously; because the preceding and succeeding moments do not perceive one another, they cannot act as adversaries to eliminate each other.

Thus, although the functioning of delusion does not arise due to the emergence of a single moment of the mind of liberation, the seeds of defiled delusion still persist within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and have not yet been extinguished.
Therefore, when that single moment of the mind of liberation ceases, the functioning of delusion arises once more. Such is the nature of the moments of liberation and delusion.
When mindfulness arises repeatedly, its cognitive function gradually perfumes the mind, increasing the power of the nature of understanding and thereby forming the seeds of that cognitive function.
At the very moment those seeds of cognitive function are perfumed, they simultaneously cause the portions of the seeds of afflictive defilements to diminish bit by bit,
just as when one perfumes a foul-smelling garment with incense, the fragrance adheres to the garment incrementally.

At that time, the foul odor vanishes bit by bit; the seeds of delusion (*kleśa-bīja*) are likewise. As the seeds of liberation (*mokṣa-bīja*) develop part by part, delusion is extinguished part by part.

Because the seeds of delusion are extinguished bit by bit, the activity of delusion gradually weakens; because the seeds of liberation increase bit by bit, the activity of liberation becomes increasingly strong. This is how they are eliminated.
It is not like the "elimination through opposition" (*pratipakṣa-nirhāra*) taught in the Hīnayāna, which consists of mere words without substance. However, as for that...
The Hīnayāna also attempts to eliminate [afflictions] through perfuming, yet it does not understand this principle.

The answer is divided into four parts. First, it directly clarifies that they cannot be eliminated as opposites, because the understanding (*jñāna*) and the affliction (*kleśa*) do not exist simultaneously.
Second, fearing the objection: "If it is said that there are no afflictions at the time of understanding, why is it that the one who understands has not yet [attained liberation]?"...

"Are the afflictions completely severed? Now, this is explained: because the seeds of the afflictions still remain, the functioning of the afflictions arises again at the time of their cessation through understanding.
A third doubt may arise: "Since understanding and afflictions alternate in arising, how can one use understanding to eliminate the afflictions?
Now, this is explained: the functioning of understanding gradually perfumes the mind, causing the seeds of understanding to be formed; thus, it is able to diminish and extinguish [the afflictions].
The seeds of delusion are like a foul-smelling garment permeated by fragrance. Fourth, one might fear and doubt:

"If they are removed through gradual perfuming, why does the Hīnayāna speak of 'removal through opposition,' claiming that [the antidote] can also sever the afflictions? We now explain: the Hīnayāna also effects removal through perfuming;
it is simply that they themselves do not realize this, and thus falsely reckon it to be removal through opposition. This is the resolution of the confusion regarding understanding and delusion.
There is no logical principle that contradicts this; therefore, there are merely words without meaning. II. Discerning the Cause for Infusing the Mind. Question:
When explaining the infusion of the mind, does one attain the infusion of the mind by perceiving the pure mind, or is there yet another cause for attaining the infusion of the mind?
Answer: All functions of both delusion and awakening arise based upon the single mind. For this reason, [the infusion occurs].

The function of resolving delusions and attaining enlightenment does not depart from the mind. Because it does not depart from the mind, at the moment its function arises, it immediately perfumes the mind itself;
there is no other source. This is like the function of waves, which do not depart from water: when the waves move, they move the very substance of the water.
Thus, because the movement of the preceding wave moves the water, subsequent waves arise once more. This is the nature of resolving delusions and attaining enlightenment.
The perfuming [of this] is also like this; it may be understood by analogy.
When one understands the perfuming of the mind, one does not perceive a pure mind, nor is there anything else from which it arises.
This is because the pure mind is not a perceptible characteristic, and because there is no other dharma external to the mind that can serve as a basis. Thus, both delusion and awakening are...
It arises based on the mind and, in turn, perfumes the mind; it is just like waves arising based on water and, in turn, moving the water.
△ Third, distinguishing the characteristics of the stages and grounds.
Question: Do these three natures (trisvabhāva) have specific stages and grounds for their śamatha and vipaśyanā, or do they have no such stages and grounds? Answer: They are not fixed. If...

From the perspective of a single interpretation: the practice of cessation is accomplished within the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) during the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*);

it is accomplished within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) during the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*); and it is accomplished within the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) when the fruit of Buddhahood is fulfilled.

Alternatively, according to another interpretation: the practice of cessation is accomplished within the *parikalpita-svabhāva* prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*); it is accomplished within the *paratantra-svabhāva* upon the stages (*bhūmi-gata*); and the fruit of Buddhahood is likewise fulfilled therein.

The practice of cessation (*śamatha*) is perfected within the true nature (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), one possesses the practice of cessation characterized by the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) according to one's respective capacity;

on the stages themselves, one likewise possesses the practice of cessation characterized by the three natures; and at the stage of Buddhahood, the practice of cessation characterized by the three natures is ultimately fulfilled.

Moreover, in each successive stage, the practices are conjoined with the three types of cessation; even an ordinary person who has first resolved to attain enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika*) likewise conjoins the practice of cessation characterized by the three natures.
There is only a distinction between clarity and obscurity; there is no difference in their reliance upon the Dharma.

When the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and *śamatha-vipaśyanā* are correlated with the stages (*bhūmi*) of the bodhisattvas, they may be arranged vertically, horizontally, inclusively, or selectively;

therefore, they are not fixed. First, speaking from the perspective of a single characteristic, this refers to the vertical arrangement. "Ten Resolutions" (*daśa-adhimukti*) refers specifically to the ten stages (*daśa-vihāra*).

Because they have permanently severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *kleśa-kleśa*), the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*)—referring both to the distinct [Vaipulya] ten dedications and the circular ten faiths—are so named;
for they have permanently severed the afflictions of the "dust-like sands" (*rajas*) while simultaneously suppressing the afflictions of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The Buddha-fruit refers to the distinct stages and the circular stage of Abiding, all of which are termed "partial realization"; reaching the ultimate position constitutes the "fulfillment," because one has permanently severed the afflictions of ignorance.

Next, another interpretation is as follows: it encompasses both the vertical and horizontal dimensions. On the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*), because it is "cultivation through conditions," the cessation and practice of the two types—the defiled and the pure—of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) are accomplished.
On the grounds themselves, because it is "true cultivation," the cessation and practice of the two types—the defiled and the pure—of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) are accomplished.

At the stage of Buddhahood, because it is "fulfilled realization," the cessation and practice of the two types—the defiled and the pure—of the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) are accomplished.
Furthermore, regarding the stages prior to the [first] ground and so forth, there is both a horizontal and a vertical dimension.

This is because, based solely on the other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one inherently possesses all three natures. Therefore, those who practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* must also cultivate them in a comprehensive manner.

However, for those prior to the grounds, this is called "partial possession," because ignorance (*avidyā*) is suppressed but not yet severed. For those on the grounds and above, it is called "full possession," because the three delusions are simultaneously severed and the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) are manifested.

For these reasons, the stage of Buddhahood is termed "ultimate fulfillment. Through the ultimate fulfillment of the practice of analytical cessation (*vibhāga-śamatha*), the liberation virtue of the Nirmāṇakāya is accomplished;
through the ultimate fulfillment of the practice of dependent cessation (*paratantra-śamatha*), the prajñā virtue of the Saṃbhogakāya is accomplished.
Because the practice of true cessation (śamatha) is ultimately fulfilled, one accomplishes the merit of the Tathatā-dharmakāya.
Next, furthermore, in each and every stage, it is neither vertical nor horizontal, yet both horizontal and vertical.

From the very beginning, within the stage of names and letters, one understands the present, momentary thought of this very instant, as well as the provisional and real dharmas of the ten realms and the ten suchnesses; according to what is seen, there is...

All phenomena that accord with the mind are, in their entirety, phenomena of the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). These phenomena, in their essential substance, lack reality;

they are thus phenomena of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). The dependent nature, moreover, lacks intrinsic nature; it is simply the true mark of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-lakṣaṇa*), which constitutes the phenomenon of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Therefore, at the very moment one first generates the aspiration for enlightenment, one attains the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) practiced in tandem. However, even within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), [one still...]

It is obscure; it becomes clear within the stage of semblance. Even within the stage of semblance it remains somewhat obscure, yet it becomes increasingly clear within the stage of partial realization.
Within the stage of partial realization it still carries traces of obscurity, but only in the ultimate stage does it become perfectly clear.

Nevertheless, from beginning to end, there are no instances where the dharmas of the three natures are not taken as the object of observation; therefore, it is said that there is no separate [object] apart from the dharmas.
△ Fourth, the summary of the concise exposition.

Furthermore, this provides a general explanation of how the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) removes obstacles and brings about benefits. That is to say:

because the practice of *śamatha* regarding the three natures is perfected, one leaves behind the conduct of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Because the practice of *vipaśyanā* regarding the three natures is perfected, one leaves behind the conduct of the Śrāvakas. This is called "removing obstacles. [The practice of] *śamatha* regarding the three natures...

Because the practice is accomplished, one attains the bliss of quiescence as self-benefit; because the practice of contemplating the three natures is accomplished, its functioning as an object-condition serves as benefit for others.
This constitutes the attainment of benefits. Thus concludes the fourth section: the cessation and attainment of śamatha and vipaśyanā.

Someone asked: "If 'stopping' (śamatha) merely accomplishes the departure from the practices of ordinary beings and is simply the intention of entering emptiness, and if 'contemplation' (vipaśyanā) merely accomplishes the departure from the practices of śrāvakas and is simply the intention of emerging into the provisional, then—since these exist between the Shared and Distinct [teachings]—is it not excessive to explain them as Perfect and Sudden?
The answer was: "If one were to discuss stopping and contemplation solely in terms of the defiled and turbid nature of discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva), that would be acceptable."

However, this pertains to the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya*). If one discusses *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* solely in terms of the two natures—parikalpita and paratantra—it may be understood as the Separate Teaching connecting to the Shared (*bie-tong-jie*).
If one discusses *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* solely in terms of the sequence of the three natures as defiled and turbid, it may be understood as being exclusively the Separate Teaching.
Now, since this [text] fully addresses both the defiled and pure aspects of the three natures, and furthermore fully discusses both the sequential and...

This does not follow the two types of sequential cultivation methods. Furthermore, within each of the [three] natures, one always practices contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) first and then cessation (*śamatha*), rather than cessation first and contemplation later.
Moreover, even ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) can simultaneously cultivate both cessation and contemplation at this very moment;

how could this not be the Perfect and Sudden Teaching? One must understand that there is a distinction between ordinary beings and *śrāvakas* regarding the internal and external realms, as well as birth through segmented succession (*pariccheda-jāti*).
The practice of ordinary beings within the realm of death; the practice of ordinary beings outside the realm of transformative birth-and-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*).
The practice of *śrāvakas* who stagnate in the realm of mere emptiness; the practice of *śrāvakas* who stagnate in the realm of mere *madhyamaka*.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "There are *śrāvakas* of the *śrāvaka-vehicle*; there are *pratyekabuddhas* of the *śrāvaka-vehicle*; there are [others] of the *śrāvaka-vehicle*."
There are śrāvakas of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, there are pratyekabuddhas of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and there are bodhisattvas of the pratyekabuddha vehicle.
There are śrāvakas of the bodhisattva vehicle, there are pratyekabuddhas of the bodhisattva vehicle, and there are bodhisattvas of the bodhisattva vehicle.

The Great Master Zhi explained this as follows: the first three [stages] correspond to the Three Vehicles of the Tripitaka Teaching; the next three correspond to the Three Vehicles of the Shared Teaching;
and the subsequent three correspond to the stages prior to the Grounds and the Grounds themselves in the Distinct Teaching.

Practitioners today, from their very first aspiration, practice the three types of cessation and the three types of contemplation, thereby immediately departing from the conduct of ordinary beings and Śrāvakas—this is what is called the five grades of the Perfect Teaching.

Stage. Having perfectly subdued the afflictions of the five abodes, although this is still the fleshly eye, it is already termed the Buddha-eye. One has already transcended the ten stages of returning [of] the Separate Teaching.

It must be understood that the preceding four sections concerning the stages have their primary intent solely in the fourth, which discusses the horizontal and vertical in terms of being neither horizontal nor vertical.
△ Fifth, explaining the function of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, in three parts: first, the direct explanation; second...
Verse: The Three Bonds. In the first [section], there are three parts: first, fully manifesting the function; second, again clarifying the basis;

third, once more indicating the expedient means. The first part has four sub-sections: first, the function of realizing the whole essence and great utility; second, the function of dual negation and dual illumination;
third, the function of being free from faults and possessing virtues; fourth, the function of fusing identity and difference while transcending the subtle.

Application. First, we now proceed to clarify the fifth point: the functions of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). This means that because the practice of *śamatha* has been perfected, one realizes the pure mind as the essence and the nature of non-dual integration;
one’s body becomes perfectly identical in its single characteristic with all sentient beings. At this point, the Three Jewels are indistinguishably merged.
There are not three. The two truths are, from this, vast and non-dual. It is profound and still; it is deep, settled, and tranquil.
Internally lucid and quiescent, its functioning lacks the mark of functioning, and its movement lacks the mark of movement. This is because all dharmas are fundamentally equal.
Because the nature of the mind is thus by its very essence, this is the substance of the profoundly deep *dharmatā*.

That is to say, because contemplative practice is perfected, the substance of the pure mind manifests, and the unimpeded function of the *dharmadhātu* spontaneously gives rise to all capacities for both defilement and purity.

It produces great offerings that fill boundless lands, presenting them to the Triple Gem and bestowing them upon the four classes of beings, as well as [the power to] absorb the winds and store them within.

The fire emits light that shakes the earth; it draws out the short and prolongs the long, merging the many into the one. With diverse forms, it divides into the six realms of existence; with its echoes, it reaches the ten directions.

Through the manifestation of the five supernatural powers and the revelation of the three wheels of conversion, he ascends as far as the pinnacle of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and dwells below in the Tuṣita heaven.
He entrusts his shadow to the gate of wisdom-illusion and attains spiritual penetration through the path of skillful means. He brandishes his two hands...
To manifest his unique supremacy, he took seven steps to reveal his absolute transcendence. Seated upright upon the jade terrace, he contemplated beneath the jeweled trees;
he brilliantly illuminated the Universal Eye within the palaces of the six heavens and universally turned the perfect sound throughout the lands of the ten directions.
The Lotus Treasury Ocean unfolded its imperial net, while the various realms of the Sahā world were arrayed like stars in the constellations. Thus, he caused those of identical form yet different...

One sees that what is proclaimed is singular, yet what is heard is manifold; external forms manifest in various ways, and extraordinary radiance displays a chaotic spectrum of colors. Thus, while the Five Mountains shine eternally, the Eight Trees remain in hidden splendor;
the jade-like essence abides forever, while the provisional form undergoes extinction. This is entirely due to the power of the habitual perfuming of great compassion and great vows.
It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, produced by the single mind; it is precisely the function of profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Through the perfection of the practice of cessation (*śamatha*), one realizes the complete embodiment [of reality]; through the perfection of the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one is able to give rise to great function.
This is a general clarification of the primary aspects of these functions. The wisdom that is capable of realizing the three truths is called the Buddha Jewel;

the principle of the three natures that is realized is called the Dharma Jewel; and the fact that there is no wisdom outside of principle and no principle outside of wisdom is called the Sangha Jewel.

Therefore, in their fundamental unity, they are not three. To differentiate the two natures—the dependent and the imagined—is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The nature of ultimate reality is called absolute truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Furthermore, all three natures are collectively termed conventional truth, while the absence of intrinsic nature in those three natures is termed absolute truth.

Moreover, the three natures and the three absences of intrinsic nature, as established through verbal designation, are both termed conventional truth; whereas the fact that the three natures and the three absences of intrinsic nature are fundamentally only...

The single mind is called the True Truth; thus, it is vast and non-dual. The rest may be understood accordingly. △ Second, clarifying the function of simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination:

Furthermore, because the practice of cessation (*śamatha*) is perfected, the mind is equanimous and does not dwell in saṃsāra. Because the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is perfected, its virtuous functions engage with conditions.

Arising, he does not enter nirvana. Furthermore, because the practice of cessation is perfected, he abides in great nirvana; because the practice of contemplation is perfected, he dwells within birth and death.
"Neither abiding nor entering" is the simultaneous negation (shuangzhe); "being able to abide and being able to dwell" is the simultaneous illumination (shuangzhao). △ Third, clarifying detachment.
It transcends the functions of conditioned qualities.
Furthermore, because the practice of *śamatha* is perfected, one is not defiled by the world; because the practice of *vipaśyanā* is perfected, one does not stagnate in quiescence.

Moreover, because the practice of *śamatha* is perfected, one is eternally quiescent even while acting; because the practice of *vipaśyanā* is perfected, one acts even while being eternally quiescent.

Being unstained and unimpeded is the departure from faults; the functioning of quiescent functioning is the possession of virtues. △ Fourth, clarifying the subtle function of integration, identity, separation, and transcendence:

Furthermore, because the practice of cessation is perfected, one knows that birth-and-death is itself nirvana. Because the practice of contemplation is perfected, one knows that nirvana is itself [birth-and-death].
This is birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, because the practice of cessation (*śamatha*) is perfected, one knows that both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are unattainable.
Because the practice of insight (*vipaśyanā*) is perfected, one knows that the very process of transmigration is birth-and-death, while non-transmigration is nirvāṇa.
All phenomena have, from the very beginning, been characterized by constant quiescence; because they do not undergo further extinction, birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*.
Since the *nirvāṇa* realized by the two vehicles is still a flow of true permanence, it is itself "transformative birth-and-death" (*pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa*).
This is a discussion of their mutual fusion and identity based on contrast. Both types of birth-and-death are fundamentally devoid of the characteristics of birth-and-death.
Just as when waves arise they are immediately water, so birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, *nirvāṇa* lacks even the characteristic of being *nirvāṇa*;
it is like the entirety of water existing within the waves. Thus, *nirvāṇa* is itself birth-and-death. This is the non-dualistic discourse of mutual fusion and identity.
Because it is eternally unchanging while following conditions, both birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa* are equal; there is no distinction between them.
One characteristic can be apprehended, namely that its entry is detachment. Because it does not change but constantly follows conditions:
following the conditions of transmigration is called birth-and-death; following the conditions of non-transmigration is called nirvana. This is what is meant by its exit being subtle.
The initial detailed exposition of the activity is concluded. △ Second, a further clarification of the basis. Question:
At the time when a bodhisattva arises from quiescence to manifest activity, among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), upon which nature does he rely to achieve this?
Answer: Because the bodhisattva relies on the principle of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), he is able to achieve the arising of activity from within quiescence; furthermore—
He employs other natures to assist in accomplishing the path of transformation. What is the meaning of this?

It means that although he knows all phenomena exist yet are non-existent, he simultaneously knows that their non-existence does not preclude their existence; thus, there is the manifestation of what appears to be phenomena, yet they are not non-existent.

Why is this? Because it is the very nature (*dharmatā*) of dependently originated phenomena. Therefore, while the Bodhisattva constantly abides in samādhi, he is able to give rise to a mind of compassion.

One contemplates sentient beings. Furthermore, by means of the gate of contemplation on the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one knows that all sentient beings undergo great suffering and affliction.
By means of the gate of contemplation on the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one brings forth the function of gathering and transforming [beings] from the mind.

By means of the gate of contemplation on the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one knows that all sentient beings are of the same substance as oneself. By means of the gate of cessation based on the nature of discrimination... one knows.

All sentient beings can eliminate defilement and attain purity. Because they rely on the gate of cessation through the *paratantra-svabhāva*, they do not perceive the characteristics of a savior or those to be saved.
Because they rely on the gate of cessation through the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*, their own bodies and the bodies of others are fundamentally and eternally abiding in Great Parinirvāṇa.

In the response, two meanings are first indicated, followed by their respective explanations. Specifically, the passage beginning with "Although one knows all phenomena" explains the principle of relying on the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
Subsequently, the passage beginning with "Then, based on the *parikalpita*" explains how the other natures assist in accomplishing the path of transformation.

Because from *śamatha* one gives rise to *vipaśyanā* (insight), wishing to know that all phenomena are produced by the mind. Therefore, regarding all phenomena, there is... [omitted].

According to the capacities of sentient beings and what should be seen or heard, matters are spontaneously accomplished without the arising of intentional thought. It is, for example, like...

he does not form a mental intention regarding his activities, yet he accords with that which benefits others.
This is achieved because his practice during the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas has been thoroughly matured; there is no other method besides this.

First, the skillful means of initial practice are clarified; next, the differences between long-term practice and Buddhahood are clarified. However, without the initial practice as a cause, how could there be long-term practice?
Without long-term practice, how could one attain Buddhahood? Thus, it is known that those who wish to become Buddhas must study the skillful means of initial practice.

"The nature of the mind is inherently pure; all phenomena are but the single mind. This mind is itself sentient beings; this mind is the bodhisattva and the Buddha."
Birth and death are also the mind; nirvana is also the mind. A single mind manifests as two, yet these two still lack the characteristic of duality.
The single mind is like the great ocean: its nature is eternally of one flavor, yet it possesses all manner of meanings; it is an inexhaustible treasury of dharmas.
The first line provides a general verse on the true essence (*tattva*). The next line subsumes phenomena (*dharma*) into principle (*li*);
there is not a single phenomenon that is not entirely the mind itself. The subsequent four lines show how the entire principle manifests as phenomena;

there is not a single phenomenon that fully embodies the principle which does not further possess the various dharmas of sentient beings, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and nirvāṇa. Thus, the one mind functions as two. This is not... [text ends].

The meaning of "change" is that which constantly follows conditions (*pratyaya*). Second, the meaning of the identity of the non-dual aspects is that while following conditions, it is eternally unchanging.

This can be understood through the analogy of the ocean. △ Second, the verse on the contemplation of phenomena has three parts: first, the explanation by way of principle; second, the explanation by way of analogy; third, the application and conclusion. Now, the first part.
Therefore, practitioners should at all times observe their own body and mind, knowing that they arise entirely because the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has been perfumed by defiled karma.
Once it is known that the Tathāgatagarbha manifests as worldly phenomena through such perfuming, one should understand the true nature of sentient beings.

All are the Tathāgatagarbha; furthermore, one should contemplate the true mind as the treasury. According to the perfuming, it produces worldly phenomena; if perfumed by pure karma, the treasury will surely produce the fruit of Buddhahood.
Observing one’s own body and mind means practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* with respect to the defiled discriminative nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Knowing that all [phenomena] arise because the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is perfumed by defiled karma means practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* with respect to the defiled dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

One should understand that the essence of sentient beings is entirely the Tathāgatagarbha; this is practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* with respect to the defiled perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, one contemplates the four phrases beginning with "the true nature of the storehouse" (*tathāgatagarbha*). By using the defiled as an analogy for the pure, one thus cultivates *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* based on the three natures of purity.
Furthermore, that the *tathāgatagarbha* manifests as worldly phenomena through the influence of perfuming (*vāsanā*) demonstrates that it is unchanging while constantly following conditions.
That the essence of sentient beings is entirely the *tathāgatagarbha* is the understanding that while it follows conditions, it is eternally unchanging.
Since the worldly dharmas are thus, the same applies by analogy to the fruit of Buddhahood. In terms of their nature (*dhātu*), they are one in true equality;

in terms of cultivation, the cause is fulfilled and the fruit is perfected. Therefore, one must necessarily rely upon the single mind and diligently practice wondrous *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. △ Second, the explanation by way of analogy.
It is like seeing a golden snake; knowing it was fashioned by hammering gold, one immediately understands that the substance of the snake is nothing but refined and malleable gold.

Furthermore, one reflects that as the gold followed the artisan to take the form of a snake or an insect, so too one knows that the gold constituting the body of the snake will follow the artisan to become a Buddha image.
The snake metaphor represents the defiled discriminative nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). The beating [of the gold] metaphor represents the defiled dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The fact that the body of the snake is purely malleable gold represents the defiled true nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Furthermore, the metaphor of beating gold to form a snake illustrates "following conditions without changing" (*avikṛta-anuvartana*).

The analogy of the snake’s body being pure gold illustrates that which remains unchanged despite following conditions. The snake’s body being gold represents the nature of the mind in the present moment.
The artisan represents the dharma-gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. The completion of the Buddha image represents the realization of the pure Dharmakāya, free from obstructions.
△ Third, the synthesis and conclusion.

The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is like pure gold; it possesses both the nature of opposition and compliance, and can manifest the fruits of ordinary beings and sages according to defiled or pure karma.
Just as gold can be fashioned into a snake or an image—thus possessing the dual natures of snake and image—it can accordingly be beaten by a craftsman into the form of a snake.
The storehouse consciousness is likewise: fundamentally possessing the two natures of opposition and compliance, it can accordingly follow either the defiled or the pure.
Karma manifests as both the fruits of ordinary beings and sages; yet, while it is manifesting as a snake, its nature as an image remains. Therefore, one can transform the snake into the image.
Thus, we know that while one is in a state of defilement, the pure nature remains, and so one can transform from an ordinary being into a sage.
The snake-image is not the Buddha-image, and thus requires cultivation and realization. But the gold of the Buddha is the very gold of the snake; therefore, they are eternally equal.

Those who cling to nature while abandoning cultivation, or who cling to cultivation while obscuring nature, how could they know the Dharma-gate of the Dharma-realm that is both eternally identical and eternally distinct?
The two verses on the contemplation of the Dharma are concluded. △ Third, the verses on the exhortation to practice.
For this reason, quickly cultivate untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) to perfume the pure mind, so that you may swiftly achieve impartial virtue.
Therefore, at this very moment, do not despise yourself, nor treat others with contempt; for ultimately, all shall together attain Buddhahood.

A pure mind is the cause, and pure karma is the condition. Since a cause must rely upon conditions, one must swiftly cultivate the conditions of untainted karma to perfume the true cause of the pure mind, thereby bringing forth its originally inherent, equal, and wondrous virtue.
Since my own mind is identical to Buddha-nature, how can I treat it with contempt? "Treat" (yu) means to employ.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; how can I despise others? Since I neither disparage myself nor despise others, this is called the equal Buddha-virtue. △ Third, the conclusion.

Because it is produced by the power of the practitioner’s own mind. It is like a person who, upon seeing a beautiful woman, conceives a passionate thought. Question: The first instance of offering you mentioned may indeed have a valid basis and be no different from making an offering in the presence [of the Buddha].
However, this subsequent instance of visualizing the Buddha’s body lacks such a basis. Why? Because one does not actually see the Buddha’s body;
to visualize it as being seen is merely a characteristic of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Answer: When the Buddha was in the world, all...
The Buddhas seen before one by sentient beings are likewise produced by the sentient beings' own minds. Therefore, the sutra says:
"The mind creates all Tathāgatas. For this reason, when one immediately brings a Buddha to mind through mental visualization, it is identical to seeing a Buddha appearing before one.
△ Second, it is far superior to the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

Furthermore, it even surpasses those of the Two Vehicles who perceive the Buddha through direct vision. Why is this? Because the Buddhas perceived by those of the Two Vehicles are actually produced from the mind;
due to ignorance, they have distorted views born of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), claiming that [the Buddha] comes from the outside, rather than being the mind itself.
Because it is thus constructed, it is a perversion and does not accord with the meaning of the mind-nature’s dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Therefore, a sutra states: "The śrāvakas have crooked views. Furthermore, another sutra states: "These people walk upon a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.

That which is called the Tathāgata is the pure mind of true suchness (*tathatā*) manifested as the fruit of dependent origination through the influence of perfuming (*vāsanā*); for this reason, it is named the Tathāgata. He...
This means that because [the Buddha] comes from something external and distinct from the mind, it is said that one cannot see Him.

The various Buddhas whom I now perceive, although produced by the conceptualizing mind, are nonetheless known to manifest within the mind due to the perfuming of the true mind by my own thoughts and recollections of the Buddhas.
Therefore, the Buddhas who are seen do not exist outside the mind; they are solely the manifestations of the true mind. To say they "exist" is itself a negation.
Existence and non-existence are themselves existence; it does not destroy true quiescence, nor does it destroy dependent origination. Therefore, it surpasses the direct vision of the two vehicles.

The two vehicles do not realize that all is mind-only, whereas this [realization] does; this is the first excellence. When the two vehicles enter quiescence, they [thereby] destroy [dependent origination].
Regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): this does not subvert dependent origination; this is the second excellence. △ Third, [the analogy of] the path being level with a bodhisattva:

Furthermore, if one were to say that because the true mind is perfumed by the conceptualizing mind, the nature of the true mind arises to manifest the Buddhas, and thus these are merely false imaginings—then the assembly at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) all perfumes the true mind through the karma of seeing the Buddha; thus, Vairocana...
That Buddha appears within the true mind. Those bodhisattvas are likewise products of deluded thought (*vikalpa*).
If the Buddhas seen by those bodhisattvas truly arise from the mind, they would know at the very moment of seeing them that they do not come from without; thus, they would not be deluded thoughts.
Since the Buddhas I now see also arise from the mind and I likewise know they do not come from without, why do you say [they are deluded thoughts]?
This is delusion. Furthermore, all the karmic practices for seeing the Buddha cultivated by those bodhisattvas are entirely created by the mind and, in turn, perfumes the mind.
My current thought of mindfulness of the Buddha is likewise created by the mind and, in turn, perfumes the mind.
Since these two are equal, if theirs is not delusory, then mine is truly real.

The first section, "Elucidating that Conceptualization is Not False," is concluded. △ Second, "Elucidating that Response and Induction are Both Accomplished," in four parts: First, further elucidating the nature of the mind as being of one substance;
second, elucidating how one sees the True Buddha through the power of conceptual thought; third, discussing the mutual permeation of the mind in the context of producing and becoming a Buddha;
fourth, concluding that response and induction are non-dual. Now, the first part.
Question: If all Buddhas are produced solely by the minds of sentient beings themselves, then there would be no actual Buddhas appearing in the world.
Answer: This does not preclude the appearance of all Buddhas in the world; rather, their appearance is precisely what is produced by the minds of sentient beings themselves.
Why is this? It is because all Buddhas and all sentient beings share the same pure mind (*viśuddha-citta*).

Because it is the essence. Thus, this pure mind manifests its entire substance as a single sentient being, yet it does not hinder its entire substance from simultaneously manifesting as all ordinary and holy beings.
Just as one sentient being is the manifestation of the entire substance of the pure mind, so it is for every single ordinary or holy being.
They exist at once as a single substance without mutual obstruction. Therefore, if one relies exclusively on a single...
Regarding those who discuss the mind: the substance of this mind is capable of producing all ordinary beings and sages.
This meaning is explained within the discussion on the identity and difference of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). For this reason, all Buddhas are produced solely by my own mind.
However, because of the meaning of consciousness as both common and uncommon characteristics, although my own mind is capable of becoming all Buddhas,
there is the principle of seeing and not seeing, as is clearly explained within the discussion of consciousness as common and uncommon characteristics.
That which is produced by the minds of sentient beings is itself the Real Buddha; the Real Buddha is itself that which is produced by the minds of sentient beings.

This is because all Buddhas and all sentient beings have the same pure mind as their essence. If one realizes the meaning of the identity and difference of the essence and the storehouse mentioned in the preceding text, then one will not conceive of the Real Buddha as being outside of one's own mind. If one realizes...
Regarding the meaning of common and uncommon characteristics as perceived by consciousness, one will no longer doubt that sentient beings have both seeing and not seeing [the Buddha].
△ Second, clarifying that through the perception based on thought, one can see the true Buddha.
For this reason, if one can employ skillful means to engage in mental visualization, this visualization will permeate the true mind (*tathatā-citta*).
Because it accords with the permeation of the Buddhas' compassion and wisdom, the Buddhas appear within the true mind, and one naturally perceives them.
These manifested Buddhas arise because one's own karmic activity of visualizing the Buddha through mental construction accords with the Buddhas' activity of benefiting others.
Because it arises from the perfuming of the mind, this Buddha is one with whom I share a common recognition.
Since he is one with whom I share a common recognition, he is the true, supramundane Buddha perceived by me.
If there were no karma of seeing the Buddha and no perfuming of the mind corresponding to the Buddha’s virtue of benefiting others, then although all Buddhas are produced by my own pure mind, I—
One constantly fails to see the Buddha.
Taking "inspiration" (gan) as the capacity to evoke and "compassionate wisdom" (bei-zhi) as the capacity to respond:

because one evokes the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings, there is no Buddha outside the mind; because one responds to the sentient beings within the minds of the Buddhas, the appearance of the Buddha is truly real. △
The Buddhas of the three periods mutually discourse upon the perfuming of the mind.
Therefore, if one were to rely solely on the Buddhas to discuss the pure mind, it would mean that the pure minds of all Buddhas constitute all sentient beings;
however, because the Buddhas possess the power of wisdom and compassion to perfume the mind, they are able to perceive all sentient beings. If one were to rely solely on...
Sentient beings take their pure mind as the discourse; thus, the pure mind of sentient beings constitutes all Buddhas.
It is simply because sentient beings possess the karma for seeing the Buddhas, which perfumes their minds, that they are able to see all Buddhas.
The Buddha is the Dharma-realm; therefore, there are no sentient beings outside the Buddha-mind. Sentient beings are the Dharma-realm; therefore, there is no Buddha outside the sentient-being mind.
Since they are mutually perfumed and mutually perceived by themselves, what cause for doubt could there be? △ Fourth, concluding that response and stimulus are non-dual.
Therefore, for one whose mind is permeated by mental imagery, the Buddhas manifest within the very mind. The Buddha who is thus seen is the true, supramundane Buddha.

If one does not understand this meaning and instead asserts that Śākyamuni Tathāgata is a real Buddha existing outside the mind, or that the Buddha created by mental visualization is a Buddha produced through deluded conceptualization—such a person, even if they see Śākyamuni...
Even the Tathāgata Kāśyapa does not recognize him.
It is conventionally conceived that the sentient being is the "sender" (the one who evokes) and the Real Buddha is the "respondent" (the one who answers).

Since the Real Buddha who is evoked does not exist outside the mind of the sentient being, how could the sentient being who is responded to exist outside the mind of Śākyamuni? This is what is meant by the non-duality of response and evocation.

Furthermore, if one calculates erroneously that Śākyamuni truly exists outside the mind, and that what is conceived is not the true Buddha, such a person walks the path of deviance and cannot see the Tathāgata.
The above concludes the Contemplation of the Buddha’s Body. △ Second, the Contemplation of the Offerings.
Furthermore, since the practitioner has thus realized that all Buddhas are produced by the mind,

they should know that both the body and the offering implements likewise arise from the concentrated mind. For this reason, one should visualize one's own body and mind as being like the King of Fragrance-Treasuries (Gandhagarbharāja),
with clouds of fragrant smoke flowing forth from within every pore of the body— clouds so inconceivable that they fill [all space].
In the lands of the ten directions, before each of the Buddhas, great fragrant pavilions are formed.
Within these fragrant pavilions, immeasurable fragrance-devas hold exquisite incense in their hands to make offerings to the Most Victorious Ones.

Or again, one may visualize oneself pervading the lands of the ten directions, with as many bodies as there are Buddhas, personally attending the Tathāgatas. Each of those individual bodies is like...
The Great Brahmā King, whose physical form was most sublime and wondrous, prostrated with his five limbs at the Honored One’s feet.
He knew that both his body and the offerings were entirely produced by a single mind, and he gave rise to no deluded attachments, such as thinking they existed apart from the mind.

Furthermore, he knew that all the offering implements possessed by the various bodhisattvas were entirely given to all sentient beings, so that they might make offerings to the Buddhas; therefore, those offering implements are themselves—
"I already possess [these things]. Because I know they are my own, I hold them to offer to all Tathāgatas.

Having created objects with my own mind, and having given them to others as my own, I further dedicate them to sentient beings to present to the Most Victorious Ones. Only by deeply entering the contemplation of dependent origination can one perform this deed.
This is the gate of contemplation for bowing to the Buddha."

The text consists of eight sections. First, from "Furthermore, the practitioner... onwards: having realized that it is the mind that creates the Buddha, one may then create the body and the offering implements from the mind.
Second, the three verses beginning with "One should imagine one's own body and mind... describe the pervasiveness of the offerings being made.
Third, the two verses beginning with "Or again, one should imagine one's own body... describe the pervasiveness of the one who makes the offerings. Fourth...
1. "Knowing that the body and the ritual implements are one" (one verse) refers to the simultaneous practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

2. "Furthermore, knowing all bodhisattvas... (the following two verses) refers to the non-duality of self and others. 3. "Creating objects with one's own mind" (one verse) refers to skillful dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). 4.
"Deeply entering the contemplation of dependent origination" (two lines) serves as a concluding praise of its efficacy. 5. "This gate of contemplation" [is] the homage.
"Buddha-phrase" (佛句) serves as a summary of the preceding text. △ Second, the Section on Cessation (止門).
Regarding worshiping the Buddha through the gate of cessation: one should know that all Buddhas, as well as one's own body and all ritual implements, are produced from the mind.
They exist yet are not existent; they are solely this single mind, and yet one must not grasp at the characteristics of this single mind.
Why is this? Because there are no phenomena external to the mind that can grasp the characteristics of this mind.
If there were such things as a grasper and a grasped, they would be merely false and devoid of intrinsic nature. To pay homage in this manner is what is called the gate of *śamatha*.
All arise from the mind; this is the nature of signlessness (*animitta*). Existence is non-existence; this is the nature of non-arising (*anutpāda*). It is solely the one mind;
this is the nature of no-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Furthermore, not grasping at the characteristics of the one mind is the nature of no-true-nature (*atattvasvabhāva*).
△ Third, the simultaneous operation.

Furthermore, one must not abandon the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) simply because one is engaged in the practice of tranquility (*śamatha*). One should practice both tranquility and contemplation together.

This means that although one knows that the Buddha’s body, one’s own body, and all objects of offering are in essence but a single mind, one nevertheless gives rise from that very mind to the functioning of dependent origination to perform fervent offerings.
And yet, even while performing these fervent offerings, one simultaneously maintains the knowledge that [all things] exist [only as such].
That which is non-existent is merely this single mind, which is equanimous and free from discursive thought. Therefore, a sutra says:

"Making offerings to the immeasurable billions of Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions, one perceives no marks of distinction between the Buddhas and one's own body. This is the simultaneous practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā.

The first section, explaining *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* during the time of prostrating to the Buddha, is concluded. △ Second, explaining *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* during the time of eating, in two parts:

first, the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); second, the gate of stillness (*śamatha*). Within the first [the gate of contemplation], there are two parts: first, the contemplation of universal offering; second, the contemplation of eliminating greed. Within the first [of these], there are again two parts: first, the contemplation of transforming the coarse into the sublime;
second, the contemplation of transforming the little into the much. This is the first [of those].
In all instances of eating, there are likewise two gates: cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding what is called "contemplation":
when first obtaining food, for the sake of making an offering to the Buddha, one should immediately reflect that this food is created by my own mind.
I should now transform the appearance of this coarse food into a sublime flavor. Why? Because one knows that all phenomena originally arise from the mind and, in turn, return to the mind.
Having made this reflection, he then visualizes the vessel that contains [the food] as a bowl made of the seven precious substances;
he visualizes the food and drink within it as the supreme flavors of the heavens, or as nectar (*amṛta*), or as non-glutinous rice, or as rock honey (*śarkarā*).

Or [one may visualize] ghee, curd, various excellent foods, and so forth. Having formed this visualization, one then takes these imagined foods and offers them to all sentient beings, together with whom one makes offerings to the Triple Gem and the four classes of beings, who partake of them.
One should then keep in mind all Buddhas and worthy sages, thinking: "May they all know that we have performed this offering; may they all accept our such [offering]."
One should make offerings. Having performed these offerings, one may then eat. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Offer a single meal to all beings;
having made offerings to all Buddhas and the worthy sages, one may then eat. Question: Since it has already been given to the Triple Gem, why is it permissible to eat it oneself?
Answer: When one offers to all sentient beings together with making offerings to the Triple Gem, [it becomes permissible].
He then shares this food with all sentient beings together, for the eighty thousand families of worms within his own body are included among the number of sentient beings;
therefore, he may eat it himself to bring peace and happiness to those worms, not for his own sake.
△ Second, the contemplation of transforming the few into the many.
Furthermore, one visualizes a single bowl of food; each individual grain of rice, in turn, becomes a bowl of the finest delicacies.
Within all those bowls, each individual grain of rice again becomes a bowl of the finest delicacies. In this manner, it continues to expand.
Visualize that there arise bowls made of jewels, filling the worlds of the ten directions, all brimming with food and drink of the finest flavor.
Having formed this visualization, offer this imagined food to all sentient beings, enabling them to make offerings to the Triple Gem, the four types of birth, and so forth.
Having formed this visualization, you may then eat yourself, causing the various worms within your own body to be fully satiated.
The universal offering visualization is complete. △ Second, the visualization for eliminating craving.
When one wishes to eliminate craving for flavors, even if one obtains fine food, one should imagine it as various kinds of impure substances and eat them.
Furthermore, one should know that these fine or coarse foods are all created by the mind; they are empty appearances without reality. Why is this so?
"I have understood. Because I previously conceived the thought of impurity regarding the fine food in my bowl, when I looked at it, I saw only impurity;
since I did not see any purity at all, I know that the pure food of the original time was likewise so.
This is the work of the mind. This is the gate of contemplation."
△ Second, the Gate of Stopping (*śamatha*).

Regarding eating food through the gate of stopping: one should contemplate the flavor of the food being eaten, the person serving the food, the mouth that eats, the tongue that distinguishes flavors, and so forth.
Contemplating each of these individually, one realizes that they all arise from the mind; thus, they are merely manifestations of the mind. They exist [only as such].
It is thus non-existent. Its essence is the single mind alone, yet one must not grasp at the characteristics of this single mind. Why?

Because there is no phenomenon external to the mind that can grasp the characteristics of this mind. If there were a grasper and a grasped, these would be mere delusions, lacking inherent existence in themselves.
This is called the gate of cessation (*śamatha*).
This is applied to the gate of cessation according to the three natures, as can be understood from the text. Second, the explanation of cessation and contemplation during meals is complete.

△ Third, the explanation of cessation and contemplation during defecation and urination has two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the resolution of doubts. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the gate of contemplation.
II. The Section on Cessation (*śamatha*). First, regarding the initial [section]:
In all instances of defecating or urinating, there is likewise *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. As for what is called *vipaśyanā*, one should form this thought while at a place of impurity:
"All such impurities are created by the mind; they exist yet are not existent. I should now transform these impurities..."
Purify it so that it becomes clean. Then, visualize this impure place as a jeweled pond and jeweled channels, filled with pure scented water or overflowing with ghee and curd.
Visualize your own body as a body made of the seven precious jewels; thus, the excrement and urine you discard become fragrant milk, ghee, honey, and so forth.
Having formed this visualization, offer it to all sentient beings. Then, one further understands that this appearance of purity is merely...
This mind creates them; their empty appearances have no reality. This is called the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
All such impurities are created by the mind; their conceptualization is fundamentally empty. Existence is non-existence, for they lack intrinsic nature through dependence on others.
When transformed into purity, this is the contemplation of the pure conceptualized nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Pure appearances are merely mind. Purity...

This is the contemplation of the pure dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Its false appearances lack reality; this is the contemplation of the pure true nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). △ Second, the gate of cessation (*śamatha*).
As for what is called the gate of cessation: it is to know that these impure places, as well as the impure things discarded by the body, are merely...
This impure appearance that can be seen is manifested because past evil karma has perfumed the mind. However, this mental state exists yet is not existent;
it is solely the one mind, equal and without thought—this is what is called the gate of *śamatha*.

Through *vipaśyanā* (insight), one transforms the nature of defilement and turbidity into the nature of purity. Through *śamatha* (calm abiding), one merely eliminates the three natures of defilement and turbidity to enter the three non-natures.
Because evil karma perfumes the mind, impurity appears; yet this mental characteristic exists and yet is not existent.

By eliminating the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), one enters the *niṣparikalpita-svabhāva* (non-imagined nature). It is solely this single mind. By eliminating the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), one enters...
It is the nature of non-arising. It is equanimity and thoughtlessness. By removing the nature of reality (*tathatā*), one enters the nature of non-nature.
△ Second, resolving doubts, in two parts: first, directly resolving the doubt; second, applying the principle to all phenomena. Now, the first part.
Question: All pure and impure phenomena mentioned above, though produced by the mind, all arise from the perfuming of past karma.
How can they be transformed through present conceptualization and thus proceed from the mind? Answer:
The essence of the mind is fully endowed with the nature of all phenomena, yet it does not arise without conditions. Therefore, the impure appearances within a latrine arise due to past karma.
Manifesting, the jewel-pools of ghee and curd do not fail to appear for any lack of conditions.

If one can apply the mind with pure thoughts, this is the karma of the jewel-pools and ghee permeating the mind; thus, pure appearances arise. This includes the mind of revulsion and the mind of the contemplation of emptiness.
This is precisely the elimination of the conditions for impurity; because the mind is perfumed by purity, defiled appearances are extinguished accordingly.
This is because past karma was certainly able to perfume the mind and give rise to appearances, while present-life practice likewise perfumes the mind to manifest its sublime function.
The mind of pure contemplation (*śubha-saṃjñā*) points to the gate of *vipaśyanā* (insight). The mind of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā*) points to the gate of *śamatha* (calm abiding).

The mind of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) points to both gates simultaneously. This refers to the cessation and insight within true reality (*tathatā*), which is the so-called absence of reality in empty appearances and the state of equality free from conceptualization.
Part Two: Applying this analogy to all phenomena has three sections: First, the formal explanation establishing the skillful means; Second, the explanation of the view.
The reason for not seeing [them] is due to the three explanations regarding the distinctions of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). First:

just as one transforms the mind through mental cultivation (*parikalpa*) at the sites of excrement and urine, so too must one cultivate the mind through such mental cultivation regarding all other pure and impure objects, thereby altering their former characteristics; thus, they are eliminated in the present.
It removes hatred and attachment, and can also serve as a skillful means for attaining the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

However, for a beginner practitioner who has not yet attained the stage where phenomena follow the turning of the mind, one may only practice by closing the eyes and forming mental images. After a long time, through mastery and refinement, all phenomena will shift and transform in accordance with one's thoughts.
For this reason, even the great Bodhisattvas, the practitioners of the two vehicles, the lesser sages, and the seers possessing the five supernormal powers [rely upon this].
One is able to effect immediate transformation of phenomena: that which does not exist appears as existing.

By conceiving the impure as pure, one can eliminate aversion; by conceiving the pure as impure, one can eliminate attachment. When both aversion and attachment are entirely eliminated, one achieves the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
When skillful mental construction becomes fully matured and the mind turns in accordance with the dharma, one achieves the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and transcends the world.
What skillful means could surpass this? △ Second, explaining the reasons for seeing and not seeing.
Question: When the various sages manifest diverse transformations, why is it that sentient beings sometimes see them and sometimes do not?
Answer: One sees by means of shared consciousness (*sādhāraṇa-vijñāna*), and does not see by means of unshared consciousness (*asādhāraṇa-vijñāna*).
△ Third, the explanation of the distinctions among the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Question: What is the difference between the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of a Bodhisattva and those of the followers of the Two Vehicles?

Answer: The supernormal powers of the followers of the Two Vehicles are achieved solely through conceptual construction (*parikalpa*). Because they perceive phenomena as existing external to the mind, their powers are limited and finite.

The supernormal powers of a Bodhisattva arise from the knowledge that all phenomena are created by the mind alone; there are only mental appearances, and no phenomena exist external to the mind. Therefore, they are limitless.

It is immeasurable. Furthermore, when a bodhisattva first studies and attains mastery, they also practice by means of conceptualization; however, they immediately realize that all phenomena are produced by the single mind.

Those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) cultivate mastery solely through conceptualization; they speak only of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and not of the production by the mind.
According to the principles of the treatises, these are equally produced by the mind, but because those of the two vehicles do not know this, there is a distinction between them.
The bodhisattva’s cultivation of supernormal powers likewise proceeds from conceptualization; the meditative power of the two vehicles is also merely a product of the mind.

It is solely due to knowing or not knowing that their respective capacities become so vastly different. Thus, should those who cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā not first awaken to the single mind as the basis for their practice?
The essential heart of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is subtle and difficult to know; I now explain a small portion according to my ability.
May I dedicate this merit to all living beings, That they may together attain birth in peace and fulfillment on the path to enlightenment.
*The Essential Commentary on the Mahāyāna Śamatha-Vipaśyanā Dharma Gate*, Fascicle Four (End).
Epilogue to the *Essential Explanation of Mahāyāna Śamatha and Vipaśyanā*:

In the Way of the Great Learning of our Confucian tradition, nothing takes precedence over the extension of knowledge and the investigation of things. If the source of the mind-nature has not been thoroughly penetrated, [the goal cannot be achieved].
Where has one ever seen what is called "the investigation of things leading to the perfection of knowledge"?

When Master Ouyi was propagating the *Lotus Sūtra* at Pude Monastery, Chen Shu saw that his expositions—both horizontal and vertical—were direct, incisive, and penetrating. Consequently, Shu asked for instruction on the expedient means for entering the path.

The Master presented him with the four fascicles of the *Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā Dharmaparyāya* (The Mahāyāna Method of Calming and Contemplation) from Mount Nanyue and told Shu: "That which I take as my own standard is the [teaching of] Tian..."
This is the source from which the Tiantai school emerged. Its text is concise yet its meaning is profound; for a long time it has been locked away within the Tripitaka.

Previously, while lecturing, I once provided a summary of its essentials. Layman, why not devote yourself to its study? When I had the opportunity to read it at length, it was as if I had obtained a supreme treasure.
By taking the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as the objects of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one performs the work of investigating things to exhaustively attain knowledge. To fully comprehend [this]—

The absence of intrinsic nature in the three natures is the very effect of the principle that "things are investigated and knowledge reaches its consummation. Unable to bear the thought of private self-interest, I have therefore planned this carving [of the blocks].
Reflecting upon my own meager strength, I considered that solitary cultivation is not as good as sharing it with others, and sharing with a few is not as good as sharing it with the many.

Thus, I gathered various resources and together we have carved this into printing blocks. I have heard in private that even before Master Liu (Lianhua) left the household life, he had already exerted himself to master the teachings of the Chan school.
Now, opening my breast, I style myself the "Master of the Seat. This is because I take the teachings as the seal of the school; thus, I rely upon the teachings to manifest the school.
My wish for those who read this book is that they do not regard it as mere words and letters, yet they must not seek liberation apart from words and letters.
If one sees words and letters as being no different from non-words and non-letters, then one sees the lotus root.
One also sees Great Master Yi, one also sees Great Master Nanyue, one also sees Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and one also sees the fundamental mind-nature within ourselves.
Please allow me to borrow a verse by Zishao to serve as a witness and seal. The verse says:
Zi Shao: The Rectification of Things; Miaoxi: Things Rectified. To understand the "One Thread":
Two Fives make Ten.
Respectfully inscribed by the disciple Zhang Cangshu.
